  • Required for Ethernet and Wi-Fi frame delivery
  • Can often be spoofed in software

MAC addresses help switches decide where to forward frames.

docs.title: IP Addresses
docs.text:
An IP address is a Layer 3 logical address used for routing between networks.

Example IPv4 address:

192.168.1.50

Example IPv6 address:

2001:db8::10

IP addresses help routers move packets toward the destination network.

docs.title: Private IP Ranges
docs.text:
Private IP addresses are used inside internal networks and are not directly routable on the public internet.

Range Common Use 10.0.0.0/8 Large private networks 172.16.0.0/12 Medium private networks 192.168.0.0/16 Home and small office networks

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Ports identify specific services or processes on a host.

Port range:

0 - 65535

Common ports:

Service Port FTP TCP 21 SSH TCP 22 DNS TCP/UDP 53 HTTP TCP 80 HTTPS TCP 443 SMB TCP 445 RDP TCP 3389

Ports matter because one IP address can host many services.

Example:

192.168.1.10:22  -> SSH
192.168.1.10:80  -> HTTP
192.168.1.10:443 -> HTTPS

docs.title: TCP
docs.text:
TCP is a connection-oriented transport protocol.

TCP focuses on reliable delivery.

Characteristics:

  • Connection-based
  • Uses acknowledgements
  • Supports retransmission
  • Maintains order
  • Provides flow control
  • More reliable than UDP
  • Usually slower than UDP

Common TCP services:

Service Port SSH 22 HTTP 80 HTTPS 443 SMB 445

docs.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
docs.text:
TCP uses a three-way handshake to establish a connection.

Client -> SYN -> Server
Client <- SYN/ACK <- Server
Client -> ACK -> Server

After the handshake, data can be exchanged.

docs.title: Common TCP Flags
docs.text:
Flag Purpose SYN Start a connection ACK Acknowledge received data FIN Gracefully close a connection RST Abruptly reset a connection PSH Push data to the application quickly

Security relevance:

  • Nmap SYN scans rely on TCP handshake behavior.
  • Firewalls track TCP connection states.
  • RST responses often indicate closed ports.

docs.title: UDP
docs.text:
UDP is a connectionless transport protocol.

UDP focuses on speed and simplicity.

Characteristics:

  • No handshake
  • No delivery guarantee
  • No built-in retransmission
  • No connection state
  • Lower overhead than TCP

Common UDP uses:

Use Case Why UDP Fits DNS Small fast queries VoIP Real-time communication Streaming Speed matters more than perfect delivery Gaming Low latency is important

Security relevance:

  • UDP scanning is slower and harder to interpret.
  • Lack of response does not always mean a port is closed.
  • Some UDP services are abused for amplification attacks.

docs.title: Transmission Modes
docs.text:
Transmission modes describe how communication flows between devices.

Mode Description Example Simplex One-way only Keyboard to computer Half-duplex Two-way, one direction at a time Walkie-talkie Full-duplex Two-way at the same time Phone call

docs.title: Network Topologies
docs.text: A network topology describes how devices are arranged or how data flows.

docs.title: Physical Topology
docs.text: Physical topology describes the actual layout of cables, devices, and wireless links.

docs.title: Logical Topology
docs.text:
Logical topology describes how traffic moves, even if the physical layout looks different.

Common topologies:

Topology Description Notes Point-to-point Direct link between two devices Simple and dedicated Bus Devices share one medium Legacy and collision-prone Star Devices connect to a central device Common in modern LANs Ring Devices form a loop Used in some legacy/token systems Mesh Devices have multiple paths High redundancy Tree Hierarchical star-like design Common in larger networks Hybrid Combination of topologies Common in real environments

docs.title: Web Request Data Flow
docs.text:
When you visit a website, several networking steps happen behind the scenes.

Example:

https://example.com

docs.title: 1. Network Configuration
docs.text:
The device needs basic network settings:

  • IP address
  • Subnet mask
  • Default gateway
  • DNS server

These are often provided by DHCP.

docs.title: 2. DNS Resolution
docs.text:
The browser needs the IP address for the domain.

example.com -> 93.184.216.34

docs.title: 3. ARP for Local Delivery
docs.text:
If the destination is outside the local network, the device sends traffic to the default gateway.

To do that, it needs the gateway MAC address.

Gateway IP -> Gateway MAC address

ARP performs this local IP-to-MAC mapping.

docs.title: 4. TCP Connection
docs.text:
For HTTPS, the browser usually connects to TCP port 443.

Client ephemeral port -> Server TCP 443

docs.title: 5. TLS and HTTP
docs.text: For HTTPS, TLS protects the communication. Then the browser sends the HTTP request through the encrypted connection.

docs.title: 6. Routing and NAT
docs.text: The packet travels through the router, ISP, and internet. If NAT is used, the router translates the private source IP to a public IP.

docs.title: 7. Response and Decapsulation
docs.text: The server responds, and each layer processes the headers until the browser receives the web content.

docs.title: View IP Configuration
docs.text:
# Linux
ip addr show

# Windows
ipconfig /all

# macOS/Linux legacy
ifconfig

docs.title: View MAC Addresses
docs.text:
# Linux
ip link show

# Windows
getmac /v

# macOS/Linux
ifconfig

docs.title: View Routing Table
docs.text:
# Linux/macOS
netstat -rn

# Linux modern
ip route

# Windows
route print

docs.title: View Active Connections
docs.text:
# Windows
netstat -ano

# Linux
ss -tulpn

docs.title: Test Connectivity
docs.text: ping 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Trace Route
docs.text:
# Linux/macOS
traceroute 8.8.8.8

# Windows
tracert 8.8.8.8

docs.title: View ARP Table
docs.text: arp -a

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Concept Layer Purpose Cable / Wi-Fi signal Layer 1 Moves bits MAC address Layer 2 Local delivery Frame Layer 2 Data link container IP address Layer 3 Routing between networks Packet Layer 3 Network layer container TCP/UDP port Layer 4 Service/process targeting TCP Layer 4 Reliable transport UDP Layer 4 Fast connectionless transport HTTP/DNS/SMTP Layer 7 Application protocols

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• A frame is used for local network delivery.
  • A packet is routed across networks.
  • MAC addresses work at Layer 2.
  • IP addresses work at Layer 3.
  • Ports work at Layer 4.
  • TCP is reliable and connection-oriented.
  • UDP is faster but does not guarantee delivery.
  • Routers forward packets between networks.
  • Switches forward frames inside a LAN.
  • DNS turns names into IP addresses.
  • ARP turns local IP addresses into MAC addresses.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
Network protocols are standardized rules that allow devices, services, and applications to communicate. They define how data is addressed, transmitted, routed, encrypted, requested, and interpreted.

This page covers common protocols and terminology used in networking, system administration, web security, and cybersecurity labs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A protocol answers questions like:

  • How should two systems start communication?
  • What port should a service listen on?
  • How should data be formatted?
  • How should errors be reported?
  • How should names resolve to IP addresses?
  • How should devices receive network configuration?

Common protocol categories:

Category Examples Transport TCP, UDP Diagnostic ICMP Addressing / Configuration DHCP, ARP, NAT Name Resolution DNS Web HTTP, HTTPS Remote Access SSH, RDP, VPN File Sharing FTP, SMB, NFS Routing / Switching OSPF, BGP, RIP, STP, VLAN

docs.title: TCP
docs.text:
Transmission Control Protocol, or TCP, is a connection-oriented transport protocol.

TCP is used when reliability matters.

Common TCP use cases:

  • Web browsing
  • SSH
  • File transfers
  • Email
  • Remote desktop
  • SMB file sharing

docs.title: TCP Characteristics
docs.text: Characteristic Description Connection-oriented Establishes a session before sending data Reliable Uses acknowledgements and retransmission Ordered Reassembles data in the correct order Stateful Tracks connection state Higher overhead More control traffic than UDP

docs.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
docs.text:
Before data is exchanged, TCP establishes a connection.

Client -> SYN -> Server
Client <- SYN/ACK <- Server
Client -> ACK -> Server

Common TCP flags:

Flag Purpose SYN Starts a connection ACK Acknowledges received data FIN Gracefully closes a connection RST Resets or abruptly terminates a connection PSH Pushes data to the application quickly

Security relevance:

  • Port scanners use TCP behavior to infer open, closed, and filtered ports.
  • Firewalls often track TCP connection states.
  • Unexpected RST packets can indicate closed ports, filtering, or connection resets.

docs.title: UDP
docs.text:
User Datagram Protocol, or UDP, is a connectionless transport protocol.

UDP is used when speed matters more than guaranteed delivery.

Common UDP use cases:

  • DNS
  • VoIP
  • Video streaming
  • Online gaming
  • Some VPN traffic
  • Service discovery

docs.title: UDP Characteristics
docs.text:
Characteristic Description Connectionless No handshake before sending data Fast Lower overhead than TCP Stateless Does not track sessions by default No delivery guarantee Packets may be lost No ordering guarantee Packets may arrive out of order

Security relevance:

  • UDP scans are harder to interpret than TCP scans.
  • No response does not always mean a UDP port is closed.
  • Some UDP services can be abused for amplification attacks.

docs.title: ICMP
docs.text:
Internet Control Message Protocol, or ICMP, is used for network diagnostics and error reporting.

ICMP does not usually carry application data. Instead, it reports network conditions.

Common ICMP uses:

  • Testing reachability
  • Measuring round-trip time
  • Reporting unreachable destinations
  • Tracing network paths

docs.title: Ping
docs.text:
ping uses ICMP Echo Request and Echo Reply messages.

ping 8.8.8.8

Useful for checking:

  • Whether a host is reachable
  • Round-trip time
  • Packet loss
  • Basic network connectivity

Note

A host can be online even if it does not respond to ping. Firewalls often block ICMP.

docs.title: Traceroute
docs.text:
Traceroute maps the path packets take through routers.

# Linux/macOS
traceroute 8.8.8.8

# Windows
tracert 8.8.8.8

Traceroute uses the TTL field. Each router decreases TTL by 1. When TTL reaches 0, the router drops the packet and sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message.

docs.title: Common ICMP Concepts
docs.text: Concept Purpose Echo Request Sent by ping client Echo Reply Sent by responding host Time Exceeded Used by traceroute Destination Unreachable Reports unreachable host, network, or port TTL Prevents packets from looping forever

docs.title: ARP
docs.text:
Address Resolution Protocol, or ARP, maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on a local network.

A device may know the destination IP address, but Ethernet and Wi-Fi still need a destination MAC address for local delivery.

Example:

192.168.1.1 -> aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff

docs.title: How ARP Works
docs.text:
Host: Who has 192.168.1.1?
Router: 192.168.1.1 is at aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff

View the ARP table:

arp -a

Security relevance:

  • ARP is local-network only.
  • ARP has no built-in authentication.
  • ARP spoofing can be used in man-in-the-middle attacks.

docs.title: DHCP
docs.text:
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, or DHCP, automatically assigns network configuration to devices.

DHCP commonly provides:

  • IP address
  • Subnet mask
  • Default gateway
  • DNS server
  • Lease duration

Without DHCP, administrators would need to configure IP settings manually.

docs.title: DHCP DORA Process
docs.text:
DHCP uses a four-step process often called DORA.

Step Message Description 1 Discover Client broadcasts to find DHCP servers 2 Offer DHCP server offers an available IP configuration 3 Request Client requests the offered IP address 4 Acknowledge Server confirms the lease 
Client -> DHCP Discover -> Broadcast
Server -> DHCP Offer
Client -> DHCP Request
Server -> DHCP ACK

DHCP uses UDP:

Role Port DHCP Server UDP 67 DHCP Client UDP 68

docs.title: DHCP Commands
docs.text:
# Windows: release and renew DHCP lease
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew

# Linux: release and request new lease
sudo dhclient -r
sudo dhclient

Capture DHCP traffic:

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 67 or port 68 -vv

Security relevance:

  • Rogue DHCP servers can provide malicious gateways or DNS servers.
  • DHCP starvation can exhaust the address pool.
  • DHCP logs can help identify devices joining a network.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Domain Name System, or DNS, translates human-readable names into IP addresses.

Example:

example.com -> 93.184.216.34

DNS is important because users remember names more easily than IP addresses.

docs.title: DNS Hierarchy
docs.text:
DNS is hierarchical.

www.example.com
│   │       │
│   │       └── Top-level domain: .com
│   └────────── Second-level domain: example
└────────────── Hostname/subdomain: www

Main levels:

Level Example Description Root . Top of the DNS hierarchy TLD .com Top-level domain Second-level domain example Registered domain name Subdomain / host www Specific host or service

docs.title: DNS Record Types
docs.text:
DNS can store different types of records.

Record Purpose A Maps a name to an IPv4 address AAAA Maps a name to an IPv6 address CNAME Creates an alias to another name MX Defines mail servers for a domain TXT Stores text values, often for verification or email security NS Identifies authoritative name servers PTR Reverse DNS lookup from IP to name

Examples:

# Basic DNS lookup
nslookup example.com

# Query A records
dig example.com A

# Query MX records
dig example.com MX

# Query TXT records
dig example.com TXT

docs.title: DNS Resolution Process
docs.text:
When a client needs to resolve a domain, it usually follows this process:

  1. Check local cache.
  2. Ask the configured recursive resolver.
  3. Resolver asks root servers.
  4. Root servers point to the correct TLD servers.
  5. TLD servers point to the authoritative name server.
  6. Authoritative server returns the requested record.
  7. Resolver caches the answer and returns it to the client.
Client
  -> Recursive Resolver
    -> Root Server
      -> TLD Server
        -> Authoritative Name Server

docs.title: DNS Caching and TTL
docs.text:
DNS records include a TTL, or Time To Live.

TTL controls how long a resolver or client can cache the answer.

Higher TTL = fewer lookups, slower changes
Lower TTL  = more lookups, faster changes

Security relevance:

  • DNS poisoning can redirect users to malicious destinations.
  • DNS logs are useful for threat hunting.
  • Unusual DNS queries can indicate malware or data exfiltration.

docs.title: HTTP and HTTPS
docs.text:
Hypertext Transfer Protocol, or HTTP, is used for web communication.

HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS encryption.

Protocol Default Port Security HTTP TCP 80 Unencrypted HTTPS TCP 443 Encrypted with TLS

HTTP is request-response based.

Client -> HTTP Request -> Server
Client <- HTTP Response <- Server

docs.title: HTTP Request Example
docs.text:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Accept: */*

docs.title: HTTP Response Example
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1256

docs.title: Common HTTP Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose GET Retrieve data POST Submit or create data PUT Update data PATCH Partially update data DELETE Delete data HEAD Retrieve headers only OPTIONS Show supported methods

docs.title: Common HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 200 OK 201 Created 301 Moved Permanently 302 Found / temporary redirect 400 Bad Request 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden 404 Not Found 405 Method Not Allowed 500 Internal Server Error 503 Service Unavailable

Note

HTTP is covered here as a networking protocol. Deeper web request analysis belongs in the web fundamentals section.

docs.title: NAT
docs.text:
Network Address Translation, or NAT, maps private internal addresses to public addresses.

NAT is commonly used because IPv4 addresses are limited.

Example:

Internal host: 192.168.1.25
Router public IP: 203.0.113.10

When the internal host accesses the internet, the router replaces the private source IP with the public IP and tracks the connection in a NAT table.

docs.title: Private IP Ranges
docs.text: Range Common Use 10.0.0.0/8 Large private networks 172.16.0.0/12 Medium private networks 192.168.0.0/16 Home and small office networks

docs.title: PAT / NAT Overload
docs.text:
Port Address Translation, or PAT, allows many private hosts to share one public IP by tracking unique source ports.

192.168.1.10:51514 -> 203.0.113.10:40001
192.168.1.11:51515 -> 203.0.113.10:40002

Security relevance:

  • NAT hides internal addressing from the public internet.
  • NAT is not a full security control.
  • Port forwarding exposes internal services externally.
  • Some protocols can break or require special handling through NAT.

docs.title: Routing Protocols
docs.text:
Routing protocols help routers decide where to forward packets.

Protocol Type Common Use OSPF Link-state Internal enterprise routing RIP Distance-vector Small or legacy networks EIGRP Advanced distance-vector Cisco environments BGP Path-vector Internet routing between organizations

docs.title: OSPF
docs.text:
Open Shortest Path First shares network topology information and calculates efficient paths.

Common use:

Internal enterprise networks

docs.title: RIP
docs.text:
Routing Information Protocol uses hop count to choose routes.

Limitations:

  • Simple
  • Older
  • Less scalable
  • Not ideal for large networks

docs.title: BGP
docs.text:
Border Gateway Protocol is the core routing protocol of the internet.

Common use:

ISP routing
Cloud provider routing
Large organization internet edge

Security relevance:

  • Route leaks can cause outages.
  • BGP hijacking can redirect traffic.
  • Internal routing visibility helps with network defense and troubleshooting.

docs.title: VLANs
docs.text:
A Virtual Local Area Network, or VLAN, logically separates a network at Layer 2.

VLANs allow multiple isolated broadcast domains to exist on the same physical switching infrastructure.

Example:

VLAN Purpose VLAN 10 Users VLAN 20 Servers VLAN 30 Guest Wi-Fi VLAN 40 Management

Benefits:

  • Segmentation
  • Reduced broadcast noise
  • Better organization
  • Security boundaries between groups

docs.title: Trunking
docs.text:
A trunk link carries traffic for multiple VLANs between switches.

The common trunking standard is IEEE 802.1Q.

Security relevance:

  • Misconfigured trunks can expose VLANs.
  • Native VLAN misuse can create risk.
  • Dynamic trunking should be disabled on user-facing ports.

docs.title: STP
docs.text:
Spanning Tree Protocol, or STP, prevents Layer 2 loops.

Layer 2 loops can cause broadcast storms and network instability.

STP works by blocking redundant paths while keeping backup paths available.

Security relevance:

  • STP manipulation can affect traffic flow.
  • Rogue switches can disrupt LAN stability.
  • BPDU Guard is often used to protect access ports.

docs.title: VPN
docs.text:
A Virtual Private Network creates an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network.

Common VPN types:

Type Purpose Remote access VPN Connects a user to a private network Site-to-site VPN Connects two networks Full tunnel Routes all traffic through the VPN Split tunnel Routes only selected traffic through the VPN

docs.title: IPsec
docs.text:
IPsec secures IP traffic at Layer 3.

Important components:

Component Purpose AH Authentication and integrity ESP Encryption and optional authentication IKE Key exchange and negotiation NAT-T Helps IPsec work through NAT

Common IPsec firewall requirements:

Component Port / Protocol IKE UDP 500 NAT-T UDP 4500 ESP IP protocol 50 AH IP protocol 51

Security relevance:

  • VPNs protect traffic over untrusted networks.
  • Weak VPN protocols should be avoided.
  • Split tunneling affects monitoring and traffic visibility.

docs.title: Wireless Protocols
docs.text:
Wireless networks use radio frequencies instead of cables.

Common Wi-Fi bands:

Band Characteristics 2.4 GHz Longer range, better wall penetration, more interference 5 GHz Faster, shorter range, less congestion 6 GHz Newer, high performance, shorter range

docs.title: Wi-Fi Security
docs.text:
Protocol Status WEP Broken / insecure WPA Legacy WPA2 Common modern baseline WPA3 Stronger modern option

Security relevance:

  • WEP should not be used.
  • Hidden SSIDs are not real security.
  • Weak Wi-Fi passwords can be attacked.
  • Enterprise Wi-Fi often uses EAP-based authentication.

docs.title: Common Ports
docs.text: Protocol / Service Port FTP TCP 21 SSH TCP 22 Telnet TCP 23 SMTP TCP 25 DNS TCP/UDP 53 DHCP Server UDP 67 DHCP Client UDP 68 HTTP TCP 80 NTP UDP 123 SNMP UDP 161/162 HTTPS TCP 443 SMB TCP 445 RDP TCP 3389

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Protocol Main Purpose TCP Reliable transport UDP Fast connectionless transport ICMP Diagnostics and error reporting ARP IPv4-to-MAC resolution on local networks DHCP Automatic network configuration DNS Name resolution HTTP Web communication HTTPS Encrypted web communication NAT Address translation OSPF Internal routing BGP Internet routing VLAN Logical Layer 2 segmentation STP Loop prevention VPN Encrypted tunneling

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• TCP is reliable and connection-oriented.
  • UDP is fast and connectionless.
  • ICMP is used for diagnostics, not normal application data.
  • ARP resolves local IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses.
  • DHCP automatically assigns IP configuration.
  • DNS translates names to IP addresses.
  • HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS.
  • NAT maps private addresses to public addresses.
  • VLANs segment networks logically.
  • VPNs create encrypted tunnels across untrusted networks.

docs.title: Subnetting
docs.text:
Subnetting is the process of dividing a larger IP network into smaller subnetworks.

It is used to organize networks, control traffic, improve address management, and separate systems by purpose, department, location, or security zone.

docs.title: Why Subnetting Matters
docs.text:
Without subnetting, every device could end up in one large flat network.

That can create problems:

  • Too much broadcast traffic
  • Poor organization
  • Harder troubleshooting
  • Weak separation between departments
  • Inefficient IP address usage
  • Larger impact if one segment is compromised

Subnetting helps create smaller, more manageable network segments.

Examples:

Accounting subnet
HR subnet
Server subnet
Guest Wi-Fi subnet
Security camera subnet
Management subnet

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Every IPv4 subnet has important address types.

Address Type Purpose Example Network address Identifies the subnet itself 192.168.1.0 Usable host addresses Assigned to devices 192.168.1.10 Default gateway Routes traffic to other networks 192.168.1.1 Broadcast address Sends traffic to all hosts in the subnet 192.168.1.255

Example subnet:

Network:        192.168.1.0/24
Usable hosts:   192.168.1.1 - 192.168.1.254
Broadcast:      192.168.1.255

docs.title: Subnet Mask
docs.text:
A subnet mask defines which part of an IP address is the network portion and which part is the host portion.

Example:

IP address:     192.168.1.25
Subnet mask:    255.255.255.0
CIDR:           /24

In this example:

Network portion: 192.168.1
Host portion:    25

So 192.168.1.25/24 belongs to the network:

192.168.1.0/24

docs.title: CIDR Notation
docs.text:
CIDR notation shows how many bits are used for the network portion.

192.168.1.0/24

The /24 means the first 24 bits are the network portion.

Common CIDR examples:

CIDR Subnet Mask Usable Hosts /24 255.255.255.0 254 /25 255.255.255.128 126 /26 255.255.255.192 62 /27 255.255.255.224 30 /28 255.255.255.240 14 /29 255.255.255.248 6 /30 255.255.255.252 2

Note

The number of usable hosts is usually total addresses minus 2: one for the network address and one for the broadcast address.

docs.title: Host Calculation
docs.text:
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.

Formula:

Total addresses = 2^(host bits)
Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2

Example:

/24 means 24 network bits
32 - 24 = 8 host bits
2^8 = 256 total addresses
256 - 2 = 254 usable hosts

docs.title: Example: /24 Network
docs.text:
Network:        192.168.10.0/24
Subnet mask:    255.255.255.0
Broadcast:      192.168.10.255
Usable range:   192.168.10.1 - 192.168.10.254

This is common in home and small office networks.

docs.title: Example: /26 Network
docs.text:
A /26 subnet has 64 total addresses and 62 usable hosts.

Network:        192.168.10.0/26
Subnet mask:    255.255.255.192
Broadcast:      192.168.10.63
Usable range:   192.168.10.1 - 192.168.10.62

The next /26 subnet starts at:

192.168.10.64/26

docs.title: Subnet Increments
docs.text:
The subnet increment tells you where each subnet starts.

For a /26:

Subnet mask: 255.255.255.192
Block size:  256 - 192 = 64

So the subnets are:

192.168.10.0/26
192.168.10.64/26
192.168.10.128/26
192.168.10.192/26

docs.title: Common Subnet Sizes
docs.text: CIDR Total Addresses Usable Hosts Common Use /24 256 254 Small LAN /25 128 126 Split a /24 in half /26 64 62 Department subnet /27 32 30 Small team or lab segment /28 16 14 Small service segment /29 8 6 Network devices /30 4 2 Point-to-point links

docs.title: Default Gateway
docs.text:
The default gateway is the router interface used to reach other networks.

Example:

Host IP:         192.168.1.50
Subnet mask:     255.255.255.0
Default gateway: 192.168.1.1

If the host needs to reach another subnet or the internet, it sends traffic to the default gateway.

Host -> Default Gateway -> Other Network

docs.title: Security Benefits
docs.text:
Subnetting can improve security by separating systems.

Example:

Subnet Purpose 192.168.10.0/24 User devices 192.168.20.0/24 Servers 192.168.30.0/24 Guest Wi-Fi 192.168.40.0/24 Cameras / IoT 192.168.50.0/24 Management

Benefits:

  • Guest devices can be isolated from internal systems.
  • Servers can be protected with firewall rules.
  • IoT devices can be restricted.
  • Sensitive systems can be placed in controlled segments.
  • Monitoring can be organized by subnet.

Important

Subnetting alone does not enforce security. You need routing rules, firewall rules, ACLs, VLANs, or other controls to restrict traffic between subnets.

docs.title: Subnetting and VLANs
docs.text:
Subnets and VLANs are often used together.

Concept Layer Purpose VLAN Layer 2 Separates broadcast domains Subnet Layer 3 Defines IP network boundaries

Common design:

VLAN 10 -> 192.168.10.0/24 -> Users
VLAN 20 -> 192.168.20.0/24 -> Servers
VLAN 30 -> 192.168.30.0/24 -> Guest Wi-Fi

Traffic between VLANs usually requires routing.

docs.title: Quick Method
docs.text:
When subnetting, ask:

  1. What network am I starting with?
  2. How many subnets do I need?
  3. How many hosts are needed per subnet?
  4. What CIDR size supports that number of hosts?
  5. What are the network, usable, and broadcast addresses?

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Need Suggested CIDR Around 250 hosts /24 Around 125 hosts /25 Around 60 hosts /26 Around 30 hosts /27 Around 14 hosts /28 Around 6 hosts /29 2 hosts /30

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Subnetting divides larger networks into smaller networks.
  • The subnet mask separates the network portion from the host portion.
  • CIDR notation shows how many bits belong to the network.
  • The network address identifies the subnet.
  • The broadcast address reaches all hosts in the subnet.
  • The default gateway routes traffic to other networks.
  • Smaller subnets reduce broadcast scope and improve organization.
  • Subnetting helps security, but firewall rules enforce security.

docs.title: Operating Systems
docs.text: Operating systems are the base layer that users, services, and security tools interact with. This section covers Linux and Windows fundamentals from an administration and cybersecurity perspective.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Linux — Filesystem structure, permissions, processes, services, scripting, and system management.
  • Windows — Command line usage, PowerShell, services, processes, WMI, and Windows administration basics.

docs.title: Bash Scripting
docs.text:
Bash scripting is used to automate Linux command-line tasks. A script can take user input, store values in variables, make decisions, repeat actions with loops, and save output for later analysis.

For cybersecurity work, Bash is useful for tasks such as host discovery, log parsing, file checks, simple reconnaissance, backups, and tool automation.

docs.title: Script Structure
docs.text:
A Bash script usually begins with a shebang, which tells Linux what interpreter should run the file.

#!/bin/bash

Common interpreter examples:

Shebang Meaning #!/bin/bash Run the script with Bash #!/usr/bin/env python3 Run the script with Python 3

After creating a script, make it executable:

chmod +x script.sh

Then run it:

./script.sh

docs.title: Arguments and Special Variables
docs.text:
Arguments are values passed to a script from the command line.

./scan.sh example.com

In this example, example.com becomes $1.

Variable Meaning $0 Script name $1, $2, $3 Positional arguments ${10} Tenth argument and above $# Number of arguments $@ All arguments $? Exit status of the last command $$ Process ID of the current script

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Script name: $0"
echo "First argument: $1"
echo "Number of arguments: $#"

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variables store values for reuse.

Assignment uses no spaces around =.

target="10.10.10.1"
echo "Scanning $target..."

Incorrect:

target = "10.10.10.1"

Bash will treat target as a command and fail.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays store multiple values in one variable.

domains=(www.example.com ftp.example.com mail.example.com)

echo ${domains[0]}
echo ${domains[@]}

Array indexes start at 0.

If an array item contains spaces, quote it:

files=("Config File.txt" "Log Data.log")

docs.title: Conditional Logic
docs.text:
Conditional logic lets a script make decisions.

Basic structure:

if [ condition ]
then
    command
elif [ another_condition ]
then
    command
else
    command
fi

Example: validating that the user provided one argument.

#!/bin/bash

if [ $# -eq 0 ]
then
    echo "Error: You must specify a target domain."
    echo "Usage: $0 <domain>"
    exit 1
elif [ $# -eq 1 ]
then
    domain=$1
    echo "Processing domain: $domain"
else
    echo "Error: Too many arguments."
    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Comparison Operators
docs.text: Bash uses different operators depending on whether you are comparing strings, numbers, or files.

docs.title: Integer Operators
docs.text: Operator Meaning Example -eq Equal to [ "$count" -eq 1 ] -ne Not equal to [ "$count" -ne 0 ] -lt Less than [ "$count" -lt 5 ] -gt Greater than [ "$count" -gt 5 ] -ge Greater than or equal to [ "$count" -ge 10 ]

docs.title: File Operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning -e Path exists -f Is a regular file -d Is a directory -r Is readable -w Is writable -x Is executable -s File exists and is not empty

Example:

#!/bin/bash

if [[ -e "$1" && -r "$1" ]]
then
    echo "Access granted: Reading $1..."
    cat "$1"
elif [[ -e "$1" && ! -r "$1" ]]
then
    echo "Permission error: You do not have read rights for $1."
    exit 1
else
    echo "Error: File not found."
    exit 2
fi

docs.title: Logical Operators
docs.text:
Use double brackets [[ ... ]] when combining conditions.

Operator Meaning && Logical AND || Logical OR ! Logical NOT

Example:

if [[ -e "$file" && -r "$file" ]]
then
    cat "$file"
fi

docs.title: Arithmetic Operations
docs.text:
Bash supports integer arithmetic by default.

Operator Meaning + Addition - Subtraction * Multiplication / Division % Modulus ++ Increment -- Decrement

Use arithmetic expansion when you want to print or use the result:

echo "Total: $((10 + 5))"

Use arithmetic evaluation when updating a variable:

counter=0
((counter++))
echo "$counter"

Bash does not handle decimal math by default. Use tools such as bc for floating-point calculations.

docs.title: String Length
docs.text:
Use ${#variable} to count the number of characters in a variable.

platform="HackTheBox"
echo "Length: ${#platform}"

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Functions make scripts easier to organize and reuse.

A function must be defined before it is called.

function greet {
    echo "Hello, $1!"
}

greet "John"

Alternative syntax:

greet() {
    echo "Hello, $1!"
}

Inside a function, $1, $2, and other positional parameters refer to the function arguments, not the script arguments.

docs.title: Variable Scope in Functions
docs.text:
By default, Bash variables are global.

Use local to limit a variable to a function.

calculate() {
    local result=50
    echo "$result"
}

This helps prevent accidental overwrites in larger scripts.

docs.title: Function Return Values
docs.text:
Bash functions return exit status codes, not normal data values.

Return Code Meaning 0 Success Non-zero Error or failure

Example:

check_file() {
    if [[ -f "$1" ]]
    then
        return 0
    else
        return 1
    fi
}

To return actual text or data, print it with echo and capture it with command substitution:

get_date() {
    date +%F
}

today=$(get_date)
echo "Today is $today"

docs.title: Input with read
docs.text:
The read command lets a script accept user input.

read -p "Enter target: " target
echo "Target selected: $target"

The -p option displays a prompt before waiting for input.

docs.title: Case Statements
docs.text:
A case statement is useful for menus and handling multiple fixed options.

read -p "Select your option: " opt

case $opt in
    "1")
        echo "Running scan..."
        ;;
    "2")
        echo "Running exploit..."
        ;;
    *)
        echo "Invalid option."
        exit 1
        ;;
esac

Important syntax:

Syntax Meaning case $var in Starts the case block pattern) Matches a value ;; Ends a branch *) Default catch-all branch esac Ends the case block

docs.title: Loops
docs.text: Loops repeat a block of code.

docs.title: For Loops
docs.text:
Use a for loop when you already have a known list.

for ip in 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.2 10.10.10.3
do
    ping -c 1 "$ip"
done

One-line version:

for ip in 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.2; do ping -c 1 "$ip"; done

docs.title: While Loops
docs.text:
A while loop runs while a condition is true.

counter=1

while [ $counter -le 5 ]
do
    echo "Counter: $counter"
    ((counter++))
done

docs.title: Until Loops
docs.text:
An until loop runs while a condition is false.

counter=0

until [ $counter -eq 10 ]
do
    ((counter++))
    echo "Counter is now: $counter"
done

docs.title: Loop Control
docs.text: Command Meaning break Exit the loop immediately continue Skip the current iteration and move to the next one

docs.title: Output Control with tee
docs.text:
Redirection saves output to a file but hides it from the terminal.

command > output.txt

The tee command displays output on the screen and saves it to a file at the same time.

command | tee output.txt

Append instead of overwrite:

command | tee -a output.txt

Comparison:

Method Syntax Visible in Terminal Saved to File Standard output command Yes No Redirection command > file No Yes Tee command \| tee file Yes Yes

Example:

hosts=$(host "$domain" | grep "has address" | cut -d " " -f4 | tee discovered_hosts.txt)

This prints discovered hosts to the terminal and saves them to discovered_hosts.txt.

docs.title: Practical Script Example
docs.text:
This example combines arguments, validation, functions, loops, and output logging.

#!/bin/bash

if [ $# -ne 1 ]
then
    echo "Usage: $0 <domain>"
    exit 1
fi

domain=$1
output_file="discovered_hosts.txt"

find_hosts() {
    host "$domain" | grep "has address" | cut -d " " -f4 | tee "$output_file"
}

ping_hosts() {
    while read -r ip
    do
        if ping -c 1 "$ip" > /dev/null 2>&1
        then
            echo "$ip is up"
        else
            echo "$ip is down"
        fi
    done < "$output_file"
}

find_hosts
ping_hosts

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Concept Syntax / Command Shebang #!/bin/bash First argument $1 Argument count $# All arguments $@ Last exit status $? Variable assignment name="value" Array items=(one two three) If statement if [ condition ]; then ... fi Case statement case $var in ... esac For loop for item in list; do ... done While loop while [ condition ]; do ... done Function name() { commands; } Arithmetic $((x + y)) Save and display output command \| tee file.txt

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Linux is built around a simple but powerful idea: everything is organized through a single filesystem tree, and most system interaction happens through files, processes, users, permissions, and the command line. Understanding the Linux structure and workflow is essential for administration, troubleshooting, and cybersecurity work because it explains where important files live, how commands are executed, how users interact with the system, and how permissions protect sensitive resources.

docs.title: Linux Filesystem Hierarchy
docs.text:
Unlike Windows, which uses drive letters such as C:\ and D:\, Linux uses a single root directory represented by /.

Everything on the system exists somewhere under /, including files, folders, devices, mounted drives, logs, and configuration files.

Common directories include:

Directory Purpose / Root of the entire filesystem /home User home directories /root Home directory for the root user /etc System-wide configuration files /bin Essential user commands /sbin Essential system administration commands /usr User applications, libraries, and shared files /var Variable data such as logs, caches, mail, and web content /tmp Temporary files /opt Optional third-party software /dev Device files /proc Virtual filesystem exposing process and kernel information /mnt Temporary mount points /media Auto-mounted removable media

docs.title: Important System Paths
docs.text:
Some directories are especially important during administration and security work.

Path Why It Matters /etc/passwd Lists local user accounts /etc/shadow Stores password hashes; readable only by root /etc/group Lists local groups /var/log/auth.log Authentication and sudo activity on Debian/Ubuntu /var/log/syslog General system logs /var/www/html Common Apache web root /home/<user> User files, SSH keys, shell history, and personal configs /tmp World-writable temporary directory often abused by attackers /proc/<pid> Runtime information about a specific process

docs.title: Users, Root, and Privileges
docs.text:
Linux separates normal users from the administrator account.

The administrator account is called root and has full control over the system.

Normal users usually have limited access and cannot modify critical system files unless they are granted elevated permissions.

The most common way to run administrative commands is with sudo.

sudo apt update

The sudo command allows a permitted user to run a command with elevated privileges without logging in directly as root.

You can check your current identity with:

whoami
id

The id command shows your user ID, group ID, and group memberships.

docs.title: File Ownership and Permissions
docs.text:
Linux permissions control who can read, write, or execute files.

Every file has:

  • An owner
  • A group
  • Permissions for the owner, group, and others

You can view permissions with:

ls -la

Example output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 user user 1200 Jan 10 12:00 notes.txt

The permission section breaks down like this:

Symbol Meaning r Read w Write x Execute - Permission not granted

For example:

-rwxr-xr--

Means:

Entity Permissions Owner Read, write, execute Group Read, execute Others Read only

docs.title: Changing Permissions
docs.text:
The chmod command changes file permissions.

chmod +x script.sh

This makes a script executable.

Numeric permissions are also common:

chmod 644 file.txt
chmod 755 script.sh

Common permission values:

Value Meaning 600 Owner can read/write; no access for others 644 Owner can read/write; others can read 700 Owner has full access; no access for others 755 Owner has full access; others can read/execute 777 Everyone has full access; dangerous

[!WARNING] Avoid using chmod 777 unless you fully understand the risk. It gives every user full control over the file or directory.

docs.title: Changing Ownership
docs.text:
The chown command changes the owner of a file or directory.

sudo chown user:user file.txt

To change ownership recursively:

sudo chown -R user:user /path/to/folder

This is useful when fixing broken permissions or assigning files to the correct service account.

docs.title: Working with Files and Directories
docs.text:
Basic navigation and file management are part of everyday Linux workflow.

Command Purpose pwd Show current directory ls List files ls -la List all files with details cd Change directory mkdir Create directory touch Create empty file cp Copy files mv Move or rename files rm Delete files cat Print file contents less Read long files page by page head Show first lines of a file tail Show last lines of a file

Examples:

pwd
ls -la
cd /var/log
cat auth.log
tail -f /var/log/syslog

The tail -f command is especially useful for watching logs in real time.

docs.title: Searching the Filesystem
docs.text:
Linux provides several tools for finding files and searching content.

Command Purpose find Search for files by name, type, size, permissions, etc. locate Fast filename search using an indexed database grep Search text inside files which Show the path of a command whereis Locate binary, source, and manual files

Examples:

find / -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null
find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null
grep -Ri "password" /var/www 2>/dev/null
which bash

The 2>/dev/null part hides permission errors, which keeps output cleaner.

docs.title: Processes and Jobs
docs.text:
A process is a running program. Every process has a unique Process ID, called a PID.

Useful commands include:

Command Purpose ps aux Show running processes top Live process viewer htop Improved interactive process viewer kill Send a signal to a process jobs Show background jobs in the current shell fg Bring a job to the foreground bg Resume a job in the background

Examples:

ps aux
top
kill 1234

To run a command in the background, add &:

ping 8.8.8.8 &

To stop a foreground process, press:

CTRL + C

To suspend it, press:

CTRL + Z

docs.title: Services and Systemd
docs.text:
Modern Linux systems commonly use systemd to manage services.

A service is a background process, often called a daemon, that provides functionality such as SSH, web hosting, logging, or networking.

The main tool for managing services is systemctl.

Command Purpose systemctl status <service> Check service status sudo systemctl start <service> Start a service sudo systemctl stop <service> Stop a service sudo systemctl restart <service> Restart a service sudo systemctl enable <service> Start service automatically at boot sudo systemctl disable <service> Prevent service from starting at boot

Examples:

systemctl status ssh
sudo systemctl restart apache2
sudo systemctl enable ssh

To view service logs:

journalctl -u ssh --no-pager

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Environment variables store values used by the shell and programs.

Common variables include:

Variable Purpose $HOME Current user's home directory $USER Current username $PATH Directories searched for executable commands $SHELL Current shell $PWD Current working directory

Examples:

echo $HOME
echo $PATH
echo $SHELL

The $PATH variable is important because it controls where Linux looks when you type a command.

docs.title: Shell Workflow
docs.text:
The shell is the command-line interface used to interact with Linux.

Common shells include:

Shell Description sh Basic Unix shell bash Common default Linux shell zsh Advanced interactive shell fish User-friendly shell with modern features

A typical Linux workflow involves:

  • Navigating directories
  • Inspecting files
  • Checking permissions
  • Running commands
  • Redirecting output
  • Searching with grep
  • Managing processes and services
  • Reading logs

Example workflow:

whoami
id
pwd
ls -la
cd /var/log
sudo tail -f auth.log

docs.title: Input, Output, and Redirection
docs.text:
Linux commands use three standard data streams:

Stream Number Purpose STDIN 0 Input STDOUT 1 Normal output STDERR 2 Error output

Redirection allows you to control where output goes.

Operator Purpose > Redirect output and overwrite file >> Redirect output and append to file 2> Redirect errors 2>/dev/null Hide errors | Pipe output into another command

Examples:

ls -la > files.txt
echo "new line" >> notes.txt
find / -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null
cat auth.log | grep "Failed password"

docs.title: Package Management
docs.text:
Linux distributions use package managers to install, update, and remove software.

Debian and Ubuntu use apt.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx
sudo apt remove nginx

Red Hat-based systems use dnf or yum.

sudo dnf install nginx
sudo yum install nginx

Package managers are important because they handle dependencies and install software from trusted repositories.

docs.title: Mounting and Devices
docs.text:
Linux treats devices as files, usually located under /dev.

Examples:

Device Description /dev/sda First disk /dev/sda1 First partition on first disk /dev/null Discards output /dev/random Random data source

Mounting attaches a filesystem to the Linux directory tree.

sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb

Unmount before removing devices:

sudo umount /mnt/usb

docs.title: Security Perspective
docs.text:
For security work, Linux structure and workflow help with both defense and offense.

Important security checks include:

id
sudo -l
find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null
cat /etc/passwd
ls -la ~/.ssh
cat ~/.bash_history
ps aux
ss -tulpen

These commands help identify:

  • Current privileges
  • Sudo permissions
  • SUID binaries
  • Local users
  • SSH keys
  • Command history
  • Running processes
  • Listening ports

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text: Mistake Why It Matters Running everything as root Increases damage if a command is wrong or compromised Using chmod 777 Gives everyone full control Ignoring logs Misses signs of errors or compromise Leaving secrets in history Exposes passwords and tokens Misconfiguring services Can expose sensitive ports or files Not checking permissions Can create privilege escalation paths

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command Show current user whoami Show user and groups id Show current directory pwd List files ls -la View file cat file.txt Read large file less file.txt Search text grep -i "text" file.txt Find files find / -name file.txt 2>/dev/null Show processes ps aux Show listening ports ss -tulpen Check service systemctl status ssh View logs journalctl -xe Update packages sudo apt update Install package sudo apt install <package>

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Linux uses a single filesystem tree starting at /.

Most system configuration lives in /etc, logs live in /var/log, and user data lives in /home.

Permissions are central to Linux security.

The shell is the main workflow tool for administration, automation, troubleshooting, and security testing.

Understanding Linux structure makes later topics like privilege escalation, service management, log analysis, and scripting much easier.

docs.title: Linux System Management
docs.text:
Linux system management covers the daily administrative tasks needed to operate, secure, and maintain a Linux host. This includes managing users and privileges, controlling services and processes, scheduling automated jobs, configuring network-facing services, maintaining backups, managing storage, reviewing logs, and applying hardening controls.

For security work, these skills matter because the same mechanisms administrators use to maintain systems are often abused by attackers for privilege escalation, persistence, lateral movement, and data access.

docs.title: User Management and Privileges
docs.text:
Linux separates normal users from the administrative user known as root. Standard users are restricted from modifying sensitive system files and services, while root can change nearly anything on the system.

This separation is one of Linux’s core security controls.

docs.title: Root and Standard Users
docs.text:
A standard user can usually:

  • Work inside their own home directory.
  • Run normal applications.
  • Read files they have permission to access.
  • Execute commands available to them.

A root user can:

  • Modify system configuration files.
  • Install or remove software.
  • Create, delete, and modify users.
  • Read sensitive files such as /etc/shadow.
  • Start, stop, enable, or disable system services.

docs.title: sudo
docs.text:
The sudo command allows a permitted user to run a command with elevated privileges, usually as root.

sudo cat /etc/shadow

Without sudo, a standard user trying to read /etc/shadow will normally receive a permission denied error.

cat /etc/shadow

The benefit of sudo is that users can perform administrative actions without logging in as root directly. This is safer, more auditable, and easier to control.

docs.title: su
docs.text:
The su command switches the current shell session to another user.

su -

Using su - attempts to switch to the root account and load root’s environment. Unlike sudo, this requires the target user’s password, usually the root password.

docs.title: Essential User and Group Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose sudo Run a command as another user, usually root. su Switch to another user account. useradd Create a new user. userdel Delete a user. usermod Modify an existing user. passwd Change a user’s password. addgroup Create a new group. delgroup Delete a group.

docs.title: Common Examples
docs.text:
Create a new user:

sudo useradd alex

Set or change a password:

sudo passwd alex

Modify a user and add them to a group:

sudo usermod -aG sudo alex

Delete a user:

sudo userdel alex

Delete a user and their home directory:

sudo userdel -r alex

docs.title: Security Notes
docs.text:
User and group management is important for both administration and security monitoring. Unexpected user creation, privilege changes, or password changes can indicate persistence or account compromise.

Important files to know:

File Purpose /etc/passwd Stores user account information. /etc/shadow Stores password hashes. Requires root privileges. /etc/group Stores group membership information. /etc/sudoers Controls who can use sudo.

docs.title: Service and Process Management
docs.text:
Linux services, also called daemons, are background processes that provide system functionality. Examples include SSH, web servers, databases, logging services, and scheduled task managers.

Modern Linux distributions usually manage services with systemd using the systemctl command.

docs.title: Managing Services with systemctl
docs.text:
The systemctl command controls systemd services.

Action Command Description Start service systemctl start <service> Starts a service immediately. Stop service systemctl stop <service> Stops a running service. Restart service systemctl restart <service> Stops and starts a service again. Enable service systemctl enable <service> Starts the service automatically at boot. Disable service systemctl disable <service> Prevents the service from starting at boot. Check status systemctl status <service> Shows service state, PID, and recent logs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Start SSH:

sudo systemctl start ssh

Enable SSH at boot:

sudo systemctl enable ssh

Check SSH status:

systemctl status ssh

Stop Apache:

sudo systemctl stop apache2

Restart Apache:

sudo systemctl restart apache2

docs.title: Troubleshooting Services with journalctl
docs.text:
Systemd logs service activity through the journal. The journalctl command allows administrators to inspect these logs.

View logs for a specific service:

journalctl -u ssh.service --no-pager

Follow logs live:

journalctl -u ssh.service -f

Show recent logs:

journalctl -u apache2.service -n 50

This is useful when a service fails to start or behaves unexpectedly.

docs.title: Process Management
docs.text:
Every running program on Linux is a process. Each process has a unique PID, or Process ID.

Useful commands include:

Command Purpose ps aux Show running processes. top Interactive real-time process viewer. htop Improved interactive process viewer, if installed. pgrep Find process IDs by name. kill Send a signal to a process. jobs Show background jobs in the current shell. fg Bring a background job to the foreground. bg Resume a suspended job in the background.

docs.title: Process States
docs.text: State Meaning Running The process is executing or ready to execute. Waiting The process is waiting for a resource, such as disk or network I/O. Stopped The process has been suspended. Zombie The process has finished but has not been cleaned up by its parent.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
Processes are controlled using signals.

Signal ID Shortcut / Command Purpose SIGINT 2 Ctrl+C Interrupts a process. SIGKILL 9 kill -9 <PID> Forcefully kills a process. SIGTERM 15 kill <PID> Gracefully asks a process to terminate. SIGTSTP 20 Ctrl+Z Suspends a process.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Find a process:

ps aux | grep apache

Find a PID by process name:

pgrep ssh

Gracefully stop a process:

kill <PID>

Force kill a process:

kill -9 <PID>

docs.title: Foreground and Background Jobs
docs.text:
A command normally runs in the foreground, meaning it occupies the terminal until it finishes.

Run a command in the background by adding &:

ping 8.8.8.8 &

List background jobs:

jobs

Suspend a running foreground process:

Ctrl+Z

Resume it in the background:

bg

Bring it back to the foreground:

fg

docs.title: Command Chaining
docs.text:
Linux shells allow commands to be chained together.

Operator Meaning Example ; Run the next command regardless of success or failure. echo A; ls fakefile; echo B && Run the next command only if the previous command succeeds. mkdir test && cd test || Run the next command only if the previous command fails. ls fakefile || echo "File missing" | Pipe output from one command into another. ps aux | grep ssh

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Run commands unconditionally:

echo "Starting"; whoami; hostname

Run the second command only if the first succeeds:

mkdir reports && cd reports

Run fallback logic if a command fails:

cat missing.txt || echo "File does not exist"

Pipe output into another command:

ps aux | grep apache

docs.title: Task Scheduling: Cron and Systemd Timers
docs.text:
Task scheduling allows administrators to automate repeated work such as backups, updates, log rotation, and maintenance scripts.

From a security perspective, scheduled tasks are also important because attackers commonly abuse them for persistence.

Linux commonly uses two scheduling systems:

Scheduler Description Cron Traditional time-based scheduler. Systemd Timers Modern systemd-based scheduler with better logging and event-based triggers.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Cron uses text files called crontabs to define scheduled jobs.

Edit the current user’s crontab:

crontab -e

List the current user’s crontab:

crontab -l

docs.title: Crontab Format
docs.text:
A cron job uses five time fields followed by the command.

* * * * * command
│ │ │ │ │
│ │ │ │ └── day of week, 0-7
│ │ │ └──── month, 1-12
│ │ └────── day of month, 1-31
│ └──────── hour, 0-23
└────────── minute, 0-59

docs.title: Common Cron Examples
docs.text: Schedule Syntax Every minute * * * * * /path/script.sh Every 6 hours 0 */6 * * * /path/script.sh Every day at midnight 0 0 * * * /path/script.sh Every Sunday at midnight 0 0 * * 0 /path/script.sh First day of every month 0 0 1 * * /path/script.sh At reboot @reboot /path/script.sh

docs.title: Security Notes for Cron
docs.text:
Cron is a common persistence location. Review these locations during investigations:

/etc/crontab
/etc/cron.d/
/etc/cron.daily/
/etc/cron.hourly/
/etc/cron.weekly/
/var/spool/cron/

Suspicious cron jobs often:

  • Run from /tmp, /dev/shm, or hidden directories.
  • Use curl, wget, bash, or python to download payloads.
  • Use @reboot for persistence.
  • Run as root unexpectedly.

docs.title: Systemd Timers
docs.text:
Systemd timers are a modern alternative to cron. They use two files:

File Purpose .service Defines what command or script runs. .timer Defines when it runs.

docs.title: Example Timer Unit
docs.text:
Location:

/etc/systemd/system/mytimer.timer

Example:

[Unit]
Description=Runs my script every hour

[Timer]
OnBootSec=3min
OnUnitActiveSec=1hour

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

docs.title: Example Service Unit
docs.text:
Location:

/etc/systemd/system/mytimer.service

Example:

[Unit]
Description=My scheduled task

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Activating a Timer
docs.text:
Reload systemd after creating or modifying unit files:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload

Start the timer:

sudo systemctl start mytimer.timer

Enable it at boot:

sudo systemctl enable mytimer.timer

List active timers:

systemctl list-timers

docs.title: Cron vs Systemd Timers
docs.text: Feature Cron Systemd Timers Simplicity Very simple More complex Granularity Minute-based Seconds and event-based Logging Limited Integrated with journalctl Configuration Single crontab line Requires .timer and .service Security controls Basic Can use systemd sandboxing options

docs.title: Network Services
docs.text:
Network services expose functionality over the network. They are essential for administration and application hosting, but they also increase attack surface.

Common Linux network services include:

Service Purpose SSH Encrypted remote command-line access. NFS Network file sharing. Apache / Nginx Web hosting. VPN Encrypted remote network access.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
SSH is the standard protocol for secure remote administration.

Install OpenSSH server:

sudo apt install openssh-server -y

Check service status:

systemctl status ssh

Connect to a server:

ssh user@192.168.1.10

Connect using a private key:

ssh -i id_rsa user@192.168.1.10

docs.title: SSH Configuration
docs.text:
The SSH server configuration file is:

/etc/ssh/sshd_config

Common hardening settings include:

PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes

After editing the SSH configuration, restart SSH:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
NFS, or Network File System, allows a remote directory to be mounted locally.

The NFS server defines shared directories in:

/etc/exports

Example export:

/var/backups 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync)

docs.title: Common NFS Options
docs.text:
Option Meaning Security Relevance rw Read/write access. Dangerous if broadly allowed. ro Read-only access. Safer for shared data. sync Writes are committed before replies. Safer for data integrity. no_root_squash Remote root remains root on the share. Very dangerous if misconfigured.

Mount an NFS share:

mkdir local_mount
sudo mount 192.168.1.10:/shared local_mount

docs.title: Security Note
docs.text: The no_root_squash option is especially dangerous. If an attacker can mount the share as root, they may be able to create files with root ownership or abuse SUID permissions.

docs.title: Web Services
docs.text: Apache and Nginx are common Linux web servers. For quick testing and file transfer, Python can also run a simple temporary web server.

docs.title: Apache
docs.text:
Install Apache:

sudo apt install apache2 -y

Start Apache:

sudo systemctl start apache2

Enable Apache at boot:

sudo systemctl enable apache2

Default web root:

/var/www/html

Default main configuration paths include:

/etc/apache2/apache2.conf
/etc/apache2/sites-available/

docs.title: Python HTTP Server
docs.text:
Serve the current directory on port 8000:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Serve on port 80:

sudo python3 -m http.server 80

This is useful for quickly transferring files in labs and assessments.

docs.title: Command-Line Web Clients
docs.text: Linux systems commonly use curl and wget to interact with web services.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
curl transfers data to or from a server and prints output to the terminal by default.

Fetch a page:

curl http://example.com

View headers only:

curl -I http://example.com

Download a file:

curl -O http://example.com/file.txt

docs.title: wget
docs.text:
wget is designed for file downloads.

Download a file:

wget http://example.com/file.txt

Download recursively:

wget -r http://example.com

docs.title: curl vs wget
docs.text: Tool Best For curl Inspecting responses, headers, APIs, and raw output. wget Downloading files and mirroring content.

docs.title: Backup and Restore
docs.text:
Backups protect against accidental deletion, disk failure, ransomware, and destructive attacker activity.

Linux commonly uses tools such as:

Tool Description rsync Efficient file synchronization. duplicity Encrypted backup tool. Deja Dup User-friendly graphical backup tool based on duplicity.

docs.title: Rsync
docs.text:
Rsync is a powerful tool for copying and synchronizing files. It only transfers differences between source and destination, making repeated backups efficient.

Install rsync:

sudo apt install rsync -y

Basic backup:

rsync -av /source/directory/ /backup/directory/

Remote backup over SSH:

rsync -avz -e ssh /source/directory/ user@backup-server:/backup/directory/

Useful options:

Option Purpose -a Archive mode. Preserves permissions, timestamps, and symlinks. -v Verbose output. -z Compress data during transfer. --delete Delete files from destination if they no longer exist in source. --backup Keep backup copies of overwritten or deleted files. --backup-dir Store changed/deleted files in a separate backup directory.

Example with deleted files preserved:

rsync -avz --backup --backup-dir=/backup/old --delete /source/ user@backup-server:/backup/current/

docs.title: Automating Backups
docs.text: Backups should be automated to avoid relying on manual execution.

docs.title: SSH Key Setup
docs.text:
Generate a key pair:

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 2048

Copy the public key to the backup server:

ssh-copy-id user@backup-server

docs.title: Backup Script
docs.text:
Example script:

#!/bin/bash
rsync -avz -e ssh /home/user/documents/ user@backup-server:/backups/documents/

Make it executable:

chmod +x backup.sh

Schedule it with cron:

crontab -e

Example cron entry to run every hour:

0 * * * * /path/to/backup.sh

docs.title: File System Management
docs.text: Linux stores all files under a single directory tree beginning at /. Storage devices are attached to this tree through mounting.

docs.title: File Systems
docs.text:
Common Linux file systems include:

File System Description Common Use ext4 Stable, journaling file system. Default for many Linux systems. ext2 Older file system without journaling. Flash drives or simple use cases. XFS High performance with large files. Enterprise storage and databases. Btrfs Supports snapshots and advanced features. Systems needing snapshots or integrity features. NTFS Windows file system. Shared drives or dual-boot environments.

docs.title: Inodes
docs.text:
An inode stores metadata about a file, including:

  • Owner.
  • Permissions.
  • Timestamps.
  • File size.
  • Pointers to data blocks.

The filename itself is stored in the directory entry, not inside the inode.

A system can run out of inodes even if disk space remains, especially when millions of tiny files are created.

Check inode usage:

df -i

docs.title: Disk and Partition Management
docs.text:
List disks and partitions:

sudo fdisk -l

List block devices:

lsblk

Show disk usage:

df -h

Show directory size:

du -sh /var/log

docs.title: Mounting and Unmounting
docs.text:
Create a mount point:

sudo mkdir /mnt/usb

Mount a device:

sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb

Unmount the device:

sudo umount /mnt/usb

If unmounting fails because the target is busy, find processes using the mount:

lsof | grep /mnt/usb

docs.title: Persistent Mounts with /etc/fstab
docs.text:
To make mounts persist after reboot, configure:

/etc/fstab

Example:

UUID=3d6a020d-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 /data ext4 defaults 0 2

Typical fields are:

Field Meaning Device UUID or device path. Mount point Where the device is mounted. File system type Example: ext4, xfs, ntfs. Options Example: defaults, noauto, ro. Dump Backup utility field, usually 0. Pass File system check order.

docs.title: Swap Space
docs.text:
Swap is disk space used as overflow memory when RAM is full.

Create swap on a partition:

sudo mkswap /dev/vda2

Enable swap:

sudo swapon /dev/vda2

View swap usage:

swapon --show

Swap is slower than RAM, but it can prevent crashes when memory is exhausted.

docs.title: Containerization
docs.text:
Containerization packages an application and its dependencies into an isolated runtime environment.

Unlike a virtual machine, a container does not run a full separate operating system. It shares the host kernel while isolating user space.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Docker is the most widely used container platform.

Core concepts:

Concept Meaning Image Read-only template used to create containers. Container Running instance of an image. Dockerfile Text file containing image build instructions. Registry Repository where images are stored, such as Docker Hub.

docs.title: Example Dockerfile
docs.text:
FROM ubuntu:22.04

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y apache2 openssh-server

RUN useradd -m docker-user && echo "docker-user:password" | chpasswd

EXPOSE 80 22

CMD service ssh start && apache2ctl -D FOREGROUND

Build the image:

docker build -t my_web_server .

Run the container:

docker run -p 8080:80 -d my_web_server

docs.title: Docker Management Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose docker ps List running containers. docker ps -a List all containers. docker stop <id> Stop a container. docker rm <id> Remove a stopped container. docker rmi <image> Remove an image. docker logs <id> View container logs.

docs.title: Docker Security Notes
docs.text:
Containers provide isolation, not full virtualization. Security risks include:

  • Shared kernel exposure.
  • Containers running as root.
  • Misconfigured privileged containers.
  • Exposed Docker APIs.
  • Sensitive host directories mounted into containers.

Avoid running containers with:

--privileged

unless absolutely necessary.

docs.title: LXC
docs.text:
LXC, or Linux Containers, is more system-oriented than Docker. It behaves more like a lightweight virtual machine and can run a full init system with multiple services.

Feature Docker LXC Focus Application containers System containers Common use Microservices and app deployment Lightweight Linux environments State Often ephemeral Often persistent Management style Run one main process Manage like a small server

Resource limits can be enforced with cgroups to prevent containers from exhausting the host.

docs.title: Network Configuration and Hardening
docs.text:
Linux networking can be managed with both legacy and modern tools.

Action Legacy Tool Modern Tool View interfaces ifconfig ip addr Bring interface up ifconfig eth0 up ip link set eth0 up Assign IP ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.2 ip addr add 192.168.1.2/24 dev eth0 View routes route ip route Add default gateway route add default gw <ip> ip route add default via <ip>

docs.title: Common Network Commands
docs.text:
View IP addresses:

ip addr

View routes:

ip route

Test reachability:

ping 8.8.8.8

View listening sockets:

ss -tuln

Trace network path:

traceroute 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Linux Access Control Models
docs.text:
Linux security can be described through different access control models.

Model Meaning DAC Discretionary Access Control. File owners control permissions. MAC Mandatory Access Control. System policy restricts access. RBAC Role-Based Access Control. Permissions are based on roles.

Standard Linux permissions are mostly DAC. SELinux and AppArmor provide MAC.

docs.title: SELinux and AppArmor
docs.text: Mandatory Access Control systems restrict what applications can access, even if standard permissions would allow it.

docs.title: SELinux
docs.text:
SELinux uses labels and policies to define which processes can access which files, ports, and resources.

It is powerful and granular, but can be complex to configure.

docs.title: AppArmor
docs.text:
AppArmor uses application profiles based on paths. It is common on Ubuntu and Debian-based systems and is generally easier to understand than SELinux.

These systems are useful because if a service like Apache is compromised, MAC can prevent it from reading sensitive files or launching unexpected programs.

docs.title: Linux Firewalls
docs.text:
Linux firewalls control network traffic entering, leaving, or passing through the host.

Common firewall tools include:

Tool Description iptables Traditional interface to the Netfilter firewall framework. nftables Modern replacement for iptables. UFW Simpler frontend commonly used on Ubuntu. firewalld Common on RHEL, CentOS, and Fedora.

docs.title: Iptables Basics
docs.text: Iptables uses tables, chains, rules, matches, and targets.

docs.title: Main Tables
docs.text: Table Purpose filter Basic allow and deny rules. nat Network Address Translation. mangle Packet modification. raw Connection tracking exemptions.

docs.title: Common Chains
docs.text: Chain Purpose INPUT Packets destined for the local system. OUTPUT Packets generated by the local system. FORWARD Packets routed through the system. PREROUTING Packets before routing decisions. POSTROUTING Packets after routing decisions.

docs.title: Common Targets
docs.text:
Target Meaning ACCEPT Allow the packet. DROP Silently discard the packet. REJECT Block and notify the sender. LOG Log the packet details.

Allow incoming SSH:

sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

Set default INPUT policy to DROP:

sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP

List rules with line numbers:

sudo iptables -L --line-numbers

docs.title: UFW Basics
docs.text:
UFW is easier to use than raw iptables.

Enable UFW:

sudo ufw enable

Allow SSH:

sudo ufw allow ssh

Allow HTTP:

sudo ufw allow 80/tcp

Check status:

sudo ufw status verbose

docs.title: Linux System Logs
docs.text:
Linux logs are usually stored in:

/var/log/

They are essential for troubleshooting and incident response.

Log Purpose /var/log/syslog General system messages on Debian/Ubuntu. /var/log/auth.log Authentication and sudo events on Debian/Ubuntu. /var/log/kern.log Kernel messages. /var/log/ufw.log UFW firewall events. /var/log/apache2/access.log Apache access logs. /var/log/nginx/access.log Nginx access logs.

docs.title: Authentication Log Example
docs.text:
Feb 28 15:04:22 server sshd[3010]: Failed password for htb-student from 10.14.15.2 port 50223 ssh2
Feb 28 15:07:19 server sshd[3010]: Accepted password for htb-student from 10.14.15.2 port 50223 ssh2

A high number of failed login attempts followed by a successful login may indicate brute force activity.

docs.title: Useful Log Commands
docs.text:
View recent log entries:

tail /var/log/syslog

Follow a log live:

tail -f /var/log/auth.log

Search authentication failures:

grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log

Search successful SSH logins:

grep "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log

Search compressed rotated logs:

zgrep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log.*.gz

docs.title: Log Management Best Practices
docs.text:
Logs should be protected and maintained.

Important practices include:

  • Enable log rotation.
  • Send logs to a remote log server.
  • Monitor authentication logs.
  • Monitor service failures.
  • Review firewall logs.
  • Protect logs from unauthorized modification.

The logrotate utility prevents logs from consuming excessive disk space by rotating and compressing old logs.

Remote logging is important because attackers often try to delete local logs after compromise.

docs.title: Linux Security and Hardening
docs.text: Linux hardening reduces the attack surface and limits damage if compromise occurs.

docs.title: Core Hardening Practices
docs.text:
Practice Purpose Keep systems updated Patches known vulnerabilities. Disable unused services Reduces attack surface. Enforce least privilege Limits unnecessary access. Disable SSH root login Prevents direct root access. Use SSH keys Reduces password brute-force risk. Use firewalls Restricts network exposure. Enable MAC systems Limits service behavior after compromise. Audit SUID/SGID files Finds dangerous privilege escalation paths. Centralize logs Protects evidence from local tampering.

Update the system:

sudo apt update && sudo apt dist-upgrade

Find SUID files:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Find SGID files:

find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null

docs.title: Security Auditing Tools
docs.text:
Useful Linux auditing and security tools include:

Tool Purpose Lynis System hardening audit. chkrootkit Rootkit checks. rkhunter Rootkit and suspicious file checks. auditd Kernel-level auditing. fail2ban Blocks repeated failed login attempts.

Install fail2ban:

sudo apt install fail2ban -y

Check fail2ban status:

sudo systemctl status fail2ban

docs.title: Remote Desktop Protocols on Linux
docs.text:
Although SSH is the standard for command-line access, Linux can also support graphical remote access.

Common protocols include:

Protocol Port Purpose X11 TCP 6000+ Remote graphical application display. VNC TCP 5900+ Full graphical desktop sharing. XDMCP UDP 177 Legacy graphical login protocol. RDP TCP 3389 Remote desktop protocol, available on Linux through xrdp.

docs.title: X11 Forwarding
docs.text:
X11 can run a graphical application on a remote machine and display it locally through SSH.

ssh -X user@192.168.1.10

Then run a graphical application:

firefox

Native X11 is insecure if exposed directly. It should be tunneled through SSH.

docs.title: VNC
docs.text:
VNC provides full graphical desktop access. It is often used for remote support or GUI-based administration.

Because many VNC setups are weakly encrypted or password-only, VNC should be tunneled through SSH or restricted by firewall rules.

docs.title: XDMCP
docs.text: XDMCP is a legacy protocol and should generally be avoided. It sends sensitive session data in cleartext and is vulnerable to interception.

docs.title: Terminal Shortcuts and Productivity
docs.text: Terminal shortcuts make command-line work much faster.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Shortcut Action Tab Auto-complete commands, paths, and filenames. Ctrl+A Jump to the beginning of the line. Ctrl+E Jump to the end of the line. Alt+B Move backward one word. Alt+F Move forward one word.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl+U Cut from cursor to start of line. Ctrl+K Cut from cursor to end of line. Ctrl+W Delete the word before the cursor. Ctrl+Y Paste the last cut text.

docs.title: Process Control
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl+C Stop the current process. Ctrl+Z Suspend the current process. Ctrl+D Send EOF or close the shell. Ctrl+L Clear the terminal screen.

docs.title: History
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl+R Reverse-search command history. Up / Down Move through previous commands.

docs.title: Users and Privileges
docs.text:
whoami
id
sudo <command>
su -
sudo useradd <user>
sudo passwd <user>
sudo usermod -aG sudo <user>

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
systemctl status <service>
sudo systemctl start <service>
sudo systemctl stop <service>
sudo systemctl enable <service>
sudo systemctl disable <service>
journalctl -u <service>

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
ps aux
top
pgrep <name>
kill <pid>
kill -9 <pid>
jobs
fg
bg

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
ip addr
ip route
ss -tuln
ping <host>
traceroute <host>

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
tail -f /var/log/auth.log
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log
journalctl -xe

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
lsblk
df -h
df -i
du -sh <path>
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb
sudo umount /mnt/usb

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt dist-upgrade
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
sudo ufw status verbose
sudo iptables -L --line-numbers

docs.title: Windows Command Line
docs.text:
The Windows Command Prompt, or CMD, is a core interface for navigating the file system, managing files, gathering host information, and performing basic system administration.

For security work, CMD is also useful for host reconnaissance, triage, and understanding what an attacker may do using built-in Windows tools.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
CMD can help answer common questions during administration, troubleshooting, or authorized security testing:

  • Where am I in the file system?
  • What files and directories exist?
  • What user am I running as?
  • What system am I on?
  • What network configuration is present?
  • What users, groups, shares, and resources exist?
  • Where are sensitive files or configuration artifacts located?
  • How can command output be filtered, redirected, or saved?

docs.title: Warning
docs.text:
Run enumeration commands only on systems you own, administer, or have explicit permission to assess.

Many commands in this page, such as systeminfo, net user, net share, and recursive file searches, may be monitored by defenders because they are commonly used during reconnaissance.

docs.title: Command Prompt Navigation
docs.text: Navigating a Windows system through CMD requires understanding drives, paths, directories, and common navigation commands.

docs.title: Listing Directory Contents
docs.text:
The dir command lists files and subdirectories in the current location.

dir

Common output fields include:

Field Meaning <DIR> The entry is a directory Size File size in bytes Timestamp Last modified date and time

Useful options:

:: Show hidden files
dir /ah

:: Recursively list files and directories
dir /s

:: Show all files, including hidden and system files
dir /a

docs.title: Current Working Directory
docs.text:
The current working directory is the folder your shell is currently operating from.

cd

Running cd by itself prints the current directory.

docs.title: Absolute and Relative Paths
docs.text:
Path Type Description Example Absolute path Starts from the drive root and includes the full path C:\Windows\System32 Relative path Starts from the current location .\Pictures

Examples:

:: Move to an absolute path
cd C:\Windows\System32

:: Move to a relative path
cd .\Pictures

docs.title: Navigation Shortcuts
docs.text:
:: Move up one directory
cd ..

:: Move to the root of the current drive
cd \

:: Move up multiple levels
cd ..\..

:: Change to another drive
D:

docs.title: Visualizing Directory Structure
docs.text:
The tree command displays a visual directory hierarchy.

:: Show folders only
tree

:: Show folders and files
tree /f

Large directory trees can generate a lot of output. Use Ctrl+C to stop the command if needed.

docs.title: File and Directory Management
docs.text: CMD provides built-in commands for creating, deleting, moving, copying, renaming, and viewing files.

docs.title: Creating Directories
docs.text:
mkdir reports
md logs

mkdir and md perform the same function.

docs.title: Removing Directories
docs.text:
:: Remove an empty directory
rmdir reports

:: Remove a directory and all contents
rmdir /s reports

:: Remove without confirmation prompts
rmdir /s /q reports
